# Spinors and the Dirac operator {#sec-spinors-dirac-operator}

A rotation by $2\pi$ is the identity on vectors, but there are objects in geometry and physics that change sign under
it and return to themselves only after a rotation by $4\pi$. These objects are **spinors**: they carry representations
not of the rotation group $SO(n)$ or the Lorentz group $SO(1, d - 1)$ but of their double covers, the spin groups, and
they are built from the **Clifford algebra**, the algebra generated by vectors whose squares are their lengths. On a
curved manifold spinors are sections of a bundle that exists only when a topological condition holds, and the natural
first-order operator acting on them is the **Dirac operator**, a square root of the Laplacian corrected by the
curvature. Its spectrum is a fine geometric invariant, and the number of its zero modes is a topological one, counted
by the index theorem of Atiyah and Singer. This chapter develops all of this on explicit spaces and computes every
spectrum it states.

Clifford algebras constructs the algebras and their matrix representations in every dimension and signature: the
gamma matrices, the chirality matrix and the charge-conjugation matrices, and the classification of reality
conditions with its period eight. Spin groups and spinor representations realises the spin groups inside the Clifford
algebra and describes Dirac, Weyl, Majorana and Majorana-Weyl spinors, in ten and eleven dimensions in particular, and
how a spinor of $d$ dimensions decomposes under $SO(1, 3) \times SO(n)$. Spin structures and the spin connection puts
spinors on manifolds: the obstruction to a spin structure, the spin structures of circles and tori, the spin
connection computed on the sphere, and the spin-c structures that rescue the complex projective plane. The Dirac
operator on flat spaces and spheres defines the operator, proves the Lichnerowicz formula and its vanishing theorem,
and derives the spectrum on tori for every spin structure and twist and on the spheres $S^2$, $S^3$ and $S^n$. Dirac
operators on compact spaces treats group manifolds, coset spaces with Frobenius reciprocity and Parthasarathy's
formula, Kähler and Calabi-Yau manifolds, and orbifolds. Twisted Dirac operators and index theorems couples the
operator to gauge fields, computes the index on the sphere with a monopole by hand, and states the index theorem with
the $\hat A$ genus. The chirality problem shows why zero modes of one chirality do not appear without gauge fields and
how gauge backgrounds produce them.

The main sources are the textbook of @zhelnorovich2019spinors (Chapters 1-4 and 6) for the algebra and the spinor
connection, the lecture notes of @vanproeyen1999 for spinors in arbitrary dimension, @trautman1995 for spin structures
and the spectrum on spheres, @camporesi1995 for the spectrum on spheres from representation theory, @dolan2003 for
coset spaces with gauge fields, @bilal2008 for the index theorem, and @aspinwall1996 for $K3$ surfaces. Every statement
is followed by at least three examples of increasing complexity and at least three exercises of increasing difficulty
with hidden solutions; the Pauli matrices, the round sphere $S^2$, the group $SU(2) = S^3$ and the monopole on $S^2$
are the running examples.

## Clifford algebras {#sec-clifford-algebras}

The Clifford algebra of a vector space with a metric is the algebra in which a vector squares to its length. Its
matrix representations are the gamma matrices, and everything about spinors (their dimension, their chirality, their
reality) is a statement about these matrices. This part defines the algebra, builds the gamma matrices in every
dimension and signature by tensor products of Pauli matrices, and classifies the charge-conjugation matrices and the
reality conditions, following @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Ch. 1] for the algebra and @vanproeyen1999 [Sec. 3] for the
classification. Signatures are written $(p, q)$, with $p$ basis vectors of square $+1$ and $q$ of square $-1$, so that
spacetime in the book's conventions has signature $(1, 3)$ (@sec-conventions-indices).

For more on this topic, see @derezinski2022mathematics [Ch. 15].

### The Clifford algebra

The quaternions, the Pauli matrices and the Dirac matrices are all algebras generated by elements that anticommute and
square to $\pm1$. The definition below captures this pattern for any metric, and the figure shows the multiplication
table of the sixteen basis elements in the case of spacetime.

![The multiplication table of the basis $\gamma_A$ of the Clifford algebra $Cl(1, 3)$, realised by the Weyl matrices
of the book ($\gamma^{01} = \gamma^0\gamma^1$, and so on). Every product $\gamma_A\gamma_B$ is $\pm\gamma_C$ for a
single basis element $\gamma_C$; the colour shows the sign. The rows of the vectors $\gamma^1, \gamma^2, \gamma^3$
start with dark entries in the columns of $\gamma^k$ because $(\gamma^k)^2 = -1$. Generated by
`figures/sd-clifford-table.sage`.](figures/sd-clifford-table.svg){#fig-sd-clifford-table width=62%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-clifford-algebra}
#### Clifford algebra

Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $d$ with a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form $\eta$ of signature $(p,
q)$ (@def-signature). The **Clifford algebra** $Cl(V, \eta) = Cl(p, q)$ is the associative real algebra with unit
generated by $V$ subject to the relations
$$
v w + w v = 2\eta(v, w)\,1 \qquad (v, w \in V),
$$ {#eq-spd-clifford-relation}
so that $v^2 = \eta(v, v)$. In an orthonormal basis $e_1, \dots, e_d$ with $\eta(e_a, e_a) = +1$ for $a \leq p$ and
$-1$ for $a > p$ the relations read $e_ae_b + e_be_a = 2\eta_{ab}$. The **complex Clifford algebra**
$Cl_{\mathbb{C}}(d) = Cl(p, q) \otimes \mathbb{C}$ depends only on $d$, since $ie_a$ squares to $-\eta_{aa}$
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.6.2, eq. (1.120)].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest Clifford algebras are familiar number systems. The first example takes a single generator and finds the
complex numbers or a pair of real lines, depending on the sign of its square.

::: {#exm-spd-cl-one-generator}
#### One generator

$Cl(0, 1)$ is spanned by $1$ and $e$ with $e^2 = -1$: it is $\mathbb{C}$, with $e = i$. $Cl(1, 0)$ is spanned by $1$
and $e$ with $e^2 = +1$; the elements $\pi_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm e)$ satisfy $\pi_\pm^2 = \pi_\pm$, $\pi_+\pi_- = 0$
and $\pi_+ + \pi_- = 1$, so $Cl(1, 0) \cong \mathbb{R} \oplus \mathbb{R}$, with $e = \pi_+ - \pi_-$. The two algebras
differ although both are two-dimensional: the sign of the metric matters for the real algebra.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

With two anticommuting generators the product $e_1e_2$ is a third element that anticommutes with both. The second
example finds Hamilton's quaternions in this way.

::: {#exm-spd-quaternions}
#### The quaternions

In $Cl(0, 2)$, $e_1^2 = e_2^2 = -1$ and $e_1e_2 = -e_2e_1$, so $(e_1e_2)^2 = -e_1e_2e_2e_1 = -1$. Setting $\mathrm{i} =
e_1$, $\mathrm{j} = e_2$, $\mathrm{k} = e_1e_2$ gives $\mathrm{i}^2 = \mathrm{j}^2 = \mathrm{k}^2 = \mathrm{ijk} = -1$:
$Cl(0, 2) \cong \mathbb{H}$, four-dimensional with basis $1, e_1, e_2, e_1e_2$. In $Cl(2, 0)$ instead $(e_1e_2)^2 = -1$
but $e_1^2 = e_2^2 = +1$, and $e_1 \mapsto \sigma_1$, $e_2 \mapsto \sigma_3$ identifies it with the real $2 \times 2$
matrices $M_2(\mathbb{R})$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In three Euclidean dimensions the Pauli matrices satisfy the relations @eq-spd-clifford-relation, as the Part II
example @exm-gamma-euclidean notes. The third example identifies the whole algebra and its centre.

::: {#exm-spd-pauli-algebra}
#### The Pauli algebra

$e_a \mapsto \sigma_a$ (@eq-pauli) represents $Cl(3, 0)$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$. The eight products $1, \sigma_a,
\sigma_a\sigma_b\,(a < b), \sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3$ span $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ over $\mathbb{R}$, since $\sigma_1\sigma_2
= i\sigma_3$ and its cyclic permutations, and $\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3 = i\,1$. So $Cl(3, 0) \cong M_2(\mathbb{C})$ as
a real algebra of dimension $8 = 2^3$; the **volume element** $e_1e_2e_3$ squares to $-1$ and commutes with everything,
playing the role of $i$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Spacetime is the case the book uses most. The fourth example places the Dirac matrices of Part II inside the Clifford
algebra of signature $(1, 3)$ and notes that the real structure of the algebra depends on the overall sign of the
metric.

::: {#exm-spd-minkowski-cl}
#### The spacetime algebra

The Weyl matrices $\gamma^\mu$ of @exm-gamma-weyl satisfy $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu + \gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu =
2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ with $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, so $e_\mu \mapsto \gamma^\mu$ is a representation of
$Cl(1, 3)$ on $\mathbb{C}^4$, and @fig-sd-clifford-table is its multiplication table. As real algebras $Cl(1, 3) \cong
M_2(\mathbb{H})$ while $Cl(3, 1) \cong M_4(\mathbb{R})$: there are real $4 \times 4$ matrices satisfying the relations
for the metric $\operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, 1, 1)$, whose products by $i$ are purely imaginary gamma matrices for our
signature (@exm-spd-majorana-four).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Clifford algebra has a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ grading by the parity of the number of vectors in a product. The first
exercise constructs it; the even part is where the spin groups of the next part live.

::: {#exr-spd-grade-involution}
#### The even subalgebra

Show that $v \mapsto -v$ on $V$ extends to an automorphism $\alpha$ of $Cl(p, q)$ with $\alpha^2 = 1$. Let $Cl^0$ and
$Cl^1$ be its $\pm1$ eigenspaces. Show that $Cl^0$ is a subalgebra spanned by products of an even number of vectors,
that $Cl^1Cl^1 \subset Cl^0$, and that $\dim Cl^0 = \dim Cl^1$ when $d \geq 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The relations @eq-spd-clifford-relation are invariant under $v \mapsto -v$, so the map extends to an algebra
homomorphism, and it squares to the identity on generators, hence everywhere. A product of $k$ vectors is multiplied
by $(-1)^k$, so $Cl^0$ (resp. $Cl^1$) is spanned by even (resp. odd) products, and parities add under multiplication.
Left multiplication by $e_1$ is invertible ($e_1^{-1} = \eta_{11}e_1$) and exchanges $Cl^0$ and $Cl^1$, so they have
the same dimension, $2^{d - 1}$ by @prp-clifford-basis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The square of the volume element decides whether it behaves like $+1$ or like $i$. The second exercise computes it in
every signature; the answer reappears in the normalisation of the chirality matrix.

::: {#exr-spd-volume-square}
#### The square of the volume element

Let $\omega = e_1e_2\cdots e_d$. Show that $\omega^2 = (-1)^{d(d - 1)/2 + q}$, that $\omega e_a = (-1)^{d - 1}e_a\omega$,
and hence that $\omega$ is central exactly when $d$ is odd. Evaluate $\omega^2$ for $Cl(3, 0)$, $Cl(1, 3)$ and
$Cl(0, 2)$ and compare with @exm-spd-pauli-algebra and @exm-spd-quaternions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Reversing the order of $d$ anticommuting factors takes $d(d - 1)/2$ transpositions, so $\omega^2 = (-1)^{d(d -
1)/2}e_1\cdots e_de_d\cdots e_1 = (-1)^{d(d - 1)/2}\prod_a\eta_{aa} = (-1)^{d(d - 1)/2 + q}$. Moving $e_a$ through
$\omega$ passes $d - 1$ factors that anticommute with it and one that commutes. For $Cl(3, 0)$: $(-1)^{3} = -1$, as
$\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3 = i$; for $Cl(1, 3)$: $(-1)^{6 + 3} = -1$, so $i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$ squares to
$+1$; for $Cl(0, 2)$: $(-1)^{1 + 2} = -1$, and indeed $\mathrm{k}^2 = -1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A multiplication table is a finite object that a computer can check completely. The third exercise builds the table of
$Cl(3, 0)$ from the Pauli matrices and reads off the centre.

::: {#exr-spd-cl3-table}
#### The table of $Cl(3, 0)$

With Sage, form the eight products $\sigma_A$ ($A \subset \{1, 2, 3\}$, in increasing order) of the Pauli matrices,
check that each product $\sigma_A\sigma_B$ equals $\pm\sigma_C$ for one $C$, and find the elements
$\sigma_A$ that commute with all the others.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every product of two basis elements is a single basis element up to sign, and the elements commuting
with the whole algebra are $1$ and $\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3 = i\,1$, as @exr-spd-volume-square predicts for odd $d$:

{{< sage exr-spd-cl3-table >}}
:::

The examples suggest that the products of distinct generators form a basis, as the figure shows for $Cl(1, 3)$. The
proposition states this and records the trace identities of @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1] that make the gamma
matrices an orthogonal basis of a matrix algebra.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-clifford-basis}
#### Basis of the Clifford algebra

For each subset $A = \{a_1 < \dots < a_k\}$ of $\{1, \dots, d\}$ let $e_A = e_{a_1}\cdots e_{a_k}$ ($e_\emptyset = 1$).
The $2^d$ elements $e_A$ form a basis of $Cl(p, q)$, and
$$
e_A^2 = (-1)^{k(k - 1)/2}\eta_{a_1a_1}\cdots\eta_{a_ka_k}, \qquad e_Ae_B = \pm e_{A \triangle B}.
$$ {#eq-spd-basis-square}
If $\gamma^a$ are matrices of order $N$ representing the $e_a$ and $d = 2\nu$ is even, then $\operatorname{tr}\gamma_A
= 0$ for $A \neq \emptyset$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma_A^{-1}\gamma_B) = N\delta_{AB}$; for $N = 2^\nu$ the
$\gamma_A$ form a basis of $M_N(\mathbb{C})$ and every matrix expands as
$$
\Psi = \frac{1}{2^\nu}\sum_A\operatorname{tr}(\gamma_A^{-1}\Psi)\,\gamma_A
$$ {#eq-spd-fierz}
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1, eqs. (1.4), (1.6)-(1.12)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions the basis has four elements and the expansion @eq-spd-fierz is the familiar expansion of a
$2 \times 2$ matrix in Pauli matrices. The first example writes it out.

::: {#exm-spd-basis-two}
#### The Pauli basis

For $d = 2$ with $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$, the basis is $1, \sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_1\sigma_2 =
i\sigma_3$, and @eq-spd-fierz reads $\Psi = \tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}\Psi + \sum_a\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\Psi)
\sigma_a)$. For $\Psi = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ the coefficients are $a + d$, $b + c$, $i(b -
c)$, $a - d$. Read as an identity for the matrix entries this is the Pauli identity
$\delta_{AB}\delta_{CD} = \tfrac12(\delta_{AD}\delta_{CB} + \sum_a(\sigma_a)_{AD}(\sigma_a)_{CB})$
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [eq. (1.19)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four dimensions the sixteen basis elements sort themselves by the number of indices. The second example gives the
grouping used in every Fierz rearrangement of particle physics.

::: {#exm-spd-dirac-basis}
#### The sixteen Dirac matrices

For $Cl(1, 3)$ the basis consists of $1$, the four $\gamma^\mu$, the six $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu$ ($\mu < \nu$), the
four triple products and $\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3 = -i\gamma_5$; the triple products are $\pm i\gamma^\mu
\gamma_5$. The counts $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$ are the binomial coefficients $\binom4k$ and add up to $16 = 4^2$, so the
gamma matrices of size $4$ span all of $M_4(\mathbb{C})$: scalar, vector, tensor, axial vector and pseudoscalar.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The squares in @eq-spd-basis-square decide which basis elements are complex structures, that is, square to $-1$. The
third example counts them in Euclidean signature, a count that returns in the symmetry of the charge-conjugation
matrices.

::: {#exm-spd-squares-count}
#### Elements squaring to minus one

In $Cl(d, 0)$, $e_A^2 = (-1)^{k(k - 1)/2}$ depends only on $k = |A| \bmod 4$: it is $+1$ for $k \equiv 0, 1$ and $-1$
for $k \equiv 2, 3 \pmod 4$. In $Cl(3, 0)$ the elements of square $-1$ are the three $e_ae_b$ and $e_1e_2e_3$; in
$Cl(4, 0)$ they are the six bivectors and four trivectors, ten in all, while the six others ($1$, four vectors and the
volume element) square to $+1$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The traces in the proposition follow from one observation: every non-trivial basis element anticommutes with some
other basis element. The first exercise carries out the argument of @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1, items 1-3].

::: {#exr-spd-trace-zero}
#### Traceless gamma products

Let $d = 2\nu$ and $A \neq \emptyset$. Show that there is a $b$ with $\gamma^b\gamma_A = -\gamma_A\gamma^b$: if $|A|$
is even take $b \in A$, if $|A|$ is odd take $b \notin A$. Deduce $\operatorname{tr}\gamma_A = 0$ from the cyclicity of
the trace, and then $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma_A^{-1}\gamma_B) = N\delta_{AB}$ from @eq-spd-basis-square.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $|A| = k$ even and $b \in A$, $\gamma^b$ anticommutes with the $k - 1$ other factors and commutes with itself, a
sign $(-1)^{k - 1} = -1$; for $k$ odd and $b \notin A$ (possible since $k < 2\nu$ when $k$ is odd), the sign is
$(-1)^k = -1$. Then $\operatorname{tr}\gamma_A = \operatorname{tr}((\gamma^b)^{-1}\gamma^b\gamma_A) =
-\operatorname{tr}((\gamma^b)^{-1}\gamma_A\gamma^b) = -\operatorname{tr}\gamma_A$. Finally $\gamma_A^{-1}\gamma_B =
\pm\gamma_{A \triangle B}$, traceless unless $A = B$, where it is $1$ with trace $N$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The expansion @eq-spd-fierz turns any matrix into its components along the sixteen Dirac matrices. The second exercise
does this for a random matrix and reassembles it.

::: {#exr-spd-expand-matrix}
#### Expanding a matrix in Dirac matrices

With Sage, take the Weyl matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl, form the sixteen products $\gamma_A$, expand a random $4 \times 4$
matrix $\Psi$ by @eq-spd-fierz and check that the sum reproduces $\Psi$. Then expand $\Psi = \gamma^0$ and $\Psi =
\tfrac12(1 - \gamma_5)$ and list their non-zero coefficients.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coefficients $2^{-2}\operatorname{tr}(\gamma_A^{-1}\Psi)$ reconstruct $\Psi$ exactly; $\gamma^0$ has the single
coefficient $1$ on $\gamma^0$, and the projector $\tfrac12(1 - \gamma_5)$ has coefficient $\tfrac12$ on $1$ and
$-\tfrac{i}{2}$ on $\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3 = -i\gamma_5$:

{{< sage exr-spd-expand-matrix >}}
:::

In odd dimension the trace argument fails for the volume element, which commutes with everything. The third exercise
finds the centre of the algebra in both parities, following @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1, item 10].

::: {#exr-spd-centre}
#### The centre

Show that the centre of $Cl(p, q)$ is spanned by $1$ when $d$ is even and by $1$ and $\omega = e_1\cdots e_d$ when $d$
is odd. Hint: expand a central element $z = \sum_Az_Ae_A$ and compare $e_bz$ with $ze_b$ using
@eq-spd-basis-square.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e_be_Ae_b^{-1} = \pm e_A$, with sign $-1$ exactly when $e_b$ anticommutes with $e_A$. Since the $e_A$ are independent,
$z$ is central iff $z_A = 0$ for every $A$ such that some $e_b$ anticommutes with $e_A$. By @exr-spd-trace-zero, for
$A \neq \emptyset$ such a $b$ exists unless $|A|$ is odd and $A$ is everything, that is $A = \{1, \dots, d\}$ with $d$
odd. So the centre is $\mathbb{R}1$ for even $d$ and $\mathbb{R}1 \oplus \mathbb{R}\omega$ for odd $d$
(@exr-spd-volume-square).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Gamma matrices in every dimension

The Pauli matrices give gamma matrices in two and three dimensions. Tensor products of Pauli matrices give them in every
dimension, doubling the size each time two dimensions are added, as the blue curve of the figure shows; the red curve
anticipates the reality conditions of the next section.

![The size $N = 2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ of the gamma matrices built by tensor products of Pauli matrices
(@def-gamma-matrices-general), and the real dimension of a minimal spinor of a Lorentzian space of dimension $d$
(@thm-majorana-classification). The size doubles every second dimension; the real dimension is halved by a
Majorana or Majorana-Weyl condition, which makes it $1$ in two dimensions, $4$ in four, $16$ in ten and $32$ in eleven.
Generated by `figures/sd-spinor-dimensions.sage`.](figures/sd-spinor-dimensions.svg){#fig-sd-spinor-dimensions width=65%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gamma-matrices-general}
#### Gamma matrices in any signature

**Gamma matrices** of signature $(p, q)$ are complex $N \times N$ matrices $\gamma^1, \dots, \gamma^d$, $d = p + q$,
with
$$
\gamma^a\gamma^b + \gamma^b\gamma^a = 2\eta^{ab}\,1_N, \qquad \eta = \operatorname{diag}(\underbrace{1, \dots,
1}_{p}, \underbrace{-1, \dots, -1}_{q}),
$$ {#eq-spd-gamma-relation}
that is, a representation of $Cl(p, q)$ on $\mathbb{C}^N$. The **standard** choice for $d = 2\nu$ is
$$
\gamma^{2k - 1} = \sigma_3^{\otimes(k - 1)} \otimes \sigma_1 \otimes 1^{\otimes(\nu - k)}, \qquad \gamma^{2k} =
\sigma_3^{\otimes(k - 1)} \otimes \sigma_2 \otimes 1^{\otimes(\nu - k)} \qquad (k = 1, \dots, \nu),
$$ {#eq-spd-tensor-gammas}
with one more matrix $\gamma^{2\nu + 1} = \sigma_3^{\otimes\nu}$ for $d = 2\nu + 1$, and with the last $q$ matrices
multiplied by $i$; it has $N = 2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ and Hermitian or anti-Hermitian $\gamma^a$ according to the sign
of $(\gamma^a)^2$ @vanproeyen1999 [eqs. (3.3)-(3.5)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions the standard choice is the pair of Pauli matrices. The first example writes it in both signatures
that contain one plus sign or two.

::: {#exm-spd-gammas-two}
#### Two dimensions

For $(p, q) = (2, 0)$: $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$. For $(1, 1)$: $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 =
i\sigma_2$, the matrices of the Part II example @exm-gamma-two-dimensions. For $(0, 2)$: $i\sigma_1$, $i\sigma_2$,
which represent the quaternions of @exm-spd-quaternions on $\mathbb{C}^2$ as $\mathrm{i} \mapsto i\sigma_1$,
$\mathrm{j} \mapsto i\sigma_2$, $\mathrm{k} \mapsto -\sigma_1\sigma_2 = -i\sigma_3$.
:::

In four dimensions the standard construction gives matrices that look different from the Weyl matrices of the book.
The second example compares them; the theorem below explains why the difference does not matter.

::: {#exm-spd-gammas-four}
#### Four dimensions

For $(4, 0)$, @eq-spd-tensor-gammas gives $\sigma_1 \otimes 1$, $\sigma_2 \otimes 1$, $\sigma_3 \otimes \sigma_1$,
$\sigma_3 \otimes \sigma_2$. For $(1, 3)$ the last three are multiplied by $i$. The Weyl matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl
are instead $\gamma^0 = \sigma_1 \otimes 1$ and $\gamma^k = i\sigma_2 \otimes \sigma_k$; both sets satisfy
@eq-spd-gamma-relation with $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$, and by @thm-pauli-uniqueness they are related
by a change of basis of $\mathbb{C}^4$.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Eleven dimensions is the largest case the book needs. The third example counts the size of its gamma matrices and
observes that in odd dimension the last matrix is fixed by the others.

::: {#exm-spd-gammas-eleven}
#### Eleven dimensions

For $(1, 10)$, $\nu = 5$ and $N = 32$: ten matrices from @eq-spd-tensor-gammas on $(\mathbb{C}^2)^{\otimes5}$ and the
eleventh $\sigma_3^{\otimes5}$, times $i$ where needed. The product $\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^{10}$ is proportional to
$\sigma_3^{\otimes5}$, so in odd dimension the last gamma matrix is the "chirality matrix" of the dimension below,
@vanproeyen1999 [after eq. (3.10)], and $\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^{11}$ is a multiple of the identity.
:::

#### Building gamma matrices

With Sage, implement @eq-spd-tensor-gammas for every $(p, q)$ with $p + q \leq 10$, check @eq-spd-gamma-relation and

All relations hold and the sizes are $1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 16, 16, 32$ for $d = 1, \dots, 10$ (for $d = 1$ the
construction gives $\gamma^1 = 1$, or $i$ in signature $(0, 1)$):

{{< sage exr-spd-build-gammas >}}

@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1, eqs. (1.38)-(1.43)] proves the existence of gamma matrices by a recursion that
adds two dimensions at a time. The second exercise asks for that recursion.

::: {#exr-spd-recursion}
#### Adding two dimensions

Let $\gamma^1, \dots, \gamma^{2\nu}$ be Euclidean gamma matrices of size $2^\nu$ and $\gamma^{2\nu + 1} =
i^\nu\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^{2\nu}$. Show that the $2\nu + 2$ matrices $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i\gamma^j \\ i\gamma^j & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $j = 1, \dots, 2\nu + 1$, are Euclidean gamma matrices
of size $2^{\nu + 1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma^{2\nu + 1}$ squares to $i^{2\nu}(-1)^{\nu(2\nu - 1)} = 1$ (@exr-spd-volume-square) and anticommutes with each
$\gamma^j$, $j \leq 2\nu$, so the $2\nu + 1$ matrices satisfy the Euclidean relations. The block matrices give
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i\gamma^j \\ i\gamma^j & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i\gamma^k \\ i\gamma^k & 0
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \gamma^j\gamma^k & 0 \\ 0 & \gamma^j\gamma^k \end{pmatrix}$, whose symmetrisation is
$2\delta^{jk}$; the first block matrix squares to $1$ and anticommutes with the others because
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i\gamma \\ i\gamma & 0 \end{pmatrix} =
\operatorname{diag}(i\gamma, -i\gamma)$ changes sign when the factors are exchanged.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The size $2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$ is not only sufficient but necessary for even $d$. The third exercise proves this from
the linear independence in @prp-clifford-basis.

::: {#exr-spd-minimal-size}
#### The minimal size

Show that gamma matrices of even dimension $d = 2\nu$ have size $N \geq 2^\nu$, and that $N$ is a multiple of $2^\nu$.
Hint: the $2^{2\nu}$ products $\gamma_A$ are linearly independent in $M_N(\mathbb{C})$; for the second part use the eigenspaces of the commuting matrices $J_k = c_k\gamma^{2k - 1}\gamma^{2k}$, with $c_k \in \{1, i\}$
chosen so that $J_k^2 = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The traces $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma_A^{-1}\gamma_B) = N\delta_{AB}$ of @prp-clifford-basis make the $\gamma_A$
independent, so $2^{2\nu} \leq \dim M_N(\mathbb{C}) = N^2$. For the second part, the $J_k$ commute (each is a product of two gamma matrices disjoint from the others)
and square to $1$; $\gamma^{2k - 1}$ anticommutes with $J_k$ and commutes with the other
$J_l$, so it maps the joint eigenspace with signs $(s_1, \dots, s_\nu)$ isomorphically onto the one with $s_k$ flipped.
All $2^\nu$ joint eigenspaces therefore have the same dimension $m$, and $N = 2^\nu m$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

In even dimension the product of all gamma matrices anticommutes with each of them and can be normalised to square to
one. This is the chirality matrix, the matrix that splits spinors into two halves.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-chirality-matrix}
#### Chirality matrix

For gamma matrices of even dimension $d$ and signature $(p, q)$ the **chirality matrix** is
$$
\gamma_* = i^{d(d - 1)/2 + q}\,\gamma^1\gamma^2\cdots\gamma^d .
$$ {#eq-spd-chirality}
It satisfies $\gamma_*^2 = 1$ and $\gamma_*\gamma^a = -\gamma^a\gamma_*$; for Euclidean signature $\gamma_* =
i^{d/2}\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eq. (1.21)], and for $(1, 3)$ it is $\gamma_5 =
i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3$. Its eigenvalues $\pm1$ are the two **chiralities**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The definition fixes the overall sign of $\gamma_*$, which other authors choose differently. The first example computes
it in two dimensions, where the choice is visible.

::: {#exm-spd-chirality-two}
#### Two dimensions

For $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$, @eq-spd-chirality gives $\gamma_* = i\sigma_1\sigma_2 = i\cdot
i\sigma_3 = -\sigma_3$. For the Lorentzian pair $\sigma_1, i\sigma_2$ the exponent is $1 + 1 = 2$ and $\gamma_* =
-\sigma_1(i\sigma_2) = +\sigma_3$, while @exr-fld-gamma-2d uses $\gamma^0\gamma^1 = -\sigma_3$: the two conventions
differ by a sign, which exchanges the names of the two chiralities. @vanproeyen1999 [eq. (3.8)] normalises with
$(-i)^{d/2 + t}$ and obtains $+\sigma_3$ in the Euclidean case.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four dimensions the chirality matrix is the $\gamma_5$ of particle physics. The second example evaluates it in the
Weyl representation, where it is diagonal.

::: {#exm-spd-gamma-five}
#### The matrix $\gamma_5$

For the Weyl matrices of @exm-gamma-weyl, $\gamma_5 = i\gamma^0\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1,
1, 1)$: the upper two components of a Dirac spinor have chirality $-1$ (left-handed) and the lower two chirality $+1$
(right-handed). The exponent in @eq-spd-chirality is $6 + 3 = 9$, and $i^9 = i$, which is why the factor in front of
the product is $i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For the standard matrices @eq-spd-tensor-gammas the chirality matrix is again a tensor product. The third example finds
it, which is how the construction of @exm-spd-gammas-eleven continues from even to odd dimension.

::: {#exm-spd-chirality-tensor}
#### Chirality of the tensor construction

For the Euclidean matrices @eq-spd-tensor-gammas, $\gamma^{2k - 1}\gamma^{2k} = 1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_1\sigma_2
\otimes \cdots = 1 \otimes \cdots \otimes i\sigma_3 \otimes \cdots$ (the $\sigma_3$ factors in front square to $1$), so
$\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^{2\nu} = (i\sigma_3)^{\otimes\nu}$ and $\gamma_* = i^\nu(i\sigma_3)^{\otimes\nu} =
(-\sigma_3)^{\otimes\nu}$. Up to sign it is the extra matrix $\sigma_3^{\otimes\nu}$ that makes the construction work
in dimension $2\nu + 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The two properties claimed in the definition follow from @exr-spd-volume-square. The first exercise derives them, explains the exponent and adds the hermiticity of $\gamma_*$.

::: {#exr-spd-chirality-properties}
#### Properties of $\gamma_*$

Show that $\gamma_*^2 = 1$ and $\gamma_*\gamma^a = -\gamma^a\gamma_*$ for even $d$. Show that if all $\gamma^a$ are
unitary then $\gamma_*$ is Hermitian, and that $\gamma_*$ commutes with every product of an even number of gamma
matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-spd-volume-square, $(\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d)^2 = (-1)^{d(d - 1)/2 + q}$, and $(i^m)^2 = (-1)^m$ with $m =
d(d - 1)/2 + q$, so $\gamma_*^2 = 1$; anticommutation is the case $d$ even of the same exercise. A unitary $\gamma_*$
with $\gamma_*^2 = 1$ satisfies $\gamma_*^\dagger = \gamma_*^{-1} = \gamma_*$. An even product picks up an even number
of signs when $\gamma_*$ moves through it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In odd dimension the product of all gamma matrices is central, so in an irreducible representation it is a number.
The second exercise computes this number and finds that it can take two values.

::: {#exr-spd-odd-product}
#### The product in odd dimension

With Sage, compute $\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d$ for the Euclidean matrices @eq-spd-tensor-gammas with $d = 3, 5, 7, 9$,
and for the matrices $-\gamma^a$. Show that $i^{-(d - 1)/2}\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d = \pm1$ with opposite signs for the
two sets.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $d = 2\nu + 1$ the product is $\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^{2\nu}\sigma_3^{\otimes\nu} = i^\nu\,1$ by
@exm-spd-chirality-tensor (so $i^{-\nu}\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d = 1$) and the opposite for $-\gamma^a$, because changing the sign of all $d$ matrices changes the product by $(-1)^d =
-1$. A matrix $T$ with $T^{-1}\gamma^aT = -\gamma^a$ would have to preserve the product and change its sign, so the two
sets are not equivalent:

{{< sage exr-spd-odd-product >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The chirality projectors split $\mathbb{C}^N$ into two halves of equal size. The third exercise proves the equality,
which is the reason Weyl spinors have half the components of Dirac spinors.

::: {#exr-spd-weyl-projectors}
#### The chirality projectors

Let $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \gamma_*)$. Show that $P_\pm$ are complementary projections, that $\operatorname{tr}
\gamma_* = 0$, and hence that each has rank $N/2$. Show that $\gamma^aP_\pm = P_\mp\gamma^a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$P_\pm^2 = \tfrac14(1 \pm 2\gamma_* + \gamma_*^2) = P_\pm$ and $P_+P_- = \tfrac14(1 - \gamma_*^2) = 0$, $P_+ + P_- =
1$. The trace of $\gamma_*$ vanishes by @prp-clifford-basis (it is a multiple of $\gamma_A$ with $A$ everything), so
$\operatorname{rank}P_\pm = \operatorname{tr}P_\pm = N/2$. Finally $\gamma^a\gamma_* = -\gamma_*\gamma^a$ gives
$\gamma^aP_\pm = P_\mp\gamma^a$: gamma matrices exchange the chiralities.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Different authors use different gamma matrices, and the results must not depend on the choice. The theorem below,
proved by @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1, items 10-11] under the name of Pauli's theorem, guarantees this in even
dimension and finds exactly two choices in odd dimension.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-pauli-uniqueness}
#### Pauli's theorem

Let $d = 2\nu$. Every set of gamma matrices of signature $(p, q)$ has size $N = 2^\nu m$ and is similar to $m$ copies
of the standard set; two sets of size $2^\nu$ are related by $\gamma'^a = T^{-1}\gamma^aT$ with $T$ unique up to a
non-zero factor, and a matrix commuting with all $\gamma^a$ of size $2^\nu$ is a multiple of $1$. Let $d = 2\nu + 1$.
There are exactly two inequivalent irreducible sets, of size $2^\nu$, related by $\gamma^a \mapsto -\gamma^a$ and told
apart by the sign of the central element $\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs. (1.28)-(1.29)],
@vanproeyen1999 [footnote 5], @trautman1995 [Prop. 2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest instance is a reordering of the Pauli matrices. The first example finds the matrix $T$ explicitly and interprets it as a reflection.

::: {#exm-spd-pauli-two}
#### Exchanging $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$

$(\sigma_1, \sigma_2)$ and $(\sigma_2, \sigma_1)$ are both Euclidean gamma matrices in two dimensions. With $T =
\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2)$, which is Hermitian with $T^2 = 1$, one finds $T\sigma_1T = \sigma_2$ and
$T\sigma_2T = \sigma_1$, so $\gamma'^a = T^{-1}\gamma^aT$ as the theorem says. The matrix $T$ is the reflection that
exchanges the $x$ and $y$ axes, lifted to spinors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem is most useful when applied to sets built from a given one by transposition or conjugation. The second
example produces three such sets and, from them, the matrices of the next section.

::: {#exm-spd-transpose-sets}
#### Transposed and conjugate sets

If $\gamma^a$ satisfy @eq-spd-gamma-relation, so do $-(\gamma^a)^T$, $(\gamma^a)^*$ and $-(\gamma^a)^*$ (transposition
reverses products, conjugation fixes the real numbers $2\eta^{ab}$). In even dimension the theorem gives invertible
matrices $C$ and $B$ with $(\gamma^a)^T = -C\gamma^aC^{-1}$ and $(\gamma^a)^* = B\gamma^aB^{-1}$, each unique up to a
factor @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs. (1.44), (1.127)]: they become the charge-conjugation and reality matrices of
@def-charge-conjugation-matrix and @def-majorana-condition.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In three dimensions the two inequivalent sets are the Pauli matrices and their negatives. The third example shows that
no change of basis relates them.

::: {#exm-spd-odd-inequivalent}
#### Two inequivalent sets in three dimensions

$\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3 = i\,1$ while $(-\sigma_1)(-\sigma_2)(-\sigma_3) = -i\,1$. A similarity $T^{-1}(\cdot)T$
preserves products and fixes multiples of $1$, so it cannot carry one set to the other. Both sets generate the same
matrix algebra $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, but they represent $Cl(3, 0) \cong M_2(\mathbb{C}) \oplus M_2(\mathbb{C})$ (complexified)
through its two different simple summands.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [eq. (1.29)] proves the theorem by writing $T$ as an average over the group of basis elements.
The first exercise checks that formula numerically for the two four-dimensional sets of @exm-spd-gammas-four.

::: {#exr-spd-pauli-average}
#### Pauli's averaging formula

Let $\gamma_A$ and $\gamma'_A$ be the sixteen products of the two sets of @exm-spd-gammas-four, built in the same
order. With Sage, compute $T = \sum_A\gamma_A F\gamma'^{-1}_A$ for a random matrix $F$, check that $\det T \neq 0$ and
that $\gamma^aT = T\gamma'^a$ for all $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Multiplying by $\gamma^a$ permutes the products $\gamma_A$ up to signs, and the same signs appear for the primed set,
so the average intertwines the two representations; for a generic $F$ it is invertible:

{{< sage exr-spd-pauli-average >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The uniqueness of $T$ up to a factor rests on a Schur-type statement about the gamma matrices themselves. The second
exercise proves it.

::: {#exr-spd-commutant}
#### Matrices commuting with the gamma matrices

Let $d = 2\nu$ and let the $\gamma^a$ have size $2^\nu$. Show that a matrix $X$ with $X\gamma^a = \gamma^aX$ for all
$a$ is a multiple of $1$, by expanding $X$ with @eq-spd-fierz. Deduce that the matrix $T$ of the theorem is unique up
to a factor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $X = \sum_Ax_A\gamma_A$. $X$ commutes with every $\gamma_B$, so $\gamma_BX\gamma_B^{-1} = \sum_A\pm x_A\gamma_A =
X$ with the sign $-1$ whenever $\gamma_B$ anticommutes with $\gamma_A$; by @exr-spd-trace-zero this happens for some
$B$ whenever $A \neq \emptyset$, which forces $x_A = 0$. If $T$ and $T'$ both intertwine, $T'T^{-1}$ commutes with all
$\gamma^a$ and is a multiple of $1$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.1, item 10].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A reducible set of gamma matrices is a direct sum of irreducible ones, and the trace of the chirality matrix tells how
it is assembled. The third exercise uses this to recognise reducible sets.

::: {#exr-spd-reducible}
#### Recognising reducible sets

Show that in even dimension $\gamma^a \otimes 1_m$ are gamma matrices of size $2^\nu m$, reducible for $m > 1$. In odd
dimension $d = 2\nu + 1$, show that $\gamma^a \oplus (-\gamma^a)$ is a set of size $2^{\nu + 1}$ in which the central
product has trace $0$, and that a set of size $2^\nu(m_+ + m_-)$ containing $m_\pm$ copies of the two irreducible sets has
$\operatorname{tr}(i^{-\nu}\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d) = 2^\nu(m_+ - m_-)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\gamma^a \otimes 1)(\gamma^b \otimes 1) = \gamma^a\gamma^b \otimes 1$, so the relations hold, and $\mathbb{C}^{2^\nu}
\otimes v$ is invariant for every $v \in \mathbb{C}^m$. In odd dimension the central element $i^{-\nu}\gamma^1\cdots
\gamma^d$ equals $+1$ on each copy of one irreducible set and $-1$ on each copy of the other (@exr-spd-odd-product), so its
trace counts $2^\nu(m_+ - m_-)$, which is $0$ for $\gamma^a \oplus (-\gamma^a)$. This sum is the representation used
by @trautman1995 [Prop. 2] under the name of Cartan spinors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Charge conjugation and reality

The transposed gamma matrices are equivalent to the original ones, and the matrix that relates them pairs spinors into
invariants. Whether the complex conjugate spinor can be identified with the spinor itself depends on the signature
modulo $8$, and the figure displays the answer for all signatures up to eleven dimensions.

![The reality conditions available in signature $(p, q)$, $d = p + q \leq 11$: Majorana-Weyl (MW), Majorana (M),
symplectic Majorana-Weyl (SMW) or only symplectic Majorana (SM), computed from explicit matrices $B$ with
$(\gamma^a)^* = \pm B\gamma^aB^{-1}$. The number in each cell is the real dimension of a minimal spinor. The pattern
depends only on $p - q \bmod 8$ (@thm-majorana-classification): Lorentzian signature is the row $q = d - 1$, and the
green cells at $d = 2$, $10$ in that row are the Majorana-Weyl spinors of two and ten dimensions. Generated by
`figures/sd-majorana-table.sage`.](figures/sd-majorana-table.svg){#fig-sd-majorana-table width=72%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-charge-conjugation-matrix}
#### Charge-conjugation matrix

A **charge-conjugation matrix** for gamma matrices $\gamma^a$ of signature $(p, q)$ is an invertible $C$ with
$$
(\gamma^a)^T = -\eta_C\,C\gamma^aC^{-1} \quad (a = 1, \dots, d), \qquad C^T = -\epsilon_C\,C,
$$ {#eq-spd-charge-conjugation}
for signs $\eta_C, \epsilon_C \in \{1, -1\}$. In even dimension one exists for each $\eta_C$ (and $C_{-} \propto
C_{+}\gamma_*$); in odd dimension for one value of $\eta_C$ only. The sign $\epsilon_C$ is determined by $d \bmod 8$ and
$\eta_C$, and then $C\gamma_A$ is symmetric or antisymmetric according to $|A| \bmod 4$ @vanproeyen1999 [eqs.
(3.11)-(3.14), Table 1], @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs. (1.44)-(1.55)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions both charge-conjugation matrices can be found by inspection. The first example does this and reads
off their symmetry.

::: {#exm-spd-charge-two}
#### Two dimensions

For $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$: $\sigma_1^T = \sigma_1$, $\sigma_2^T = -\sigma_2$. The matrix $C_+ =
\sigma_2$ gives $-\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2 = \sigma_1$ and $-\sigma_2\sigma_2\sigma_2 = -\sigma_2$, so $\eta_C = +1$; it
is antisymmetric, $\epsilon_C = +1$. The matrix $C_- = \sigma_1 \propto C_+\gamma_*$ gives $\sigma_1\sigma_a\sigma_1 =
(\sigma_a)^T$, so $\eta_C = -1$, and it is symmetric, $\epsilon_C = -1$, in agreement with the row $d = 2$ of
@vanproeyen1999 [Table 1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four dimensions the charge-conjugation matrix is the one that turns a particle spinor into an antiparticle spinor
in the Dirac theory. The second example gives it in the Weyl representation.

::: {#exm-spd-charge-four}
#### Four dimensions

For the Weyl matrices, $C = i\gamma^2\gamma^0$ satisfies $C\gamma^\mu C^{-1} = -(\gamma^\mu)^T$, that is
@eq-spd-charge-conjugation with $\eta_C = +1$, and $C^T = -C$, so $\epsilon_C = +1$; $C\gamma_5$ gives $\eta_C = -1$ and is
again antisymmetric. Accordingly $C$ and $C\gamma_5$ and $C\gamma^\mu\gamma_5$ are antisymmetric, while $C\gamma^\mu$
and $C\gamma^{\mu\nu}$ are symmetric: there are $4 + 6 = 10$ symmetric products, the number of components of the
anticommutator of two four-component Majorana spinors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The symmetric products $C\gamma_A$ are the possible terms in the anticommutator of two supercharges. The third example
counts them in eleven dimensions, where the result is a famous number.

::: {#exm-spd-charge-eleven}
#### Eleven dimensions

For $d = 11$ only $\eta_C = +1$ occurs, $C$ is antisymmetric, and $C\gamma_A$ is symmetric for $|A| = 1, 2, 5$ (and
their duals $10, 9, 6$, which give nothing new since $\gamma_A$ with $|A| \geq 6$ is a multiple of one with $11 -
|A|$ indices) @vanproeyen1999 [Table 1]. The number of independent symmetric matrices is $\binom{11}{1} + \binom{11}{2} +
\binom{11}{5} = 11 + 55 + 462 = 528 = \tfrac12\cdot32\cdot33$: every symmetric $32 \times 32$ matrix is a combination
of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The table of signs $(\epsilon_C, \eta_C)$ can be computed by solving the linear equations @eq-spd-charge-conjugation. The
first exercise does this for $d \leq 8$.

::: {#exr-spd-charge-table}
#### The table of signs

With Sage, solve $(\gamma^a)^TC + \eta_CC\gamma^a = 0$ for the Euclidean matrices @eq-spd-tensor-gammas with $d = 1,
\dots, 8$ and $\eta_C = \pm1$, and for each solution determine $\epsilon_C$. Compare with @vanproeyen1999 [Table 1].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $(d, \eta_C)$ has a one-dimensional solution space or none, as @thm-pauli-uniqueness predicts, and the signs
found reproduce the table: $(\epsilon_C, \eta_C) = (-1, -1)$ for $d = 1$, both $(\pm1, \pm1)$ for $d = 2$, $(1, 1)$ for
$d = 3$, $(1, \pm1)$ for $d = 4$, $(1, -1)$ for $d = 5$, $(\pm1, \mp1)$ for $d = 6$, $(-1, 1)$ for $d = 7$ and $(-1,
\pm1)$ for $d = 8$:

{{< sage exr-spd-charge-table >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The symmetry of $C\gamma_A$ follows from that of $C$ by transposing products. The second exercise derives the rule and
uses it to count symmetric matrices, as @vanproeyen1999 [eqs. (3.14)-(3.16)] does.

::: {#exr-spd-symmetric-count}
#### Symmetric products

Show that $(C\gamma_A)^T = -\epsilon_C(-\eta_C)^k(-1)^{k(k - 1)/2}C\gamma_A$ for $|A| = k$. For $d = 2\nu$ the
$C\gamma_A$ form a basis of $M_{2^\nu}(\mathbb{C})$; deduce that the number of symmetric ones is $2^{\nu - 1}(2^\nu +
1)$ and check it in $d = 4$ against @exm-spd-charge-four.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(C\gamma^{a_1}\cdots\gamma^{a_k})^T = (\gamma^{a_k})^T\cdots(\gamma^{a_1})^TC^T = (-\eta_C)^kC\gamma^{a_k}\cdots
\gamma^{a_1}C^{-1}(-\epsilon_C)C$, and reversing the order costs $(-1)^{k(k - 1)/2}$. Since $C$ is invertible the
$C\gamma_A$ are a basis of all matrices, so exactly $\tfrac12N(N + 1)$ of them are symmetric, $N = 2^\nu$. In $d = 4$
with $\eta_C = \epsilon_C = 1$ the sign is $-(-1)^k(-1)^{k(k - 1)/2}$: symmetric for $k = 1, 2$, giving $4 + 6 = 10 =
\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot5$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The symmetry of $C$ does not depend on the choice of gamma matrices. The third exercise proves this with the
transformation rule of @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eq. (1.48)].

::: {#exr-spd-charge-basis}
#### Independence of the basis

Let $\gamma'^a = T^{-1}\gamma^aT$. Show that $C' = T^TCT$ satisfies @eq-spd-charge-conjugation for the primed matrices
with the same $\eta_C$ and $\epsilon_C$, and that every charge-conjugation matrix for $\gamma'$ is a multiple of $C'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\gamma'^a)^T = T^T(\gamma^a)^T(T^T)^{-1} = -\eta_CT^TC\gamma^aC^{-1}(T^T)^{-1} = -\eta_CC'(T^{-1}\gamma^aT)C'^{-1}$,
and $C'^T = T^TC^TT = -\epsilon_CC'$. If $C''$ is another one, $C''^{-1}C'$ commutes with all $\gamma'^a$ and is a
multiple of $1$ by @thm-pauli-uniqueness.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The complex conjugate of a spinor transforms like the spinor itself, up to a fixed matrix. When this matrix squares to
the identity under conjugation one can impose a reality condition, and the spinor has half as many real components.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-majorana-condition}
#### Majorana spinor

Let $B$ be an invertible matrix with $(\gamma^a)^* = sB\gamma^aB^{-1}$ for all $a$ and a fixed sign $s$; then
$B^*B = c\,1$ with $c$ real, and $B$ can be rescaled to $c = \pm1$. If $B^*B = 1$ for some such $B$, a **Majorana
spinor** is a $\psi \in \mathbb{C}^N$ with
$$
\psi^* = B\psi .
$$ {#eq-spd-majorana}
If $B^*B = -1$ for every such $B$, one instead imposes on pairs $\psi^i$, $i = 1, 2$, the **symplectic Majorana**
condition $(\psi^i)^* = \epsilon_{ij}B\psi^j$. A **Majorana-Weyl spinor** is a Majorana spinor of definite chirality
@vanproeyen1999 [eqs. (3.19)-(3.28)], @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs. (1.135)-(1.142)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In four dimensions with our signature there is a basis in which all gamma matrices are imaginary. The first example
uses it, where the Majorana condition says simply that the spinor is real.

::: {#exm-spd-majorana-four}
#### Majorana spinors in four dimensions

In signature $(1, 3)$ the matrices $\tilde\gamma^0 = \sigma_2 \otimes \sigma_1$, $\tilde\gamma^1 = i\sigma_1 \otimes
1$, $\tilde\gamma^2 = i\sigma_2 \otimes \sigma_2$, $\tilde\gamma^3 = i\sigma_3 \otimes 1$ are purely imaginary
(@exr-spd-imaginary-rep), so $(\tilde\gamma^a)^* = -\tilde\gamma^a$: $s = -1$, $B = 1$, $B^*B = 1$, and Majorana spinors
are the real vectors of $\mathbb{C}^4$, four real components. The Dirac equation $(i\tilde\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu -
m)\psi = 0$ has real coefficients in this basis, so it preserves real solutions @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.6.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The smallest Majorana spinors of a Lorentzian space live in two and three dimensions. The second example finds the
three-dimensional ones.

::: {#exm-spd-majorana-three}
#### Three dimensions

In signature $(1, 2)$, $\gamma^0 = \sigma_2$, $\gamma^1 = i\sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = i\sigma_3$ satisfy
@eq-spd-gamma-relation and are all purely imaginary, so again $B = 1$ and Majorana spinors are real two-component
vectors. In signature $(1, 1)$ the real matrices $\sigma_1$, $i\sigma_2$ give real Majorana spinors whose two components
have opposite chirality $\gamma_* = \sigma_3$ (@exm-spd-chirality-two), so each chirality is a single real component: a Majorana-Weyl spinor
with one real degree of freedom (@fig-sd-spinor-dimensions at $d = 2$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In five Lorentzian dimensions the reality matrix squares to $-1$ and no Majorana condition exists. The third example
shows how the symplectic condition takes its place, with the same count of real components as one Dirac spinor.

::: {#exm-spd-symplectic-five}
#### Symplectic Majorana spinors in five dimensions

In signature $(1, 4)$ every matrix $B$ with $(\gamma^a)^* = \pm B\gamma^aB^{-1}$ has $B^*B = -1$ (@fig-sd-majorana-table,
cell $d = 5$, $q = 4$), so no spinor equals its own conjugate. A pair $\psi^1, \psi^2$ with $(\psi^1)^* = B\psi^2$,
$(\psi^2)^* = -B\psi^1$ is consistent, since conjugating the first gives $\psi^1 = B^*(\psi^2)^* = -B^*B\psi^1 =
\psi^1$. The pair has $2 \times 4$ complex components subject to $4$ complex conditions: $8$ real components, the
minimal spinor of five-dimensional supersymmetry.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

#### Computing $B^*B$

With Sage, for every $(p, q)$ with $p + q \leq 8$, find the matrices $B$ with $(\gamma^a)^* = sB\gamma^aB^{-1}$ for the
standard gamma matrices (they are products of the real or of the imaginary $\gamma^a$) and print the signs of $B^*B$.
Check that a positive sign occurs exactly when $p - q \equiv 0, 1, 2, 6, 7 \pmod 8$.

Each $\gamma^a$ of @eq-spd-tensor-gammas is real or imaginary, so the product of the real ones and the product of the
imaginary ones conjugate every $\gamma^a$ to $\pm(\gamma^a)^*$; the signs of $B^*B$ follow the rule:

{{< sage exr-spd-bb-sign >}}

A reality condition is useful only if spinor transformations respect it. The second exercise checks this for the
transformations generated by the products $\gamma^a\gamma^b$, which are the spin transformations of the next part.

::: {#exr-spd-majorana-invariant}
#### Invariance of the Majorana condition

Let $\Sigma^{ab} = \tfrac14[\gamma^a, \gamma^b]$ and $S = \exp(\tfrac12\omega_{ab}\Sigma^{ab})$ with real $\omega_{ab}$.
Show that $B\Sigma^{ab}B^{-1} = (\Sigma^{ab})^*$ for either sign $s$, hence $BS = S^*B$, and that $S\psi$ is Majorana
whenever $\psi$ is.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B\gamma^a\gamma^bB^{-1} = (s(\gamma^a)^*)(s(\gamma^b)^*) = (\gamma^a\gamma^b)^*$ since $s^2 = 1$, so $B\Sigma^{ab}B^{-1}
= (\Sigma^{ab})^*$; with real $\omega_{ab}$ this exponentiates to $BSB^{-1} = S^*$. Then $(S\psi)^* = S^*\psi^* =
S^*B\psi = BS\psi$ @vanproeyen1999 [eq. (3.23)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The imaginary gamma matrices of @exm-spd-majorana-four were stated without proof. The third exercise verifies them and
compares with the condition of @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.6.3] for the existence of real or imaginary
representations.

::: {#exr-spd-imaginary-rep}
#### An imaginary representation

With Sage, check that the matrices $\tilde\gamma^\mu$ of @exm-spd-majorana-four satisfy @eq-spd-gamma-relation with
$\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ and are purely imaginary. Show that for $\operatorname{diag}(-1, 1, 1, 1)$
the matrices $i\tilde\gamma^\mu$ are real.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The relations hold and every entry is imaginary; $i\tilde\gamma^\mu$ is real and squares to $-\eta^{\mu\mu}$, so it is a
real representation of $Cl(3, 1)$, the $M_4(\mathbb{R})$ of @exm-spd-minkowski-cl. @zhelnorovich2019spinors [after eq.
(1.142)] finds imaginary representations for $\nu - q' \equiv 0, 3 \pmod 4$, where $q'$ counts the directions whose
gamma matrix squares to $-1$: here $\nu = 2$, $q' = 3$, $\nu - q' = -1 \equiv 3$:

{{< sage exr-spd-imaginary-rep >}}
:::

The computations of this section combine into a classification with period eight in the signature. The theorem states
it in the form of @vanproeyen1999, which depends only on $p - q$ and so is the same for $(p, q)$ and $(q, p)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-majorana-classification}
#### Reality of spinors

Let $r = (p - q) \bmod 8$. Majorana spinors exist if and only if $r \in \{0, 1, 2, 6, 7\}$; Majorana-Weyl spinors exist
if and only if $r = 0$; for $r = 4$ there are symplectic Majorana-Weyl spinors, and for $r \in \{3, 5\}$ only symplectic
Majorana spinors. With $N = 2^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}$, the real dimension of a minimal spinor is $N/2$ for $r = 0$, $2N$
for $r \in \{3, 5\}$ and $N$ otherwise. The proof rests on $B^*B = \pm1$ and on $(\gamma_*)^* = (-1)^{(p - q)/2}
B\gamma_*B^{-1}$ @vanproeyen1999 [eqs. (3.20), (3.25), (3.28), Table 2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Lorentzian signature is the row $q = d - 1$ of @fig-sd-majorana-table. The first example reads it off for every
dimension up to twelve.

::: {#exm-spd-lorentz-table}
#### Lorentzian signature

For $(1, d - 1)$, $r = (2 - d) \bmod 8$. Majorana spinors exist for $d = 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12$ and Majorana-Weyl ones
for $d = 2, 10$. The minimal real dimensions for $d = 2, \dots, 12$ are $1, 2, 4, 8, 8, 16, 16, 16, 16, 32, 64$ (the red
curve of @fig-sd-spinor-dimensions), in agreement with @vanproeyen1999 [Table 2, column $t = 1$].
:::

Ten and eleven dimensions are the two cases where the minimal spinor has as few real components as the dimension
allows. The second example records them.

::: {#exm-spd-ten-eleven}
#### Ten and eleven dimensions

In $d = 10$, $r = 1 - 9 = -8 \equiv 0$: Majorana-Weyl spinors exist, with $32/2 = 16$ real components; the two
chiralities give inequivalent real representations of dimension $16$. In $d = 11$, $r = -9 \equiv 7$: Majorana spinors
exist, with $32$ real components, and there is no chirality. Thirty-two real components is the largest number that a
supersymmetry generator can have without fields of spin greater than two, so eleven is the largest dimension with a
single minimal supercharge @vanproeyen1999 [Sec. 4.3 and Table 3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

Compact internal spaces have Euclidean signature, the row $q = 0$. The third example reads that row, where the period
eight is visible in the Majorana-Weyl spinors of eight dimensions.

::: {#exm-spd-euclidean-table}
#### Euclidean signature

For $(d, 0)$, $r = d \bmod 8$: Majorana spinors for $d \equiv 0, 1, 2, 6, 7$, Majorana-Weyl for $d = 8$ (the two real
eight-dimensional representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(8)$), symplectic Majorana-Weyl for $d = 4$ (the Weyl spinors of
$\mathbb{R}^4$ are the pseudoreal doublets of $SU(2)$), and only symplectic Majorana spinors for $d = 3, 5$ (the
$\mathbb{C}^2$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(3) = SU(2)$ is pseudoreal).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The dimension count in the theorem is a short case analysis. The first exercise carries it out and compares with the
table of @vanproeyen1999.

::: {#exr-spd-real-dimension}
#### Counting real components

Derive the real dimension of a minimal spinor in each case of the theorem: a Dirac spinor has $2N$ real components, a
Majorana or Weyl condition halves it, and Majorana-Weyl quarters it. Explain why for $r = 4$ the answer is $N$ although
neither a Majorana nor a Majorana-Weyl condition exists, and why for $r = 3, 5$ it is $2N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $r = 0$, Majorana-Weyl: $2N/4 = N/2$. For $r \in \{1, 2, 6, 7\}$, Majorana: $N$; when $d$ is even ($r = 2, 6$) the
Weyl spinor is complex with $N/2$ complex, that is $N$ real, components, the same count. For $r = 4$, $d$ is even and a
Weyl spinor has $N$ real components; the symplectic Majorana-Weyl condition relates two Weyl spinors and leaves $N$
real components for the pair. For $r = 3, 5$, $d$ is odd, there is no Weyl condition, and the symplectic condition on a
pair leaves $2N$: one Dirac spinor's worth.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Majorana-Weyl condition combines two projections, and they are compatible only if complex conjugation preserves the
chirality. The second exercise derives the condition $r \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ for this.

::: {#exr-spd-mw-condition}
#### Compatibility of reality and chirality

Using $B\gamma^aB^{-1} = s(\gamma^a)^*$, show that $B\gamma_*B^{-1} = (-1)^{(p - q)/2}(\gamma_*)^*$ for even $d$ (for
either $s$, since $d$ is even). Deduce that $\psi \mapsto B^{-1}\psi^*$ preserves chirality iff $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod
4$, and combine with the Majorana condition to find $r = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^dB^{-1} = s^d(\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d)^* = (\gamma^1\cdots\gamma^d)^*$, while the prefactor $i^m$,
$m = d(d - 1)/2 + q$, is conjugated to $i^{-m} = (-1)^mi^m$. So $B\gamma_*B^{-1} = (-1)^m\gamma_*^*$, and $m \equiv
d/2 + q \equiv (p - q)/2 \pmod 2$ since $d(d - 1)/2 \equiv d/2$ for even $d$. If $\gamma_*\psi = \psi$ then
$\gamma_*(B^{-1}\psi^*) = (-1)^mB^{-1}\psi^*$, so the Majorana condition can be imposed on a Weyl spinor iff $m$ is even,
$r \equiv 0 \pmod 4$; among $r \in \{0, 2, 6\}$ with Majorana spinors only $r = 0$ remains @vanproeyen1999 [eq.
(3.28)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The real dimension of the minimal spinor bounds how small a supersymmetry algebra can be. The third exercise lists the
minimal numbers of real supercharges in the dimensions the book uses.

::: {#exr-spd-supercharges}
#### Minimal supercharges

Using @exm-spd-lorentz-table, give the number of real components of the smallest supersymmetry generator in Lorentzian
dimensions $d = 4, 5, 6, 10, 11$. How many four-dimensional minimal supercharges ($4$ real components each) does each
correspond to?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$4, 8, 8, 16, 32$ real components, that is $1, 2, 2, 4, 8$ four-dimensional supercharges: the minimal theories in five
and six dimensions reduce to $\mathcal{N} = 2$ in four, ten-dimensional $\mathcal{N} = 1$ reduces to $\mathcal{N} = 4$,
and eleven-dimensional supersymmetry to $\mathcal{N} = 8$, the maximum compatible with spins at most two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine the Clifford relations, the explicit gamma matrices and the reality conditions. They
prepare the spin groups of the next part, which live in the even subalgebra of the Clifford algebra.

The low-dimensional Clifford algebras are matrix algebras over $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or $\mathbb{H}$. The first
integrative exercise identifies three of them by finding explicit generators.

::: {#exr-spd-low-algebras}
#### Three small Clifford algebras

Show that $Cl(1, 1) \cong M_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $Cl(2, 0) \cong M_2(\mathbb{R})$, while $Cl(0, 2) \cong \mathbb{H}$, by
giving explicit real $2 \times 2$ matrices (or quaternions) for the generators. Which of these signatures admit
Majorana spinors according to @thm-majorana-classification, and how is this visible in the matrices?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Cl(1, 1)$: $e_1 \mapsto \sigma_1$, $e_2 \mapsto i\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, both real.
$Cl(2, 0)$: $\sigma_1$, $\sigma_3$ (@exm-spd-quaternions). Both images span $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ (four independent real
matrices). $Cl(0, 2) \cong \mathbb{H}$ (@exm-spd-quaternions). For $(1, 1)$, $r = 0$; for $(2, 0)$, $r = 2$; for
$(0, 2)$, $r = 6$: all three admit Majorana spinors. For the first two the real matrices act on $\mathbb{R}^2$; for
$(0, 2)$ the matrices $i\sigma_1, i\sigma_2$ of @exm-spd-gammas-two are not real, but $(\gamma^a)^* = sB\gamma^aB^{-1}$
is solved with $s = -1$ by $B = \sigma_1$: $\sigma_1(i\sigma_1)\sigma_1 = i\sigma_1 = -(i\sigma_1)^*$ and
$\sigma_1(i\sigma_2)\sigma_1 = -i\sigma_2 = -(i\sigma_2)^*$, with $B^*B = \sigma_1^2 = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Eleven dimensions combines everything of this part: the size $32$, the antisymmetric charge conjugation and the
Majorana condition. The second integrative exercise checks them on explicit matrices.

::: {#exr-spd-eleven-check}
#### The eleven-dimensional spinor

With Sage, build gamma matrices of signature $(1, 10)$ by @eq-spd-tensor-gammas, find $C$ with $(\gamma^a)^T =
-C\gamma^aC^{-1}$ and a matrix $B$ with $B^*B = 1$, and verify that $C$ is antisymmetric and $C\gamma^a$ symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each $\gamma^a$ of the standard set is symmetric or antisymmetric, so the product of the symmetric ones (or of the
antisymmetric ones) is a candidate for $C$; both candidates work, since in odd dimension they differ by the central
element, and $C$ comes out antisymmetric with every $C\gamma^a$ symmetric. A $B$ with $B^*B = +1$ exists, in agreement
with @exm-spd-charge-eleven and @exm-spd-ten-eleven:

{{< sage exr-spd-eleven-check >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The period eight of @fig-sd-majorana-table has a structural reason: adding eight Euclidean directions multiplies the
algebra by a real matrix algebra. The third integrative exercise proves the periodicity of the Majorana condition this
way.

::: {#exr-spd-period-eight}
#### Period eight

Let $\gamma^a$ ($a \leq d$) be gamma matrices of signature $(p, q)$ with reality matrix $B$, and $\Gamma^i$ ($i \leq 8$)
Euclidean gamma matrices of size $16$ with chirality $\Gamma_*$ and a real form ($B_8 = 1$, @exm-spd-euclidean-table).
Show that $\gamma^a \otimes \Gamma_*$ and $1 \otimes \Gamma^i$ are gamma matrices of signature $(p + 8, q)$, and that
$B \otimes 1$ (possibly times $1 \otimes \Gamma_*$) is a reality matrix with the same sign of $B^*B$. Conclude that the
type depends on $p - q \bmod 8$ only.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Gamma_*$ anticommutes with every $\Gamma^i$ and squares to $1$, so the products anticommute across the two groups and
the relations hold. In the real basis of the eight-dimensional matrices $\Gamma^i$ and $\Gamma_*$ are real, so
conjugating $\gamma^a \otimes \Gamma_*$ by $B \otimes 1$ gives $s(\gamma^a)^* \otimes \Gamma_*$ and conjugating $1
\otimes \Gamma^i$ gives $1 \otimes \Gamma^i$; if $s = -1$ one uses $B \otimes \Gamma_*$, which flips the sign on the
second group as well. In both cases $(B \otimes X)^*(B \otimes X) = B^*B \otimes X^2 = B^*B \otimes 1$. So the sign of
$B^*B$, and with it the existence of Majorana spinors, is the same for $(p, q)$ and $(p + 8, q)$, and similarly for
$(p, q + 8)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## Spin groups and spinor representations {#sec-spin-groups}

Conjugation by an invertible element of the Clifford algebra that maps vectors to vectors is an orthogonal
transformation. The elements that are products of an even number of unit vectors form the spin group, which covers the
rotation (or Lorentz) group twice, and the gamma matrices restricted to it are the spinor representation. This part
defines the spin groups following @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.2 and Sec. 3.1] and @trautman1995 [Sec. 2-3],
describes the Weyl and Majorana representations they carry with @vanproeyen1999 [Sec. 3.2], and decomposes the spinors
of a product space into spinors of the factors. The covering homomorphism $SU(2) \to SO(3)$ of
@def-covering-homomorphism is the model throughout.

For more on this topic, see @krasnov2020formulations [Sec. 1.16] and @mukunda2022continuous [Ch. 6].

### Spin groups

A rotation of $\mathbb{R}^3$ by $\varphi$ is represented on spinors by a matrix that depends on $\varphi/2$, so it
returns to the identity only after a rotation by $4\pi$. The figure compares a vector and a spinor along a rotation by
$4\pi$, and the definition below builds the group of such matrices in any signature.

![A rotation by $\varphi$ about the $x^3$ axis acting on a vector and on a spinor. Blue: the component
$\Lambda^1{}_1 = \cos\varphi$ of the rotation matrix, periodic with period $2\pi$. Red: the entry $S(\varphi)_{11} =
e^{-i\varphi/2}$ of the spinor transformation $S(\varphi) = \exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}\varphi\sigma_3)$, which covers it,
$S^{-1}\sigma_aS = \Lambda_a{}^b\sigma_b$; it reaches $S(2\pi) = -1$ and returns only at $4\pi$. Generated by
`figures/sd-spinor-rotation.sage`.](figures/sd-spinor-rotation.svg){#fig-sd-spinor-rotation width=70%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spin-group}
#### Spin group

The **spin group** $\mathrm{Spin}(p, q)$ is the set of products $S = u_1u_2\cdots u_{2k}$ in $Cl(p, q)$ of an even
number of vectors with $\eta(u_i, u_i) = \pm1$, with the Clifford product as group law. For $S \in \mathrm{Spin}(p, q)$
and $v \in V$, $\rho(S)v = SvS^{-1}$ is again a vector, $\rho(S) \in SO(p, q)$, and
$$
1 \to \{1, -1\} \to \mathrm{Spin}(p, q) \xrightarrow{\ \rho\ } SO(p, q) \to 1
$$ {#eq-spd-spin-sequence}
is exact @trautman1995 [Sec. 3.1, eqs. (2)-(5)]. In a representation by gamma matrices, $S$ acts on $\mathbb{C}^N$ and
$S^{-1}\gamma^aS = \Lambda^a{}_b\gamma^b$ with $\Lambda \in SO(p, q)$; the two matrices $\pm S$ give the same $\Lambda$
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.2.1, eqs. (1.59)-(1.61)]. We write $\mathrm{Spin}(n) = \mathrm{Spin}(n, 0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the plane the spin group is a circle that wraps twice around the rotation circle. The first example computes the
spinor matrix of a rotation, which is the formula of @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eq. (3.45)].

::: {#exm-spd-spin-two}
#### $\mathrm{Spin}(2)$

The product of the unit vectors $u_1 = e_1$ and $u_2 = \cos\tfrac\varphi2\,e_1 + \sin\tfrac\varphi2\,e_2$ is $S(\varphi)
= \cos\tfrac\varphi2 + \sin\tfrac\varphi2\,e_1e_2 = \exp(\tfrac\varphi2e_1e_2)$. With $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 =
\sigma_2$, $e_1e_2 \mapsto i\sigma_3$ and $S(\varphi) = e^{i\varphi\sigma_3/2}$; then $S^{-1}\sigma_1S = \cos\varphi\,
\sigma_1 + \sin\varphi\,\sigma_2$, a rotation by $\varphi$. So $\mathrm{Spin}(2) \cong U(1)$ and $\rho$ is $z \mapsto
z^2$: the spinor components have charges $\pm\tfrac12$ under rotations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In three dimensions the spin group is $SU(2)$, the double cover studied in @exm-iso-double-cover. The second example
writes the spinor matrix of a rotation about an arbitrary axis.

::: {#exm-spd-spin-three}
#### $\mathrm{Spin}(3) = SU(2)$

The even products of unit vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$, represented by Pauli matrices, are $S = \cos\tfrac\varphi2 -
i\sin\tfrac\varphi2\,n\cdot\sigma = \exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}\varphi\,n\cdot\sigma)$ for unit vectors $n$, the matrices of
$SU(2)$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 4.1.3]. $S$ covers the rotation by $\varphi$ about $n$ (@fig-sd-spinor-rotation
for $n = e_3$), and the rotation by $2\pi$ is covered by $S = -1$: $\mathrm{Spin}(3) \to SO(3)$ is the double cover of
@def-covering-homomorphism.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For the Lorentz group the spin transformations are no longer unitary, and boosts are covered by hyperbolic functions of
half the rapidity. The third example finds the group $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ in the Weyl representation.

::: {#exm-spd-spin-lorentz}
#### $\mathrm{Spin}(1, 3)$ and $SL(2, \mathbb{C})$

In the Weyl representation $\gamma^0\gamma^1 = \operatorname{diag}(-\sigma_1, \sigma_1)$, so $S = \exp(-\tfrac12\phi
\gamma^0\gamma^1) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{\phi\sigma_1/2}, e^{-\phi\sigma_1/2})$, and $S^{-1}\gamma^0S = \cosh\phi\,
\gamma^0 - \sinh\phi\,\gamma^1$: a boost of rapidity $\phi$ along $x^1$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 3.1.3]. In
general the identity component of $\mathrm{Spin}(1, 3)$ consists of the matrices $\operatorname{diag}(M, (M^\dagger)^{-1})$
with $M \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$; the blocks act on the two chiralities of @exm-spd-gamma-five.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The sign $S(2\pi) = -1$ is the defining property of spinors. The first exercise checks it on the generators of
rotations in every plane of $\mathbb{R}^4$.

::: {#exr-spd-four-pi}
#### Rotations by $2\pi$

With Sage, for the Euclidean gamma matrices of $\mathbb{R}^4$ and each pair $a < b$, compute $S(\varphi) =
\exp(\tfrac\varphi2\gamma^a\gamma^b)$ at $\varphi = 2\pi$ and $\varphi = 4\pi$, and the rotation $\Lambda(\varphi)$
defined by $S^{-1}\gamma^cS = \Lambda^c{}_d\gamma^d$ at $\varphi = 2\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\gamma^a\gamma^b)^2 = -1$, so $S(\varphi) = \cos\tfrac\varphi2 + \sin\tfrac\varphi2\gamma^a\gamma^b$: $S(2\pi) = -1$,
$S(4\pi) = 1$, while $\Lambda(2\pi) = 1$ for all six planes:

{{< sage exr-spd-four-pi >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

That $\rho(S)$ preserves the metric follows from the Clifford relation alone. The second exercise proves it, first for
a single unit vector, where conjugation is a reflection.

::: {#exr-spd-reflections}
#### Products of reflections

For a unit vector $u$, show that $v \mapsto -uvu^{-1}$ is the reflection in the hyperplane orthogonal to $u$:
$-uvu^{-1} = v - 2\frac{\eta(u, v)}{\eta(u, u)}u$. Deduce that $\rho(u_1u_2\cdots u_{2k})$ is a product of $2k$
reflections, hence in $SO(p, q)$, and that $\rho(-S) = \rho(S)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u^{-1} = u/\eta(u, u)$ and $uv = 2\eta(u, v) - vu$, so $-uvu^{-1} = -(2\eta(u, v) - vu)u/\eta(u, u) = v - 2\eta(u,
v)u/\eta(u, u)$, which fixes $u^\perp$ and sends $u$ to $-u$. Conjugation by $u_1\cdots u_{2k}$ is the composition of the
conjugations by the $u_i$, and the $2k$ signs cancel, so it is a product of an even number of reflections, an element
of $O(p, q)$ with determinant $+1$. Conjugation by $-S$ equals conjugation by $S$ @trautman1995 [eq. (2)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four Euclidean dimensions the spin group splits into two commuting copies of $SU(2)$, one for each chirality. The
third exercise exhibits the splitting with explicit matrices.

::: {#exr-spd-spin-four}
#### $\mathrm{Spin}(4) = SU(2) \times SU(2)$

With the Euclidean gamma matrices of @exm-spd-gammas-four and $\Sigma^{ab} = \tfrac14[\gamma^a, \gamma^b]$, define
$J^\pm_1 = -\tfrac{i}{2}(\Sigma^{23} \pm \Sigma^{14})$ and cyclically. With Sage, show that $[J^\pm_a, J^\pm_b] =
i\epsilon_{abc}J^\pm_c$, $[J^+_a, J^-_b] = 0$, and that $J^+$ acts only on one chirality and $J^-$ only on the other.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two triples close on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and commute; each annihilates one eigenspace of $\gamma_*$ and acts on the
other as spin $\tfrac12$, so the Dirac spinor of $\mathbb{R}^4$ is $(\tfrac12, 0) \oplus (0, \tfrac12)$:

{{< sage exr-spd-spin-four >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Near the identity a spin transformation is determined by the quadratic elements $\gamma^a\gamma^b$. The proposition
gives the commutation relations that make them a representation of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(p, q)$, and the
exponential that integrates them; for $(1, 3)$ it is @def-lorentz-generators of Part II.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-spin-lie-algebra}
#### The spinor generators

The matrices $\Sigma^{ab} = \tfrac14[\gamma^a, \gamma^b]$ satisfy
$$
[\Sigma^{ab}, \gamma^c] = \eta^{bc}\gamma^a - \eta^{ac}\gamma^b, \qquad [\Sigma^{ab}, \Sigma^{cd}] =
\eta^{bc}\Sigma^{ad} - \eta^{ac}\Sigma^{bd} - \eta^{bd}\Sigma^{ac} + \eta^{ad}\Sigma^{bc},
$$ {#eq-spd-sigma-algebra}
so they represent $\mathfrak{so}(p, q)$. For real antisymmetric $\omega_{ab}$, $S = \exp(\tfrac12\omega_{ab}\Sigma^{ab})
\in \mathrm{Spin}(p, q)$ and $S^{-1}\gamma^aS = \Lambda^a{}_b\gamma^b$ with $\Lambda = \exp(\omega)$, $\omega$ the matrix
$(\omega^a{}_b)$; infinitesimally $S = 1 + \tfrac14\delta\omega_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs.
(1.66)-(1.69), (3.44)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In three dimensions the generators are multiples of Pauli matrices. The first example relates them to the generators
$T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ of the book's conventions (@sec-conventions-lie).

::: {#exm-spd-so3-generators}
#### Rotations in three dimensions

For $\gamma^a = \sigma_a$, $\Sigma^{ab} = \tfrac14[\sigma_a, \sigma_b] = \tfrac{i}{2}\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c =
-\epsilon_{abc}T_c$. The rotation by $\varphi$ about $e_3$ has $\omega_{12} = -\omega_{21} = \varphi$, so that $\Lambda = e^\omega$ has
$\Lambda^1{}_1 = \cos\varphi$, $\Lambda^1{}_2 = \sin\varphi$, and
$S = \exp(\varphi\Sigma^{12}) = \exp(\tfrac{i}{2}\varphi\sigma_3)$, the matrix of @exm-spd-spin-two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.
