The number of independent generators is the dimension of the rotation algebra. The second example lists it for the
dimensions the book uses and compares with the size of the spinor.

::: {#exm-spd-generator-count}
#### Counting generators

$\mathfrak{so}(p, q)$ has dimension $d(d - 1)/2$: $3$ for $d = 3$, $6$ for $d = 4$, $15$ for $d = 6$, $45$ for $d =
10$, $55$ for $d = 11$. The $\Sigma^{ab}$ are linearly independent (they are distinct basis elements $\tfrac12\gamma_{\{a,
b\}}$ of @prp-clifford-basis), so the spinor representation is faithful on the Lie algebra, although $2^{\lfloor
d/2\rfloor}$ grows much faster than $d(d - 1)/2$: for $d = 11$, $55$ generators act on $\mathbb{C}^{32}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Lorentz boosts and rotations of Part II are the cases $(a, b) = (0, k)$ and $(j, k)$. The third example identifies
them in the Weyl representation, where they are block diagonal.

::: {#exm-spd-lorentz-blocks}
#### Boosts and rotations on Weyl spinors

In the Weyl representation $\Sigma^{jk} = -\tfrac{i}{2}\epsilon_{jkl}\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_l, \sigma_l)$ and
$\Sigma^{0k} = \tfrac12\gamma^0\gamma^k = -\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_k, -\sigma_k)$. Rotations act in the same way on both chiralities, boosts with opposite signs: with $\beta_k = \omega_{0k}$ and
$\theta_l = \tfrac12\epsilon_{jkl}\omega_{jk}$, the left-handed spinor transforms with $M = \exp(-\tfrac12\beta\cdot\sigma -
\tfrac{i}{2}\theta\cdot\sigma)$ and the right-handed one with $\exp(\tfrac12\beta\cdot\sigma - \tfrac{i}{2}\theta\cdot\sigma)
= (M^\dagger)^{-1}$, the two inequivalent representations
$(\tfrac12, 0)$ and $(0, \tfrac12)$ of $\mathfrak{so}(1, 3)_{\mathbb{C}} \cong \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C}) \oplus
\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{C})$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first relation in @eq-spd-sigma-algebra says that the gamma matrices transform as a vector. The first exercise
derives it from the Clifford relation.

::: {#exr-spd-sigma-gamma}
#### The gamma matrices are a vector

Derive $[\gamma^a\gamma^b, \gamma^c] = 2\eta^{bc}\gamma^a - 2\eta^{ac}\gamma^b$ from @eq-spd-gamma-relation, and deduce
the first relation in @eq-spd-sigma-algebra. Then use it, together with $\Sigma^{cd} = \tfrac14[\gamma^c, \gamma^d]$, to
obtain the second.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma^c = \gamma^a(2\eta^{bc} - \gamma^c\gamma^b) = 2\eta^{bc}\gamma^a - (2\eta^{ac} -
\gamma^c\gamma^a)\gamma^b$, so $[\gamma^a\gamma^b, \gamma^c] = 2\eta^{bc}\gamma^a - 2\eta^{ac}\gamma^b$. For $a \neq b$,
$\Sigma^{ab} = \tfrac12\gamma^a\gamma^b$, which gives the first relation (both sides vanish for $a = b$). For the second,
$[\Sigma^{ab}, \gamma^c\gamma^d] = [\Sigma^{ab}, \gamma^c]\gamma^d + \gamma^c[\Sigma^{ab}, \gamma^d]$; inserting the first
relation and antisymmetrising in $c, d$ gives the four terms.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The commutation relations can be checked by brute force in any dimension. The second exercise does so in five
dimensions, where the spinor has four components.

::: {#exr-spd-sigma-commutators}
#### Checking the algebra

With Sage, build the Euclidean gamma matrices for $d = 5$ and verify both relations of @eq-spd-sigma-algebra for all
indices. How many independent matrices $\Sigma^{ab}$ are there, and what Lie algebra of $4 \times 4$ matrices do they
span?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both relations hold for all $5^3$ and $5^4$ index combinations. The ten $\Sigma^{ab}$ are independent anti-Hermitian
traceless $4 \times 4$ matrices closing under commutators: they span $\mathfrak{so}(5) \cong \mathfrak{sp}(2)$, a
ten-dimensional subalgebra of $\mathfrak{su}(4)$:

{{< sage exr-spd-sigma-commutators >}}
:::

The relation $\Lambda = \exp(\omega)$ can be tested on a random element of the algebra. The third exercise does this in
three dimensions, recovering the rotation matrix from the spinor matrix by traces.

::: {#exr-spd-lambda-from-s}
#### The rotation from the spinor matrix

For a random real antisymmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix $\omega$, compute $S = \exp(\tfrac12\omega_{ab}\Sigma^{ab})$ with
$\gamma^a = \sigma_a$, then $\Lambda^a{}_b = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}\sigma_aS\sigma_b)$, and compare with the
matrix exponential $\exp(\omega)$ (indices lowered with $\delta$). Check that $\Lambda$ is orthogonal with determinant
$1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace formula uses $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\sigma_b) = \delta_{ab}$, and the two matrices agree to machine
precision:

{{< sage exr-spd-lambda-from-s >}}
:::

### Dirac, Weyl and Majorana spinors

The gamma matrices restricted to the spin group give the Dirac spinor representation. In even dimension it splits into
two halves, labelled by the eigenvalue of the chirality matrix, and the figure shows the weights of the two halves for
$\mathrm{Spin}(4)$ and $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$.

![The weights $(h_1, \dots, h_\nu)$ of the Dirac spinor of $\mathrm{Spin}(2\nu)$, the eigenvalues of the commuting
generators $h_k = -i\Sigma^{2k - 1, 2k}$, which are diagonal for the matrices @eq-spd-tensor-gammas. All $2^\nu$
combinations $(\pm\tfrac12, \dots, \pm\tfrac12)$ occur once; the colour is the chirality $\gamma_* = (-1)^\nu\prod_k2h_k$.
Left: $\mathrm{Spin}(4)$, whose two Weyl spinors are the doublets of the two factors $SU(2)$. Right: $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$,
in an oblique projection of the cube of weights; each chirality has four weights, those of the representations
$\mathbf{4}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{4}}$ of $SU(4)$. Generated by `figures/sd-weyl-weights.sage`.](figures/sd-weyl-weights.svg){#fig-sd-weyl-weights width=78%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weyl-representation}
#### Weyl spinor

The **Dirac representation** of $\mathrm{Spin}(p, q)$ is $S \mapsto S$ on $\mathbb{C}^N$, for irreducible gamma
matrices. For even $d$ the generators $\Sigma^{ab}$ commute with $\gamma_*$, so the eigenspaces $S_\pm = \{\psi :
\gamma_*\psi = \pm\psi\}$, of dimension $N/2$, are invariant; the representations on $S_+$ and $S_-$ are the two
**Weyl representations** (semispinor representations), and a **Weyl spinor** is an element of $S_+$ or $S_-$
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 1.5], @trautman1995 [Prop. 2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions the Weyl spinors are the two components of a Dirac spinor. The first example finds their charges
under $\mathrm{Spin}(2) = U(1)$, which return when spinors are put on the sphere.

::: {#exm-spd-weyl-two}
#### Two dimensions

With $\gamma_* = -\sigma_3$ (@exm-spd-chirality-two) the Weyl spinors are $(0, \psi_2)$ ($\gamma_* = +1$) and $(\psi_1,
0)$ ($\gamma_* = -1$). The rotation $S(\varphi) = e^{i\varphi\sigma_3/2}$ of @exm-spd-spin-two multiplies them by
$e^{-i\varphi/2}$ and $e^{i\varphi/2}$: the two Weyl representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(2) = U(1)$ have charges
$\mp\tfrac12$, and they are complex conjugate to each other.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four Lorentzian dimensions the Weyl spinors are the left- and right-handed two-component spinors of the standard
model. The second example identifies the two representations.

::: {#exm-spd-weyl-four}
#### Left- and right-handed spinors

In the Weyl representation $\gamma_5 = \operatorname{diag}(-1, -1, 1, 1)$, so a Dirac spinor is $\psi = (\psi_L,
\psi_R)$ with $\gamma_5\psi_L = -\psi_L$, $\gamma_5\psi_R = \psi_R$. By @exm-spd-spin-lorentz, $\psi_L \mapsto M\psi_L$
and $\psi_R \mapsto (M^\dagger)^{-1}\psi_R$, $M \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$: the representations $(\tfrac12, 0)$ and $(0,
\tfrac12)$, of complex dimension $2$ each.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In ten dimensions the Weyl and Majorana conditions combine (@thm-majorana-classification). The third example counts the real components that remain after both conditions.

::: {#exm-spd-weyl-ten}
#### Ten dimensions

For $(1, 9)$, $N = 32$ and the Weyl representations $\mathbf{16}$ and $\mathbf{16}'$ have complex dimension $16$. Since
$p - q = -8 \equiv 0 \pmod 8$, each admits a Majorana condition, and a Majorana-Weyl spinor has $16$ real components:
the supercharge of ten-dimensional supersymmetry with $16$ real components. Theories with two Majorana-Weyl
supercharges of the same or of opposite chirality are the two maximal supersymmetries of ten dimensions
@vanproeyen1999 [Table 3].
:::

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The invariance of the Weyl subspaces rests on one commutation. The first exercise proves it and its consequence for the
Dirac operator of later parts.

::: {#exr-spd-weyl-invariant}
#### Invariance of the Weyl subspaces

Show that $\gamma_*$ commutes with every $\Sigma^{ab}$ and with every $S \in \mathrm{Spin}(p, q)$ for even $d$, so that
$P_\pm S = SP_\pm$. Show that a single $\gamma^a$ maps $S_+$ to $S_-$, so an operator of the form $\gamma^a\partial_a$
exchanges the chiralities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Sigma^{ab}$ is a product of two gamma matrices, and $\gamma_*$ anticommutes with each, so it commutes with the product
(@exr-spd-chirality-properties); the same holds for any even product of unit vectors, hence for $S$. $\gamma^aP_\pm =
P_\mp\gamma^a$ (@exr-spd-weyl-projectors) shows that $\gamma^a$ maps $S_\pm$ to $S_\mp$, and so does
$\gamma^a\partial_a$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The weights of @fig-sd-weyl-weights can be read off in any even dimension. The second exercise computes them and checks
the rule that relates them to chirality.

::: {#exr-spd-weights-chirality}
#### Weights and chirality

With Sage, for $\nu = 2, 3, 4, 5$ list the diagonal entries of $h_k = -i\Sigma^{2k - 1, 2k}$ and of $\gamma_*$ in the
standard Euclidean matrices of dimension $2\nu$, and check that $\gamma_* = (-1)^\nu\prod_k2h_k$. How many weights of
each chirality are there?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$h_k$ is $\tfrac12\sigma_3$ in the $k$th factor (up to the sign of $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = i\sigma_3$), so the weights are
all sign choices, and $\gamma_* = (-\sigma_3)^{\otimes\nu}$ (@exm-spd-chirality-tensor) gives the product rule; each
chirality has $2^{\nu - 1}$ weights, those with an even (for $\gamma_* = +1$) or odd number of entries $+\tfrac12$:

{{< sage exr-spd-weights-chirality >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The half-integral weights distinguish spinors from tensors, all of whose weights are integers. The third exercise uses
this to show that no tensor representation contains a spinor.

::: {#exr-spd-spinors-not-tensors}
#### Spinors are not tensors

Show that the weights of the vector representation of $\mathfrak{so}(2\nu)$ are $\pm\epsilon_k$ (one entry $\pm1$, the
others $0$) and that the weights of a tensor product of vectors are integral. Deduce that the Dirac spinor, whose
weights are half-integral, is not contained in any tensor representation, and that $-1 \in \mathrm{Spin}(2\nu)$, which
acts as $-1$ on spinors, acts as $+1$ on every tensor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $\mathbb{C}^{2\nu}$ the rotation generator in the plane $(2k - 1, 2k)$ has eigenvalues $\pm i$ on $e_{2k - 1} \mp
ie_{2k}$ and $0$ on the other directions, so the weights are $\pm\epsilon_k$. Weights add under tensor products, so
tensors have integral weights, while spinor weights $(\pm\tfrac12, \dots)$ are not integral. The element $-1 =
\exp(2\pi\Sigma^{12})$ acts as $e^{2\pi ih_1}$, which is $-1$ on half-integral and $+1$ on integral weights.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Complex conjugation of spinors either preserves or exchanges the two Weyl representations, depending on the signature.
The proposition states the rule, which is the computation of @exr-spd-mw-condition read as a statement about
representations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-weyl-conjugation}
#### Conjugation of Weyl spinors

Let $d$ be even and $B$ as in @def-majorana-condition. Then $\psi \mapsto B^{-1}\psi^*$ commutes with the action of
$\mathrm{Spin}(p, q)$ and maps $S_\pm$ to $S_{\pm(-1)^{(p - q)/2}}$. Hence for $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ each Weyl
representation is equivalent to its complex conjugate (real for $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod 8$, pseudoreal for $p - q \equiv
4$), and for $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ the two Weyl representations are complex conjugates of each other @vanproeyen1999
[eq. (3.28) and the paragraph before it].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In four Lorentzian dimensions $p - q = -2$, and the conjugate of a left-handed spinor is right-handed. The first example
uses this to write a Majorana spinor in terms of a single Weyl spinor.

::: {#exm-spd-conjugate-four}
#### Left and right are conjugate

For $(1, 3)$, $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, so the conjugate of $\psi_L$ transforms like $\psi_R$: explicitly
$\sigma_2M^*\sigma_2 = (M^\dagger)^{-1}$ for $M \in SL(2, \mathbb{C})$ (take the complex conjugate of $\sigma_2M^T\sigma_2
= M^{-1}$ and invert). Hence $\psi = (\chi, \sigma_2\chi^*)$ is a Dirac spinor built from one left-handed $\chi$, and it
satisfies $\psi^* = \gamma^2\psi$, the Majorana condition with $B = \gamma^2$, $s = -1$, $B^*B = 1$: four real components,
as in @exm-spd-majorana-four.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four Euclidean dimensions $p - q = 4$ and each Weyl representation is pseudoreal. The second example identifies it
with the doublet of $SU(2)$.

::: {#exm-spd-conjugate-euclid-four}
#### Pseudoreal doublets

For $(4, 0)$ the Weyl representations are the doublets of the two factors of $\mathrm{Spin}(4) = SU(2) \times SU(2)$
(@exr-spd-spin-four). The doublet is equivalent to its conjugate, $\sigma_2U^*\sigma_2 = U$ for $U \in SU(2)$, but there
is no basis in which $U$ is real: the structure map $\psi \mapsto \sigma_2\psi^*$ squares to $-1$. This is the
symplectic Majorana-Weyl case $r = 4$ of @thm-majorana-classification.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In six Euclidean dimensions $p - q = 6 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and the two Weyl spinors are conjugate to each other. The
third example identifies them with the fundamental and antifundamental of $SU(4)$.

::: {#exm-spd-conjugate-six}
#### $\mathrm{Spin}(6) = SU(4)$

The Weyl representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$ have dimension $4$. Their weights (@fig-sd-weyl-weights, right) are
exchanged by $h \mapsto -h$, which is complex conjugation, so $S_- \cong \overline{S_+}$. The fifteen generators
$\Sigma^{ab}$ restricted to $S_+$ span $\mathfrak{su}(4)$ (@exr-spd-six-su4), and $S_\pm$ are the $\mathbf{4}$ and
$\bar{\mathbf{4}}$ of $SU(4) \cong \mathrm{Spin}(6)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition can be checked with the matrices $B$ of @exr-spd-bb-sign. The first exercise does so in all even
dimensions up to ten.

::: {#exr-spd-conjugation-check}
#### Which chirality is conjugate

With Sage, for the standard gamma matrices of signatures $(d, 0)$ and $(1, d - 1)$, $d = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10$, take a matrix
$B$ with $(\gamma^a)^* = \pm B\gamma^aB^{-1}$ and test whether $B\gamma_*B^{-1}$ equals $+\gamma_*^*$ or $-\gamma_*^*$.
Compare with $(-1)^{(p - q)/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The sign is $(-1)^{(p - q)/2}$ in every case: conjugation preserves chirality in Euclidean dimensions $4, 8$ and
Lorentzian dimensions $2, 6, 10$, and exchanges it otherwise:

{{< sage exr-spd-conjugation-check >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The formula $\psi = (\chi, -i\sigma_2\chi^*)$ was asserted without checking the Majorana condition. The second exercise
verifies it in the Weyl representation.

::: {#exr-spd-majorana-from-weyl}
#### A Majorana spinor from a Weyl spinor

In the Weyl representation show that $B = \gamma^2$ satisfies $(\gamma^\mu)^* = -B\gamma^\mu B^{-1}$ and $B^*B = 1$, and
that $\psi = (\chi, \sigma_2\chi^*)$ satisfies $\psi^* = B\psi$ for every two-component $\chi$. Show that every Majorana
spinor has this form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the Weyl representation $\gamma^0, \gamma^1, \gamma^3$ are real and $\gamma^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma_2 \\
-\sigma_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is imaginary. $\gamma^2$ commutes with itself and anticommutes with the others, so
$-\gamma^2\gamma^\mu(\gamma^2)^{-1}$ is $-\gamma^2 = (\gamma^2)^*$ for $\mu = 2$ and $\gamma^\mu = (\gamma^\mu)^*$ otherwise;
$B^*B = (\gamma^2)^*\gamma^2 = -(\gamma^2)^2 = 1$. For $\psi = (\chi, \xi)$, $B\psi = (\sigma_2\xi, -\sigma_2\chi)$, so
$\psi^* = B\psi$ means $\chi^* = \sigma_2\xi$ and $\xi^* = -\sigma_2\chi$; the first gives $\xi = \sigma_2\chi^*$, and then
the second holds automatically because $\sigma_2^* = -\sigma_2$. So the Majorana spinors are exactly the $(\chi,
\sigma_2\chi^*)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Six Euclidean dimensions give the identification of $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$ with $SU(4)$. The third exercise checks it numerically on the fifteen generators $\Sigma^{ab}$.

::: {#exr-spd-six-su4}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(6) = \mathfrak{su}(4)$

With Sage, restrict the fifteen $\Sigma^{ab}$ of the Euclidean gamma matrices of dimension $6$ to $S_+$ and show that
they are traceless anti-Hermitian $4 \times 4$ matrices spanning a space of real dimension $15$, hence all of
$\mathfrak{su}(4)$. Show that the restrictions to $S_-$ are the complex conjugates up to a change of basis.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The restrictions are anti-Hermitian, traceless and independent over $\mathbb{R}$, fifteen in number, so they fill
$\mathfrak{su}(4)$; on $S_-$ the eigenvalues of each generator are the negatives of those on $S_+$, as for the conjugate
representation:

{{< sage exr-spd-six-su4 >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Decomposition under subgroups

When a space is a product, its spin group contains the product of the spin groups of the factors, and a spinor of the
whole space decomposes into products of spinors of the factors. The proposition gives the decomposition for spacetime
times a Euclidean space of dimension $n$, which is the case of a $d$-dimensional spinor seen from four dimensions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-spinor-branching}
#### Spinors of a product

Let $\gamma^\mu$ be gamma matrices of signature $(1, 3)$ with $\gamma_5$ as in @def-chirality-matrix, and $\gamma^a_K$,
$a = 1, \dots, n$, Euclidean gamma matrices of size $N_K = 2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. Then
$$
\Gamma^\mu = \gamma^\mu \otimes 1, \qquad \Gamma^{3 + a} = i\gamma_5 \otimes \gamma^a_K
$$ {#eq-spd-product-gammas}
are gamma matrices of signature $(1, 3 + n)$ of size $4N_K = 2^{\lfloor D/2\rfloor}$, $D = 4 + n$, and
$\mathrm{Spin}(1, 3) \times \mathrm{Spin}(n)$ acts by $S_4 \otimes S_K$. The Dirac spinor of $D$ dimensions is the tensor
product of the Dirac spinors of the factors; for even $n$, $\Gamma_* = \gamma_5 \otimes \gamma_*^K$, so the Weyl spinor
of positive chirality in $D$ dimensions is $(\psi_R \otimes S_K^+) \oplus (\psi_L \otimes S_K^-)$
@vanproeyen1999 [eqs. (3.3), (3.8)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Six dimensions split as four plus two is the smallest case with chirality on both sides. The first example works it
out with the charges of @exm-spd-weyl-two.

::: {#exm-spd-branch-six}
#### Six as four plus two

For $n = 2$, $\Gamma^M$ have size $8$ and $\Gamma_* = \gamma_5 \otimes \gamma_*^K$ with $\gamma_*^K = -\sigma_3$. A Weyl
spinor of positive chirality in six dimensions is $\psi_R \otimes (0, 1) + \psi_L \otimes (1, 0)$: a right-handed spinor
with $\mathrm{Spin}(2)$ charge $-\tfrac12$ and a left-handed one with charge $+\tfrac12$. Four complex components, which
is the Weyl spinor $\mathbf{4}$ of $SO(1, 5)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Ten as four plus six is the case of ten-dimensional supersymmetry on a six-dimensional space. The second example
combines the proposition with the identification $\mathrm{Spin}(6) = SU(4)$.

::: {#exm-spd-branch-ten}
#### Ten as four plus six

For $n = 6$ the positive-chirality Weyl spinor $\mathbf{16}$ of $SO(1, 9)$ decomposes as $(\psi_R \otimes \mathbf{4})
\oplus (\psi_L \otimes \bar{\mathbf{4}})$, in Lorentz notation $(0, \tfrac12; \mathbf{4}) \oplus (\tfrac12, 0;
\bar{\mathbf{4}})$ of $SL(2, \mathbb{C}) \times SU(4)$. The Majorana-Weyl condition identifies the second summand with the
conjugate of the first, so a Majorana-Weyl spinor of ten dimensions is equivalent to four left-handed Weyl spinors of
four dimensions in the $\bar{\mathbf{4}}$ of $SU(4)$; @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 4.1, eq. (89)] carries out the analogous
decomposition of the ten-dimensional spinor under $\mathfrak{so}(1, 5) \oplus \mathfrak{so}(4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In eleven dimensions the internal space is odd-dimensional and there is no chirality to split. The third example counts
the four-dimensional spinors in an eleven-dimensional one.

::: {#exm-spd-branch-eleven}
#### Eleven as four plus seven

For $n = 7$, $N_K = 8$ and $\Gamma^M$ have size $32$; the spinor is $\mathbf{4} \otimes \mathbf{8}$. The Majorana condition
of eleven dimensions combines the Majorana condition of four dimensions with the reality of the spinor $\mathbf{8}$ of
$\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ (signature $(7, 0)$, $r = 7$), so the $32$ real components form eight four-dimensional Majorana
spinors: eight supercharges, the $\mathcal{N} = 8$ of @exr-spd-supercharges.
:::

The proposition is an explicit statement about matrices, which the first exercise checks numerically. It also checks
the sign of the chirality matrix, which decides which four-dimensional chirality pairs with which internal one.

::: {#exr-spd-branch-check}
#### Checking the product construction

With Sage, build @eq-spd-product-gammas from the Weyl matrices and the Euclidean matrices for $n = 2, 4, 6$, check the
Clifford relations of signature $(1, 3 + n)$, and compare $\Gamma_*$ of @def-chirality-matrix with $\gamma_5 \otimes
\gamma_*^K$.

The relations hold and $\Gamma_* = \gamma_5 \otimes \gamma_*^K$ exactly, without a sign, for all three $n$; the exponent
$m$ of @eq-spd-chirality combines with the factors $i$ of @eq-spd-product-gammas into a multiple of $4$:

{{< sage exr-spd-branch-check >}}

The product gamma matrices split the Dirac operator of the product into a four-dimensional part and an internal part.
The second exercise derives the four-dimensional mass of a mode from the eigenvalue of the internal operator.

::: {#exr-spd-branch-mass}
#### Masses from the internal operator

Let $D_K = i\gamma^a_K\partial_a$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ (or a torus) and $\Psi = \chi(x) \otimes \eta(y)$ with $D_K\eta =
\lambda\eta$. Show that $i\Gamma^M\partial_M\Psi = 0$ becomes $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu + i\lambda\gamma_5)\chi = 0$, and
that $\chi = e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4}\chi'$ turns it into the Dirac equation $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - m)\chi' = 0$ with
$|m| = |\lambda|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$i\Gamma^{3 + a}\partial_a\Psi = i(i\gamma_5\chi) \otimes \gamma^a_K\partial_a\eta = i(i\gamma_5\chi) \otimes (-i\lambda\eta)
= i\lambda\gamma_5\chi \otimes \eta$, using $\gamma^a_K\partial_a\eta = -iD_K\eta$. Since $\gamma_5$ anticommutes with
$\gamma^\mu$, $i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4}\chi' = e^{i\pi\gamma_5/4}i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi'$; multiplying
the equation by $e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4}$ gives $i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi' + i\lambda\gamma_5e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/2}\chi' = 0$,
and $e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/2} = -i\gamma_5$, so the mass term is $i\lambda\gamma_5(-i\gamma_5) = \lambda$: $m = -\lambda$.
Massless four-dimensional spinors come from the zero modes of $D_K$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Chirality in four dimensions is tied to chirality in the internal space by the proposition. The third exercise turns
this into a counting rule for massless chiral spinors, which the index theorems of a later part evaluate.

::: {#exr-spd-branch-chirality-count}
#### Net chirality from the internal space

Let $n$ be even and suppose the internal operator $D_K$ has $n_\pm$ zero modes of chirality $\gamma_*^K = \pm1$. Show
that a $D$-dimensional Weyl spinor of positive chirality gives $n_+$ massless right-handed and $n_-$ massless left-handed
four-dimensional spinors, so the net number of right-handed minus left-handed massless spinors is $n_+ - n_-$. What is it
when $D_K$ anticommutes with $\gamma_*^K$ and is self-adjoint on a space without boundary?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @prp-spinor-branching the Weyl spinor is $(\psi_R \otimes S_K^+) \oplus (\psi_L \otimes S_K^-)$, and by
@exr-spd-branch-mass the massless modes are those with $\lambda = 0$; a zero mode of chirality $+1$ is paired with
$\psi_R$, one of chirality $-1$ with $\psi_L$. Hence $n_R - n_L = n_+ - n_-$. Since $D_K$ exchanges $S_K^+$ and $S_K^-$,
its non-zero eigenvalues pair up across chiralities, and $n_+ - n_-$ is the index of $D_K$ restricted to $S_K^+$
(@def-fredholm-operator): it is not forced to vanish, and computing it is the subject of @sec-dirac-index.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine the spin groups, the Weyl and Majorana representations and the decomposition of
spinors of a product. They prepare the next part, where spinors become fields on curved spaces.

The covering map $\mathrm{Spin}(3) \to SO(3)$ can be written in closed form. The first integrative exercise computes it
and its kernel.

::: {#exr-spd-cover-formula}
#### The covering map in closed form

For $S \in SU(2)$ show that $\Lambda_{ab}(S) = \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(S^{-1}\sigma_aS\sigma_b)$ defines a
homomorphism to $SO(3)$, that its kernel is $\{\pm1\}$, and compute $\Lambda$ for $S = \exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}\varphi\sigma_1)$.
With Sage, check $\Lambda(S_1S_2) = \Lambda(S_1)\Lambda(S_2)$ in the order fixed by the convention $S^{-1}\gamma^aS =
\Lambda^a{}_b\gamma^b$ for random $S_1, S_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S^{-1}\sigma_aS$ is traceless Hermitian, so it is $\Lambda_{ab}\sigma_b$ with real $\Lambda_{ab}$ given by the trace
formula; it preserves $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, so $\Lambda \in O(3)$, and continuity from $S = 1$ gives
$\det\Lambda = 1$. With this convention $(S_1S_2)^{-1}\sigma_a(S_1S_2) = \Lambda(S_1)_{ab}S_2^{-1}\sigma_bS_2 =
(\Lambda(S_1)\Lambda(S_2))_{ac}\sigma_c$. The kernel consists of $S$ commuting with all $\sigma_a$, that is $S = \pm1$
(@exr-spd-commutant); for $S = \exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}\varphi\sigma_1)$, $\Lambda$ is the rotation by $\varphi$ in the
$(2, 3)$ plane:

{{< sage exr-spd-cover-formula >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Five dimensions is the first case of an odd number of internal dimensions over four. The second integrative exercise
decomposes the five-dimensional spinor and its Dirac operator.

::: {#exr-spd-five-four}
#### Five as four plus one

For $n = 1$ the internal gamma matrix is $\gamma^1_K = 1$ and @eq-spd-product-gammas gives $\Gamma^4 = i\gamma_5$. Show
that the Dirac spinor of $(1, 4)$ is a four-dimensional Dirac spinor, that there is no chirality in five dimensions, and
that a mode $e^{iky}\chi(x)$ on a line has four-dimensional mass $|k|$. Which reality condition does the
five-dimensional spinor admit (@exm-spd-symplectic-five)?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Gamma^M$ are $4 \times 4$, the size $2^2$ of five dimensions; $(i\gamma_5)^2 = -1$ and $i\gamma_5$ anticommutes with
$\gamma^\mu$. In odd dimension the product of all $\Gamma^M$ is central (@exr-spd-centre), so there is no chirality
matrix. With $D_K = i\partial_y$, $D_Ke^{iky} = -ke^{iky}$, and @exr-spd-branch-mass gives $|m| = |k|$. The spinor is
symplectic Majorana: $p - q = -3 \equiv 5 \pmod 8$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The weights of a decomposed spinor are sums of weights of the factors. The third integrative exercise uses the weights
of @fig-sd-weyl-weights to redo the decomposition of @exm-spd-branch-ten.

::: {#exr-spd-weights-branching}
#### Branching by weights

The Dirac spinor of $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$ (Euclidean, for simplicity) has weights $(\pm\tfrac12)^5$ and $\gamma_* =
(-1)^5\prod_k2h_k$. Restricting to $\mathrm{Spin}(4) \times \mathrm{Spin}(6)$ (weights $(h_1, h_2)$ and $(h_3, h_4,
h_5)$), show that the sixteen weights of chirality $+1$ are the products of the chirality $\pm$ weights of
$\mathrm{Spin}(4)$ with the chirality $\pm$ weights of $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$, with matching signs, and count them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(-1)^5\prod_{k \leq 5}2h_k = [(-1)^2\prod_{k \leq 2}2h_k][(-1)^3\prod_{3 \leq k \leq 5}2h_k]$, so the chirality of a
weight of $\mathrm{Spin}(10)$ is the product of the chiralities of its two parts. Chirality $+1$ arises from $(+, +)$ or
$(-, -)$: $2 \times 4 + 2 \times 4 = 16$ weights, the decomposition $\mathbf{16} = (\mathbf{2}_+, \mathbf{4}) \oplus
(\mathbf{2}_-, \bar{\mathbf{4}})$, which becomes that of @exm-spd-branch-ten once the first factor is made Lorentzian.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

## Spin structures and the spin connection {#sec-spin-structures}

On a curved manifold a spinor is described in a local orthonormal frame, and its components change by a spin
transformation when the frame is rotated. Because a rotation determines its spin transformation only up to sign, the
signs must be chosen consistently over the whole manifold, and this is possible only when a topological condition
holds. This part defines spin structures following @trautman1995 [Sec. 4.1], computes them on circles, tori and
spheres, constructs the covariant derivative of spinors from the Levi-Civita connection in a frame following
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 2.2-2.3], and describes the spin-c structures that exist on manifolds without a spin
structure, with the complex projective plane as the example of @dolan2003 [Sec. 2]. The frames of @def-frame, the
connections of @sec-connections and the vector bundles of @def-vector-bundle are used throughout.

### Spin structures

On the circle a spinor field can return to itself or to its negative after one turn, and both choices are consistent.
The figure shows the lowest modes of the two kinds of field; the definition below explains in general which choices
exist.

![The two spin structures of the circle. Spinor fields are functions of the angle that are periodic (blue, modes
$e^{ik\theta}$ with $k \in \mathbb{Z}$) or antiperiodic (red, $k \in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac12$); the plot shows real parts
over two turns. The Dirac operator $i\,d/d\theta$ has eigenvalues $-k$, so only the periodic structure has a zero mode.
Generated by `figures/sd-circle-spin-structures.sage`.](figures/sd-circle-spin-structures.svg){#fig-sd-circle-spin-structures width=70%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spin-structure}
#### Spin structure

Let $M$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ and $SO(M) \to M$ the principal $SO(n)$-bundle of oriented
orthonormal frames (@def-principal-bundle). A **spin structure** on $M$ is a principal $\mathrm{Spin}(n)$-bundle
$\mathrm{Spin}(M) \to M$ with a bundle map $\chi : \mathrm{Spin}(M) \to SO(M)$ such that $\chi(qS) = \chi(q)\rho(S)$
for the covering $\rho$ of @eq-spd-spin-sequence. Equivalently, in an atlas of local orthonormal frames with transition
functions $\Lambda_{ij} : U_i \cap U_j \to SO(n)$, it is a choice of lifts $S_{ij}$ with $\rho(S_{ij}) = \Lambda_{ij}$ and
$S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki} = 1$. The **spinor bundle** is the vector bundle $\mathrm{Spin}(M) \times_{\mathrm{Spin}(n)}
\mathbb{C}^N$ (@def-vector-bundle), and a **spinor field** is a section of it @trautman1995 [Sec. 4.1, eqs. (13)-(14)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Flat space has a global frame, so the frame bundle is a product and one lift suffices. The first example records the
consequence: spinor fields on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are just vector-valued functions.

::: {#exm-spd-spin-flat}
#### Euclidean space

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the Cartesian frame $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n$ trivialises $SO(\mathbb{R}^n) = \mathbb{R}^n
\times SO(n)$, and $\mathrm{Spin}(\mathbb{R}^n) = \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathrm{Spin}(n)$ is a spin structure; it is the
only one because $\mathbb{R}^n$ is simply connected. Spinor fields are functions $\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}^N$, and a
rotation of the coordinates acts on them by $\psi(x) \mapsto S\psi(\Lambda^{-1}x)$ with $\rho(S) = \Lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The circle is the simplest manifold with more than one spin structure. The second example finds both, following
@trautman1995 [Sec. 6.1].

::: {#exm-spd-spin-circle}
#### The circle

For $n = 1$, $SO(1)$ is trivial and $\mathrm{Spin}(1) = \{\pm1\}$, so a spin structure on $S^1$ is a double cover of
$S^1$: either the trivial cover $S^1 \times \{\pm1\}$ or the connected cover $S^1 \to S^1$, $z \mapsto z^2$
@trautman1995 [Sec. 6.1]. Spinor fields are correspondingly periodic or antiperiodic functions of the angle
(@fig-sd-circle-spin-structures). The circle as the boundary of the disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$ inherits the connected one
(@exr-spd-circle-bounding).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A torus is a product of circles, and its spin structures are products of the structures of the circles. The third
example counts them.

::: {#exm-spd-spin-torus}
#### Tori

$T^n = \mathbb{R}^n/2\pi\mathbb{Z}^n$ has the global frame $\partial_1, \dots, \partial_n$, and a spin structure is fixed
by a sign $(-1)^{s_i}$, $s_i \in \{0, 1\}$, for each generator of the lattice: spinor fields satisfy $\psi(y + 2\pi e_i)
= (-1)^{s_i}\psi(y)$. There are $2^n$ spin structures: $4$ on $T^2$, labelled $(P, P)$, $(P, A)$, $(A, P)$, $(A, A)$ with
$P$ for periodic and $A$ for antiperiodic. Only $(P, \dots, P)$ admits constant spinor fields.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Spheres of dimension at least two are simply connected, so a spin structure, if it exists, is unique. The fourth example
shows that it exists by restricting the spin structure of the surrounding Euclidean space.

::: {#exm-spd-spin-sphere}
#### Spheres

$S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$, $n \geq 2$: an oriented frame of $S^n$ together with the outward normal is an oriented
frame of $\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$, which embeds $SO(S^n)$ into $S^n \times SO(n + 1)$; the preimage in $S^n \times
\mathrm{Spin}(n + 1)$ is a spin structure, and the spinor bundle is trivial, $S^n \times \mathbb{C}^{N}$ with the spinors of
$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$ or half of them @trautman1995 [Sec. 6, Prop. 5]. It is the only one since $S^n$ is simply
connected.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The bounding spin structure of the circle comes from the rotation of the tangent frame as one goes round. The first
exercise computes the sign that this rotation produces on spinors.

::: {#exr-spd-circle-bounding}
#### The circle bounds the disc

Along the unit circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$ the frame (tangent, normal) at angle $\theta$ is the Cartesian frame rotated by
$\theta$. Using @exm-spd-spin-two, show that the components of a constant spinor of $\mathbb{R}^2$ in this frame are
$e^{\pm i\theta\sigma_3/2}\psi_0$ and conclude that the induced spin structure on the circle is the antiperiodic one.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rotating frame is $\Lambda(\theta)$ applied to the Cartesian one, and the spinor transformation covering it is
$S(\theta) = e^{i\theta\sigma_3/2}$ (with one choice of sign convention for components, $e^{-i\theta\sigma_3/2}$ with the
other). Components of a fixed spinor in the rotated frame are $S(\theta)^{\mp1}\psi_0$, which at $\theta = 2\pi$ are
$-\psi_0$: the restriction of the spin structure of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the connected double cover, as @trautman1995 [Sec.
6.1] states for immersions $z \mapsto z^n$ with $n$ odd.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Two spin structures differ by a sign attached to each closed loop, multiplicatively. The second exercise turns this into
the count $2^n$ for tori and into a general statement.

::: {#exr-spd-spin-difference}
#### Differences of spin structures

Let $\{S_{ij}\}$ and $\{S'_{ij}\}$ be two systems of lifts of the same $\Lambda_{ij}$. Show that $\epsilon_{ij} =
S'_{ij}S_{ij}^{-1} \in \{\pm1\}$ satisfies $\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{jk}\epsilon_{ki} = 1$, and that the structures are
equivalent iff $\epsilon_{ij} = \delta_i\delta_j$ for signs $\delta_i$. For $M = T^n$, identify $\epsilon$ with the signs
$(-1)^{s_i}$ of @exm-spd-spin-torus.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\rho(S'_{ij}) = \rho(S_{ij})$, so $\epsilon_{ij}$ is in the kernel $\{\pm1\}$, which is central, and the two cocycle
conditions give $\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{jk}\epsilon_{ki} = S'_{ij}S'_{jk}S'_{ki}(S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki})^{-1} = 1$. Changing the
local lifts of the frames by signs $\delta_i$ changes $S_{ij}$ to $\delta_iS_{ij}\delta_j$. So spin structures differ by
$\mathbb{Z}_2$-valued cocycles modulo coboundaries, the group $H^1(M; \mathbb{Z}_2)$, which assigns a sign to each closed
loop; for $T^n$ it is $\mathbb{Z}_2^n$, one sign per circle, the $(-1)^{s_i}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Real projective spaces are the simplest manifolds where the count of spin structures is neither one nor a power of two
times one. The third exercise reads off the answers of @trautman1995 [Sec. 4.3] and checks them against the
classification of the previous exercise.

::: {#exr-spd-projective}
#### Real projective spaces

@trautman1995 [Sec. 4.3] shows that $\mathbb{R}P^{4k + 1}$ has no spin structure and $\mathbb{R}P^{4k - 1}$ has two.
Using $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}P^m) = \mathbb{Z}_2$ (so $H^1(\mathbb{R}P^m; \mathbb{Z}_2) = \mathbb{Z}_2$), explain why the count
is two whenever it is not zero. Which of $\mathbb{R}P^3$, $\mathbb{R}P^5$, $\mathbb{R}P^7$ admit spin structures, and how
many?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-spd-spin-difference, once one spin structure exists the others are in bijection with $H^1(\mathbb{R}P^m;
\mathbb{Z}_2) = \mathbb{Z}_2$: exactly two. $\mathbb{R}P^3$ ($4k - 1$ with $k = 1$) and $\mathbb{R}P^7$ ($k = 2$) have two
each; $\mathbb{R}P^5$ ($4k + 1$ with $k = 1$) has none. Since $\mathbb{R}P^3 = SO(3)$ is a Lie group, it also has the
spin structure induced by a left-invariant frame, one of the two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The cocycle condition $S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki} = 1$ may fail for every choice of lifts. The theorem names the obstruction,
a cohomology class built from the transition functions of the frame bundle; @trautman1995 [Sec. 4.1, Sec. 6.1] uses it
through the Stiefel-Whitney classes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-spin-obstruction}
#### Existence of spin structures

An oriented Riemannian manifold $M$ admits a spin structure if and only if its second Stiefel-Whitney class $w_2(M) \in
H^2(M; \mathbb{Z}_2)$, the class of the $\pm1$-valued cocycle $S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki}$ for arbitrary lifts, vanishes. The
spin structures of a spin manifold are then in bijection with $H^1(M; \mathbb{Z}_2)$. For a complex manifold $w_2$ is
the reduction modulo $2$ of the first Chern class $c_1$ @trautman1995 [Sec. 4.1 and Sec. 6.1], @dolan2003 [Sec. 2,
example iii].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Surfaces are the first test. The first example shows that every closed oriented surface is spin and counts its spin
structures.

::: {#exm-spd-surfaces-spin}
#### Surfaces

A closed oriented surface $\Sigma_g$ of genus $g$ is a complex curve with $c_1 = \chi(\Sigma_g) = 2 - 2g$ times the
generator, an even number, so $w_2 = 0$: every closed oriented surface is spin. $H^1(\Sigma_g; \mathbb{Z}_2) =
\mathbb{Z}_2^{2g}$, so there are $2^{2g}$ spin structures: one on $S^2$, four on $T^2$ (@exm-spd-spin-torus), sixteen on a
surface of genus two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The complex projective plane is the standard example of a manifold without a spin structure. The second example shows
this from its first Chern class.

::: {#exm-spd-cp2-not-spin}
#### $CP^2$ is not spin

The total Chern class of $CP^m$ is $c(TCP^m) = (1 + x)^{m + 1}$ with $x$ the generator of $H^2(CP^m; \mathbb{Z})$
@aspinwall1996 [eq. (10)], so $c_1 = (m + 1)x$. For $CP^2$, $c_1 = 3x$ and $w_2 = x \bmod 2 \neq 0$: $CP^2$ has no spin
structure, although it is a compact simply connected Kähler manifold @dolan2003 [Sec. 2, example iii]. $CP^1 = S^2$
($c_1 = 2x$) and $CP^3$ ($c_1 = 4x$) are spin.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Calabi-Yau manifolds have vanishing first Chern class by definition. The third example concludes that they are spin, a
fact used when their parallel spinors are counted.

::: {#exm-spd-calabi-yau-spin}
#### Calabi-Yau manifolds and $K3$

A Calabi-Yau manifold is a compact Kähler manifold with $c_1 = 0$ (@greene1997 [Sec. 2.11]), so $w_2 = 0$ and it is
spin. The $K3$ surface is simply connected @aspinwall1996 [eq. (13)], so its spin structure is unique; the quintic
threefold in $CP^4$ is simply connected as well and also has a unique spin structure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first Chern class of $CP^m$ decides its spin structure for every $m$. The first exercise works out the pattern.

::: {#exr-spd-cpn-spin}
#### Which $CP^m$ are spin

Using $c_1(CP^m) = (m + 1)x$, show that $CP^m$ is spin if and only if $m$ is odd. For the spin cases, how many spin
structures are there?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$w_2 = (m + 1)x \bmod 2$ vanishes iff $m + 1$ is even. $CP^m$ is simply connected, so $H^1(CP^m; \mathbb{Z}_2) = 0$ and
the spin structure of $CP^1, CP^3, CP^5, \dots$ is unique by @thm-spin-obstruction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Spin structures behave well under products. The second exercise shows this and counts the spin structures of products
of spheres and tori.

::: {#exr-spd-products-spin}
#### Products

Show that $M \times N$ is spin when $M$ and $N$ are, using $SO(M \times N) \supset SO(M) \times SO(N)$ and the
homomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(m) \times \mathrm{Spin}(n) \to \mathrm{Spin}(m + n)$ given by @prp-spinor-branching. How many
spin structures do $S^2 \times T^2$, $S^3 \times S^1$ and $T^6$ have?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Lifts $S^M_{ij}$ and $S^N_{ij}$ with trivial cocycles give lifts $S^M_{ij} \otimes S^N_{ij}$ of the product frames,
again with trivial cocycle (the product map sends $(-1, -1)$ to $1$, so the construction is consistent). $H^1$ of a product
of connected spaces is $H^1(M) \oplus H^1(N)$ here: $S^2 \times T^2$ has $2^2 = 4$, $S^3 \times S^1$ has $2$, $T^6$ has
$2^6 = 64$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second Stiefel-Whitney class of a surface can also be computed from the Euler characteristic directly. The third
exercise checks @exm-spd-surfaces-spin on the sphere with the cocycle of two hemispheres.

::: {#exr-spd-sphere-cocycle}
#### The sphere from two hemispheres

Cover $S^2$ by the two hemispheres with the frames obtained by stereographic projection. The transition function on the equator is a rotation by $2\theta$ at the point of angle $\theta$ (the tangent bundle
of $S^2$ has clutching function of winding number $\chi(S^2) = 2$), a loop of winding number $2$ in $SO(2)$. Show that it lifts to a loop in $\mathrm{Spin}(2)$, so that $S_{12}S_{21} = 1$ can be arranged, and that a
winding number $1$ would not lift.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under $\rho : z \mapsto z^2$ (@exm-spd-spin-two), the loop $e^{2i\theta}$ in $SO(2) = U(1)$ lifts to the closed loop
$e^{i\theta}$, $0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi$, while $e^{i\theta}$ lifts only to the open path $e^{i\theta/2}$, which ends at
$-1$. Hence the transition function of $S^2$ lifts consistently and $w_2(S^2) = 0$; the winding number is the Euler
characteristic $\chi(S^2) = 2$, and the obstruction is its parity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### The spin connection

A spinor field that is constant in Cartesian coordinates has varying components in a rotating frame, and the spin
connection is the correction that makes its covariant derivative vanish. The figure shows the holonomy it produces
around a circle of latitude on the sphere, half the holonomy of vectors.

![Holonomy around the circle of latitude $\theta = \theta_0$ on the unit sphere, which encloses the area $A =
2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$. Vectors come back rotated by $A$ (blue, the cosine of the angle); spinors come back multiplied
by $H = \exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}A\sigma_3)$ (red, $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}H$), the lift of that rotation. At the equator the
vector holonomy is trivial but the spinor holonomy is $-1$. The curve is computed by solving the transport equation of
@exm-spd-sphere-spin-connection numerically. Generated by `figures/sd-spinor-holonomy.sage`.](figures/sd-spinor-holonomy.svg){#fig-sd-spinor-holonomy width=65%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spin-connection}
#### Spin connection

Let $e_a$ be a local orthonormal frame with dual coframe $e^a$, and let $\omega^a{}_b$ be the Levi-Civita connection
one-forms in this frame, $\nabla_Xe_b = \omega^a{}_b(X)e_a$ (the Ricci rotation coefficients of
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 2.2.1, eqs. (2.26), (2.35)]), so that $\omega_{ab} = -\omega_{ba}$ and $de^a +
\omega^a{}_b \wedge e^b = 0$. The **spin connection** is the covariant derivative of spinor fields
$$
\nabla_X\psi = X(\psi) + \tfrac14\omega_{ab}(X)\gamma^a\gamma^b\psi ,
$$ {#eq-spd-spin-connection}
in the frame components $\psi$ of the spinor field @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs. (2.56), (2.68)]. Under a change of
frame $e'_a = e_b\Lambda^b{}_a(x)$ with lift $S(x)$, it transforms covariantly @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eqs. (2.61),
(2.65)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In polar coordinates the flat plane already has a non-zero spin connection, because the polar frame rotates. The first
example computes it and the components of a constant spinor.

::: {#exm-spd-polar-plane}
#### The plane in polar coordinates

For $e^1 = dr$, $e^2 = r\,d\theta$, $de^2 = dr \wedge d\theta$ forces $\omega^2{}_1 = d\theta$, $\omega_{12} = -d\theta$.
With $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$, $\gamma^1\gamma^2 = i\sigma_3$, so $\nabla_r = \partial_r$ and
$\nabla_\theta = \partial_\theta - \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_3$. A spinor that is constant in Cartesian coordinates has polar
components $\psi(\theta) = e^{i\theta\sigma_3/2}\psi_0$, which satisfy $\nabla_\theta\psi = 0$ and are antiperiodic in
$\theta$, as in @exr-spd-circle-bounding.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The round sphere is the running example. The second example computes its spin connection in the frame of the polar
coordinates, the frame used for its Dirac operator later in the chapter.

::: {#exm-spd-sphere-spin-connection}
#### The sphere

For the unit sphere with $e^1 = d\theta$, $e^2 = \sin\theta\,d\varphi$, $de^2 = \cos\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$
gives $\omega^2{}_1 = \cos\theta\,d\varphi$ and $\omega_{12} = -\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ (the Christoffel symbols of
@prp-sphere-christoffel in the frame). Hence
$$
\nabla_\theta = \partial_\theta, \qquad \nabla_\varphi = \partial_\varphi - \tfrac{i}{2}\cos\theta\,\sigma_3 .
$$ {#eq-spd-sphere-spin-connection}
Near the poles the frame $(e_\theta, e_\varphi)$ is the polar frame of @exm-spd-polar-plane, so the frame components of
smooth spinor fields are antiperiodic in $\varphi$. Parallel transport around the latitude $\theta = \theta_0$ solves
$\partial_\varphi\psi = \tfrac{i}{2}\cos\theta_0\,\sigma_3\psi$; including the sign from the antiperiodicity, the holonomy is $H = -e^{i\pi\cos\theta_0\sigma_3} =
e^{-iA\sigma_3/2}$ with $A = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$ (@fig-sd-spinor-holonomy).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Changing the frame by a rotation that depends on the point changes the connection by a derivative term, like a gauge
transformation. The third example works it out in two dimensions, where the spin connection is an abelian gauge field.

::: {#exm-spd-frame-change}
#### Changing the frame in two dimensions

In two dimensions $\omega_{12}$ is a single one-form and $\nabla = d - \tfrac{i}{2}\omega_{12}\sigma_3$ up to the
identification $\gamma^1\gamma^2 = i\sigma_3$, a $U(1)$ connection acting with charges $\pm\tfrac12$ on the two
components. Rotating the frame by an angle $\alpha(x)$ changes $\omega_{12}$ to $\omega_{12} - d\alpha$ and the
components to $e^{\pm i\alpha\sigma_3/2}\psi$, the gauge transformation of charge $\tfrac12$ @zhelnorovich2019spinors [eq.
(2.61)]. From the Cartesian frame to the polar frame of @exm-spd-polar-plane, $\alpha = \theta$ and $\omega_{12} = 0 -
d\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The connection forms can be computed from a coframe by the structure equations or from the Christoffel symbols. The
first exercise does the latter for the sphere and confirms @eq-spd-sphere-spin-connection.

::: {#exr-spd-sphere-omega}
#### The spin connection of the sphere from the Christoffel symbols

With Sage, compute $\omega_{ab\mu} = e_a{}^\nu(\partial_\mu e_{b\nu} - \Gamma^\lambda{}_{\mu\nu}e_{b\lambda})$ for the
unit sphere with the frame $e_1 = \partial_\theta$, $e_2 = \sin^{-1}\theta\,\partial_\varphi$, and check $de^a +
\omega^a{}_b \wedge e^b = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The only non-zero component is $\omega_{12\varphi} = -\cos\theta = -\omega_{21\varphi}$, and the structure equations hold:

{{< sage exr-spd-sphere-omega >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The spin connection is designed so that Clifford multiplication by a vector field obeys the Leibniz rule. The second
exercise proves this from the first relation of @eq-spd-sigma-algebra.

::: {#exr-spd-clifford-leibniz}
#### Compatibility with Clifford multiplication

For a vector field $Y = Y^ae_a$ write $Y\cdot\psi = Y^a\gamma_a\psi$. Show that $\nabla_X(Y\cdot\psi) = (\nabla_XY)\cdot
\psi + Y\cdot\nabla_X\psi$, using $[\tfrac14\omega_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b, \gamma_c] = \omega_{ac}\gamma^a$ (with
$\omega = \omega(X)$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla_X(Y^a\gamma_a\psi) = X(Y^a)\gamma_a\psi + Y^a\gamma_aX(\psi) + Y^a\tfrac14\omega_{bc}\gamma^b\gamma^c\gamma_a\psi$.
Moving $\gamma_a$ to the left produces the commutator $[\tfrac14\omega_{bc}\gamma^b\gamma^c, \gamma_a] = \omega_{ba}\gamma^b$
(@prp-spin-lie-algebra, with $\tfrac14\omega_{bc}\gamma^b\gamma^c = \tfrac12\omega_{bc}\Sigma^{bc}$). So the right side is
$(X(Y^a) + \omega^a{}_bY^b)\gamma_a\psi + Y^a\gamma_a\nabla_X\psi$, and $X(Y^a) + \omega^a{}_b(X)Y^b$ are the components of
$\nabla_XY$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The claim that a constant Cartesian spinor has polar components $e^{i\theta\sigma_3/2}\psi_0$ can be checked
symbolically. The third exercise does so and also transports a spinor around the circle $r = 1$.

::: {#exr-spd-polar-constant}
#### Constant spinors in polar coordinates

With Sage, check that $\psi(\theta) = e^{i\theta\sigma_3/2}\psi_0$ satisfies $\nabla_\theta\psi = 0$ for the connection of
@exm-spd-polar-plane, that $\psi(2\pi) = -\psi(0)$, and that the holonomy around the circle $r = 1$, including the sign
from the antiperiodic components, is trivial, in agreement with the flatness of the plane.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\theta\psi = \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_3\psi$, so $\nabla_\theta\psi = 0$; the components change sign after one turn,
and the antiperiodicity of the frame components cancels this sign, so the true holonomy is $1$:

{{< sage exr-spd-polar-constant >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The commutator of two spinor covariant derivatives is given by the Riemann tensor contracted with the generators
$\Sigma^{ab}$. Contracting once more with gamma matrices gives the scalar curvature, the identity behind the Lichnerowicz
formula of the next part.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-spinor-curvature}
#### Curvature of the spin connection

For vector fields $X, Y$ and the curvature two-forms $R^a{}_b = d\omega^a{}_b + \omega^a{}_c \wedge \omega^c{}_b$ (the
Riemann tensor $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of @def-riemann in the frame),
$$
(\nabla_X\nabla_Y - \nabla_Y\nabla_X - \nabla_{[X, Y]})\psi = \tfrac14R_{ab}(X, Y)\gamma^a\gamma^b\psi ,
\qquad \gamma^c\gamma^d R(e_c, e_d)\psi = -\tfrac12R\,\psi ,
$$ {#eq-spd-spinor-curvature}
with $R(e_c, e_d) = \nabla_{e_c}\nabla_{e_d} - \nabla_{e_d}\nabla_{e_c} - \nabla_{[e_c, e_d]}$ and $R$ the scalar
curvature (positive on spheres) @dolan2003 [eq. (4)], @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 2.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere the curvature two-form is the area form. The first example checks both formulas of
@eq-spd-spinor-curvature in the frame of @exm-spd-sphere-spin-connection.

::: {#exm-spd-sphere-spinor-curvature}
#### The sphere

From @eq-spd-sphere-spin-connection, $[\nabla_\theta, \nabla_\varphi] = \partial_\theta(-\tfrac{i}{2}\cos\theta\,\sigma_3)
= \tfrac{i}{2}\sin\theta\,\sigma_3$, while $R^1{}_2 = d(-\cos\theta\,d\varphi) = \sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$
gives $\tfrac14(R_{12} - R_{21})\gamma^1\gamma^2 = \tfrac12\sin\theta\cdot i\sigma_3$, the same. In the frame,
$R(e_1, e_2) = \tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_3$, and $\gamma^c\gamma^dR(e_c, e_d) = 2\sigma_1\sigma_2\cdot\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_3 =
-1 = -\tfrac12R$ with $R = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The curvature generates the holonomy of small loops. The second example confirms this on the sphere: for a small cap
the holonomy is the exponential of the curvature times the area.

::: {#exm-spd-holonomy-cap}
#### Holonomy and curvature

For the latitude $\theta = \theta_0$ the holonomy of @exm-spd-sphere-spin-connection is $\exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}A\sigma_3)$, and
$-\tfrac{i}{2}A\sigma_3 = -\int_{\text{cap}}\tfrac14R_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b$ since $\tfrac14R_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b =
\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_3\,\text{area form}$ and the cap has area $A$. The sign reflects the orientation of the loop, and the
factor $\tfrac12$ relative to vectors is the factor $\tfrac12$ in $\Sigma^{ab}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Spaces of constant curvature have the simplest spinor curvature. The third example evaluates it on the round spheres
of any dimension, which the computation of their Dirac spectrum uses.

::: {#exm-spd-constant-curvature}
#### Constant curvature

On the unit sphere $S^n$, $R_{abcd} = \delta_{ac}\delta_{bd} - \delta_{ad}\delta_{bc}$, so $R(e_c, e_d)\psi =
\tfrac14(\gamma^c\gamma^d - \gamma^d\gamma^c)\psi = \tfrac12\gamma^c\gamma^d\psi$ for $c \neq d$. Then $\gamma^c\gamma^d
R(e_c, e_d) = \tfrac12\sum_{c \neq d}\gamma^c\gamma^d\gamma^c\gamma^d = -\tfrac12n(n - 1)$, which is $-\tfrac12R$ with
$R = n(n - 1)$ (@prp-sphere-curvature for $n = 2$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first formula follows from @eq-spd-spin-connection and the commutation relations of the $\Sigma^{ab}$. The first
exercise asks for the computation.

::: {#exr-spd-curvature-derivation}
#### Deriving the curvature

Write $\nabla = d + \Omega$ with $\Omega = \tfrac12\omega_{ab}\Sigma^{ab}$. Show that the curvature is $d\Omega + \Omega
\wedge \Omega$ and, using the second relation of @eq-spd-sigma-algebra, that $\Omega \wedge \Omega = \tfrac14(\omega_{ac}
\wedge \omega^c{}_b)\gamma^a\gamma^b$; conclude the first formula of @eq-spd-spinor-curvature.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\nabla_X\nabla_Y - \nabla_Y\nabla_X - \nabla_{[X, Y]})\psi = (d\Omega + \Omega \wedge \Omega)(X, Y)\psi$ as for any
connection of the form $d + \Omega$. $\Omega \wedge \Omega = \tfrac14\omega_{ab} \wedge \omega_{cd}\Sigma^{ab}\Sigma^{cd} =
\tfrac18\omega_{ab} \wedge \omega_{cd}[\Sigma^{ab}, \Sigma^{cd}]$ (the wedge of one-forms is antisymmetric), and the four
terms of @eq-spd-sigma-algebra combine into $\tfrac12\omega_{ac} \wedge \omega^c{}_b\Sigma^{ab}$. With $d\Omega =
\tfrac12d\omega_{ab}\Sigma^{ab}$ this is $\tfrac12R_{ab}\Sigma^{ab} = \tfrac14R_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The contraction to the scalar curvature uses the first Bianchi identity. The second exercise carries it out and fixes the sign with the sphere.

::: {#exr-spd-ricci-contraction}
#### The contraction

Using $\gamma^c\gamma^d\gamma^a\gamma^b$ and the Bianchi identity $R_{a[bcd]} = 0$, show that $\tfrac14R_{abcd}\gamma^c
\gamma^d\gamma^a\gamma^b = -\tfrac12R$, where $R_{abcd} = R_{ab}(e_c, e_d)$ and $R = R^{ca}{}_{ca}$ in the sign convention
of @sec-conventions-curvature.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the pair symmetry $R_{abcd} = R_{cdab}$ the expression is $\tfrac14\gamma^c(R_{cdab}\gamma^d\gamma^a\gamma^b)$. Write
$\gamma^d\gamma^a\gamma^b = \gamma^{[dab]} + \eta^{da}\gamma^b - \eta^{db}\gamma^a + \eta^{ab}\gamma^d$. The totally
antisymmetric part is killed by the Bianchi identity $R_{c[dab]} = 0$, and the last term by the antisymmetry of
$R_{cdab}$ in $a, b$. The two middle terms give $2R_{cd}{}^{d}{}_{b}\gamma^b$, a contraction of the Riemann tensor, that is
$\pm2\operatorname{Ric}_{cb}\gamma^b$. Contracting with $\gamma^c$, only the symmetric part $\eta^{cb}$ of $\gamma^c\gamma^b$
survives, because the Ricci tensor is symmetric, and the result is $\pm\tfrac12R$; the sphere
(@exm-spd-sphere-spinor-curvature) fixes the sign to $-\tfrac12R$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The holonomy formula of @exm-spd-sphere-spin-connection was obtained by solving a differential equation. The third
exercise checks it numerically and compares with the curvature integral.

::: {#exr-spd-holonomy-numeric}
#### Holonomy around latitudes

With Sage, solve $\partial_\varphi\psi = \tfrac{i}{2}\cos\theta_0\,\sigma_3\psi$ numerically for $\theta_0 = 0.3, 1.0,
\pi/2, 2.5$, multiply by $-1$ for the antiperiodicity, and compare with $\exp(-\tfrac{i}{2}A\sigma_3)$, $A = 2\pi(1 -
\cos\theta_0)$. Compute also $\int_{\text{cap}}\tfrac12R_{12}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The numerical holonomy agrees with the formula to the integration tolerance, and $\int_{\text{cap}}\tfrac12R_{12} =
\tfrac12A$:

{{< sage exr-spd-holonomy-numeric >}}

### Spin-c structures

When the second Stiefel-Whitney class does not vanish, the sign ambiguity of spinors can be compensated by the sign
ambiguity of the square root of a line bundle. The figure shows the index of the resulting Dirac operators on $CP^2$
for each charge, which is computed later in the chapter.

![The index $(Q + 1)(Q + 2)/2$ of the spin-c Dirac operator of $CP^2$ for the spin-c structure of charge $Q$ (blue), and
the number of its zero modes found from the Casimir operators of $SU(3)$ by @dolan2003 [eqs. (55)-(56)] (red crosses).
The canonical structure $Q = 0$ has a single zero mode; for $Q = -1, -2$ there are none. Generated by
`figures/sd-cp2-index.sage`.](figures/sd-cp2-index.svg){#fig-sd-cp2-index width=65%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spinc-structure}
#### Spin-c structure

The group $\mathrm{Spin}^c(n) = (\mathrm{Spin}(n) \times U(1))/\{\pm(1, 1)\}$ covers $SO(n) \times U(1)$ by $[S, z]
\mapsto (\rho(S), z^2)$. A **spin-c structure** on an oriented Riemannian manifold $M$ with a complex line bundle $L$ (the
**determinant line**) is a lift of $SO(M) \times_M U(L)$ to a principal $\mathrm{Spin}^c(n)$-bundle; locally it is a
choice of lifts $S_{ij}$ of the frame transitions and square roots $z_{ij}$ of the transition functions of $L$ with
$S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki}\,z_{ij}z_{jk}z_{ki} = 1$. Spinor fields are sections of the twisted bundle "$S \otimes L^{1/2}$",
which exists although neither factor does; a connection on $L$ adds $\tfrac12A_L$ to @eq-spd-spin-connection
@dolan2003 [Sec. 2, example iii].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a spin manifold spin-c structures are spin structures twisted by line bundles. The first example makes this precise
on the sphere, where it describes spinors in a magnetic monopole field.

::: {#exm-spd-spinc-sphere}
#### Spin-c structures on $S^2$

$S^2$ is spin, so the sign cocycles $S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki}$ can be made trivial and the $z_{ij}$ must then form a cocycle
themselves: $L^{1/2} = N$ is an honest line bundle and $L = N^2$. The spin-c spinors are spinors with values in $N$, with
$c_1(N) = m \in \mathbb{Z}$, and $L$ has even degree $2m$: spinors of charge one in the monopole field of charge $m$
(@def-chern-number).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On $CP^2$ the sign cocycle is non-trivial, so $L$ must have odd degree to cancel it. The second example lists the
choices and the one of @dolan2003 that has a single zero mode.

::: {#exm-spd-spinc-cp2}
#### Spin-c structures on $CP^2$

On $CP^2$, $w_2 = x \bmod 2$ (@exm-spd-cp2-not-spin), so a spin-c structure needs $c_1(L) \equiv x \pmod 2$: $L = \mathcal{O}(k)$
with $k$ odd. Writing $k = 2Q + 3$, the choice $Q = 0$, $L = \mathcal{O}(3) = K^{-1}$, is the canonical spin-c structure of
the Kähler manifold $CP^2$, for which "the spin exactly cancels the monopole charge" and the Dirac operator has exactly one
zero mode @dolan2003 [eqs. (55)-(56)] (@fig-sd-cp2-index).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Every Kähler manifold carries a canonical spin-c structure whose spinors are forms. The third example describes it; it
turns the Dirac operator into the Dolbeault operator in a later section.

::: {#exm-spd-spinc-kahler}
#### The canonical spin-c structure of a Kähler manifold

On a Kähler manifold of complex dimension $m$ the holonomy lies in $U(m) \subset SO(2m)$ @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.2], and
$U(m)$ lifts to $\mathrm{Spin}^c(2m)$. The spinor bundle is $\Lambda^{0, \bullet} = \bigoplus_q\Lambda^{0, q}$, the forms
of type $(0, q)$, with determinant line $K^{-1}$, $K = \Lambda^{m, 0}$ the canonical bundle; the two chiralities are the
forms of even and of odd degree. When $K$ has a square root the manifold is spin and $S = \Lambda^{0, \bullet} \otimes
K^{1/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The zero-mode counts of @fig-sd-cp2-index were obtained by @dolan2003 from representation theory and compared with the
index. The first exercise reproduces the comparison.

::: {#exr-spd-cp2-index-table}
#### Index and zero modes on $CP^2$

With Sage, tabulate $(Q + 1)(Q + 2)/2$ for $Q = -7, \dots, 5$ and the zero-mode numbers $(|Y| + 2)(|Y| + 4)/8$ of
@dolan2003 [eq. (55)] with $Y = 2Q$ for $Q \geq 0$ and $Y = 2Q + 6$ for $Q \leq -3$. Check that they agree and that the
index vanishes for $Q = -1, -2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two columns agree for every $Q$, and the index is $0$ exactly at $Q = -1, -2$, where @dolan2003 finds no zero modes:

{{< sage exr-spd-cp2-index-table >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

The cancellation of signs in the definition is the whole content of a spin-c structure. The second exercise checks it
on the cocycles.

::: {#exr-spd-spinc-cocycle}
#### Cancelling signs

Let $s_{ijk} = S_{ij}S_{jk}S_{ki} \in \{\pm1\}$ be the sign cocycle of arbitrary lifts (representing $w_2$) and
$t_{ijk} = z_{ij}z_{jk}z_{ki}$ for arbitrary square roots $z_{ij}$ of the transition functions $g_{ij}$ of $L$. Show that
$t_{ijk} \in \{\pm1\}$, that it represents $c_1(L) \bmod 2$, and that a spin-c structure exists iff the classes of $s$ and
$t$ agree.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$t_{ijk}^2 = g_{ij}g_{jk}g_{ki} = 1$, so $t_{ijk} = \pm1$; changing the square roots changes $t$ by a coboundary, and $t$ is
the obstruction to a square root of $L$, which is $c_1(L) \bmod 2$. The product $[S_{ij}, z_{ij}]$ is a cocycle in
$\mathrm{Spin}^c$ iff $s_{ijk}t_{ijk} = 1$ after a change of lifts, that is iff $[s] = [t]$: $w_2(M) = c_1(L) \bmod 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The canonical spin-c structure of @exm-spd-spinc-kahler can be compared with the spin structure on a spin Kähler
manifold. The third exercise does this on $CP^1 = S^2$.

::: {#exr-spd-spinc-cp1}
#### $CP^1$ from both sides

On $CP^1$, $K = \mathcal{O}(-2)$. Show that $\Lambda^{0, \bullet} = (\Lambda^{0, 0} \oplus \Lambda^{0, 1}) = \mathcal{O}
\oplus \mathcal{O}(2)$ (as smooth line bundles, $\Lambda^{0, 1} \cong \overline{K} \cong K^{-1}$) and $S = \Lambda^{0,
\bullet} \otimes K^{1/2} = \mathcal{O}(-1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(1)$. Interpret the charges $\mp1$ as the charges
$\mp\tfrac12$ of @exm-spd-weyl-two measured in units of the generator of $H^2$ in the frame bundle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Lambda^{0, 1}$ is spanned by $d\bar z$, which transforms like $\overline{dz}$, so $\Lambda^{0, 1} \cong \overline{K}$,
and for a line bundle $\overline{K} \cong K^{-1}$ with a Hermitian metric: $\mathcal{O}(2)$. Tensoring with $K^{1/2} =
\mathcal{O}(-1)$ gives $\mathcal{O}(-1) \oplus \mathcal{O}(1)$. The tangent bundle of $CP^1$ is $\mathcal{O}(2) = K^{-1}$, a
rotation of the frame by $\alpha$ acts on it by $e^{i\alpha}$ and on the two Weyl spinors by $e^{\mp i\alpha/2}$
(@exm-spd-weyl-two): they are the line bundles of degree $\mp\tfrac12\cdot2 = \mp1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine spin structures, the spin connection and spin-c structures. They prepare the
Dirac operator of the next part, which is built from the spin connection and whose spectrum depends on the spin
structure.

The equator of the sphere inherits a spin structure from the sphere and another from the plane. The first integrative
exercise compares the two through the holonomy.

::: {#exr-spd-equator-structure}
#### The structure induced on the equator

Show that the spin structure of $S^2$ restricted to the equator is the antiperiodic structure of the circle, using the
holonomy $H = -1$ of @fig-sd-spinor-holonomy for a spinor transported along the equator (a geodesic, along which the
tangent frame is parallel).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the equator $\omega_{12}(\partial_\varphi) = -\cos\tfrac\pi2 = 0$: the frame $(e_\theta, e_\varphi)$, normal and tangent
to the equator, is parallel along it, so a parallel spinor has constant frame components. The holonomy $H = -1$ says that
these constant components describe a spinor that comes back to its negative; equivalently, smooth spinor fields of $S^2$
have antiperiodic components in the tangent-normal frame of the equator. That is the definition of the antiperiodic spin
structure on the circle, the one that bounds the hemisphere, consistent with @exr-spd-circle-bounding.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Flat tori have vanishing spin connection in the coordinate frame, so all the information is in the spin structure. The
second integrative exercise finds the parallel spinors for each structure.

::: {#exr-spd-torus-parallel}
#### Parallel spinors on flat tori

On $T^n$ with the flat metric and the frame $\partial_i$, show that $\omega = 0$ and that the parallel spinor fields are
the constant ones. Using @exm-spd-spin-torus, show that the dimension of the space of parallel spinors is $2^{\lfloor
n/2\rfloor}$ for the periodic structure and $0$ for the other $2^n - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$de^i = d(dy^i) = 0$ with $\omega = 0$ solves the structure equations, so $\nabla_i = \partial_i$ and parallel means
constant. A constant non-zero field satisfies $\psi(y + 2\pi e_i) = (-1)^{s_i}\psi(y)$ only if all $s_i = 0$; then every
constant vector of $\mathbb{C}^N$, $N = 2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, is allowed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Spin-c spinors on $CP^2$ can be counted by the holomorphic Euler characteristic. The third integrative exercise checks
the formula of @fig-sd-cp2-index by the Riemann-Roch computation with the Todd class.

::: {#exr-spd-cp2-riemann-roch}
#### Riemann-Roch on $CP^2$

With Sage, expand $e^{Qx}\big(x/(1 - e^{-x})\big)^3$ to second order in $x$ and read off the coefficient of $x^2$, which is
$\int_{CP^2}\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal{O}(Q))\operatorname{td}(CP^2)$ since $\int_{CP^2}x^2 = 1$. Compare with $(Q + 1)(Q +
2)/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coefficient is $\tfrac12Q^2 + \tfrac32Q + 1 = \tfrac12(Q + 1)(Q + 2)$ for every $Q$: the index of the spin-c Dirac
operator of charge $Q$ is the holomorphic Euler characteristic of $\mathcal{O}(Q)$, the identification made precise in
@sec-dirac-compact-spaces:

{{< sage exr-spd-cp2-riemann-roch >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
