On the spheres of higher dimension the Casimir of $\mathrm{Spin}(n + 1)$ is given by Freudenthal's formula. The second
example combines it with @eq-spd-parthasarathy, as @camporesi1995 [eqs. (5.41)-(5.48)] does.

::: {#exm-spd-parthasarathy-sn}
#### $S^n$

For the highest weight $\lambda_l = (l + \tfrac12, \tfrac12, \dots)$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(n + 1)$, $C_2(\lambda_l) = (\lambda_l,
\lambda_l + 2\rho) = (l + \tfrac n2)^2 - \tfrac{n(n - 1)}{8}$, and with $R = n(n - 1)$, @eq-spd-parthasarathy gives $D^2 = (l +
\tfrac n2)^2$, the spectrum of @thm-sphere-dirac-spectrum @camporesi1995 [eqs. (5.44), (5.48)].
:::

The six-dimensional nearly-Kähler cosets are not symmetric, and the formula needs the replacement of $R/8$. The third
example states the setting of @dolan2003 [Sec. 3] and the cosets of @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [Sec. 2].

::: {#exm-spd-nearly-kahler}
#### The nearly-Kähler cosets

The non-symmetric six-dimensional cosets $G_2/SU(3)$, $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ and $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$ carry
$G$-invariant nearly-Kähler metrics @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [Sec. 2]. Their canonical connection has torsion $T^\alpha =
\tfrac12f^\alpha{}_{\beta\gamma}e^\beta \wedge e^\gamma$ and covariantly constant curvature, and the square of the Dirac operator
of that connection is $C_2(G, \lambda) - C_2(H, t) + C_2(H, \tau)$ @dolan2003 [eqs. (59)-(67)]. On $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$
with two monopole charges $(T, Y)$ the number of zero modes is the dimension of the $SU(3)$ representation minimising
$C_2$ @dolan2003 [eq. (70)].
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The relation $\nabla^*\nabla = C_2(G) - C_2(H)$ comes from writing the Laplacian through the generators of $G$. The first
exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-spd-casimir-laplacian}
#### The Laplacian as a difference of Casimirs

Let $T_A$ be an orthonormal basis of $\mathfrak{g}$ adapted to $\mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{m}$, acting on sections by left
translation as differential operators $D_A$. On a symmetric space, show that $\nabla_\alpha = D_\alpha$ ($\alpha$ in
$\mathfrak{m}$) for the canonical connection, so that $-\sum_\alpha D_\alpha D_\alpha = -\sum_AD_AD_A + \sum_iD_iD_i$, and
identify the two sums with $C_2(G, \lambda)$ and $C_2(H, \tau)$ (@dolan2003 [eq. (15)]).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $G \times_H S$ the generators of $\mathfrak{h}$ act on an equivariant function through $\tau$ (by the equivariance
condition), so $\sum_iD_iD_i = -C_2(H, \tau)$ in the sign convention where Casimirs of unitary representations are positive.
The generators of $\mathfrak{g}$ act on the summand $V_\lambda$ of @eq-spd-frobenius, so $-\sum_AD_AD_A = C_2(G, \lambda)$. The
canonical connection of a symmetric space is the Levi-Civita one, and its covariant derivatives along $\mathfrak{m}$ are the
$D_\alpha$ at the origin and, by invariance, everywhere. So $\nabla^*\nabla = -\sum_\alpha D_\alpha D_\alpha = C_2(G, \lambda) -
C_2(H, \tau)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

With Sage, compute $C_2(\tau) = (\tau, \tau + 2\rho_K)$ for the spinor representation of $\mathrm{Spin}(n)$ (highest weight
$(\tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac12)$) for $n = 2, \dots, 8$ in the normalisation where the vector representation has $C_2 = n - 1$,
and compare with $R/8 = n(n - 1)/8$.

$C_2(\tau) = n(n - 1)/8$ in every case, as @camporesi1995 [eq. (5.46)] states for even $n$:

On $S^4$ the formula with a gauge field gives the spectrum in an instanton background. The third exercise reproduces the case
without gauge field from the $SO(5)$ Casimirs of @dolan2003 [eqs. (36)-(43)].

::: {#exr-spd-s4-casimirs}
#### $S^4$ from $SO(5)$ Casimirs

With $C_2(p, q) = \tfrac12(p^2 + q^2) + 2p + q$ and $d(p, q) = \tfrac16(p + q + 3)(p - q + 1)(p + 2)(q + 1)$ for $SO(5)$
@dolan2003 [eqs. (36)-(37)], spinors on $S^4$ without gauge field use $(p, q) = (q + 1, q)$. With Sage, compute $C_2 +
\tfrac{R}{8}$ ($R = 12$) and $d$ for $q \leq 5$, and compare with $(q + 2)^2$ and the multiplicity of @thm-sphere-dirac-spectrum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$C_2(q + 1, q) + \tfrac32 = (q + 2)^2$, the eigenvalue squared for $l = q$, and $d(q + 1, q) = \tfrac23(q + 1)(q + 2)(q + 3) =
4\binom{q + 3}{q}$. The representation occurs twice in the spinor fields, once for each Weyl piece of $\tau$, and the $2d$ states
split into $d$ with eigenvalue $q + 2$ and $d$ with $-(q + 2)$ @dolan2003 [eq. (43)]:

{{< sage exr-spd-s4-casimirs >}}
:::

### Kähler and Calabi-Yau spaces

On a Kähler manifold the spinors are differential forms of type $(0, q)$ and the Dirac operator is the Dolbeault operator
plus its adjoint, so harmonic spinors are holomorphic objects counted by Hodge numbers. The figure shows the Hodge numbers
of the two Calabi-Yau manifolds used below.

![The Hodge diamonds of the $K3$ surface and of the quintic threefold in $CP^4$, with $h^{p, q}$ in row $p + q$ (even rows
blue, odd rows red). The Euler characteristics $\chi = \sum(-1)^{p + q}h^{p, q}$ are $24$ and $2(h^{1, 1} - h^{2, 1}) = -200$;
for $K3$ the signature is $-16$ and $\hat A = 2$. Generated by `figures/sd-hodge-diamonds.sage`.](figures/sd-hodge-diamonds.svg){#fig-sd-hodge-diamonds width=75%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dolbeault-dirac}
#### Dolbeault-Dirac operator

On a Kähler manifold $M$ of complex dimension $m$ with its canonical spin-c structure (@exm-spd-spinc-kahler), spinor fields
are forms of type $(0, \bullet)$ and the Dirac operator is the **Dolbeault-Dirac operator**
$$
D = \sqrt2\,(\bar\partial + \bar\partial^*) : \Omega^{0, \bullet}(M) \to \Omega^{0, \bullet}(M) ,
$$ {#eq-spd-dolbeault-dirac}
which maps even forms to odd ones and back, the two chiralities. If $M$ is spin, the Dirac operator of the spin structure is
@eq-spd-dolbeault-dirac acting on $\Omega^{0, \bullet}(K^{1/2})$. Harmonic spinors of positive and negative chirality are the
Dolbeault cohomology $H^{0, \mathrm{even}}$ and $H^{0, \mathrm{odd}}$ (of $K^{1/2}$ in the spin case), with dimensions given by
Hodge numbers @greene1997 [Sec. 2.9], @dolan2003 [Sec. 2, example iii].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the complex plane the identification is a computation with the flat Dirac operator. The first example carries it out.

::: {#exm-spd-dolbeault-plane}
#### The complex plane

On $\mathbb{C}$ with $z = x + iy$ and $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$, $D = i(\sigma_1\partial_x + \sigma_2\partial_y) =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2i\partial_z \\ 2i\partial_{\bar z} & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. A spinor $(f, g)$ corresponds to the form $f +
g\,d\bar z/\sqrt2$ (unit-norm basis), and $\sqrt2\bar\partial f = 2\partial_{\bar z}f\,(d\bar z/\sqrt2)$, $\sqrt2\bar\partial^*(g\,
d\bar z/\sqrt2) = -2\partial_zg$: up to the phases $i$ and $-i$ the two off-diagonal entries are $\sqrt2\bar\partial$ and
$\sqrt2\bar\partial^*$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On $CP^1 = S^2$ the twisted spinor bundles are line bundles, and zero modes are holomorphic sections. The second example
counts them, anticipating the index on the sphere.

::: {#exm-spd-dolbeault-cp1}
#### $CP^1$ with a twist

On $CP^1$, $K^{1/2} = \mathcal{O}(-1)$ (@exr-spd-spinc-cp1), so spinors with values in $\mathcal{O}(M)$ are $(0, \bullet)$-forms
with values in $\mathcal{O}(M - 1)$. Positive-chirality zero modes are holomorphic sections, $h^0(\mathcal{O}(M - 1)) = M$ for
$M \geq 1$, and negative-chirality ones are $h^1(\mathcal{O}(M - 1)) = h^0(\mathcal{O}(-M - 1)) = 0$. Without a twist ($M = 0$)
there are none, as the vanishing theorem requires.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

On $CP^2$ the canonical spin-c structure gives the single zero mode of @fig-sd-cp2-index. The third example explains it as a
Dolbeault cohomology group.

::: {#exm-spd-dolbeault-cp2}
#### $CP^2$ with its canonical spin-c structure

For $Q = 0$ the spinors are $\Omega^{0, \bullet}(CP^2)$, and the harmonic ones are $H^{0, 0} \oplus H^{0, 1} \oplus H^{0, 2}$ with
$h^{0, 0} = 1$, $h^{0, 1} = h^{0, 2} = 0$: a single zero mode of positive chirality, the constant function, and index $1$. For
general $Q$ the forms take values in $\mathcal{O}(Q)$ and the index is the holomorphic Euler characteristic $(Q + 1)(Q + 2)/2$
(@exr-spd-cp2-riemann-roch), in agreement with @dolan2003 [eq. (56)].
:::

Zero modes on $CP^1$ with a twist are polynomials of bounded degree in a coordinate. The second exercise counts them directly
and compares with the index on the sphere computed later.

::: {#exr-spd-cp1-sections}
#### Holomorphic sections on $CP^1$

A holomorphic section of $\mathcal{O}(d)$ on $CP^1$ is a holomorphic function $f(z)$ on $\mathbb{C}$ such that $z^{-d}f(z)$ is
holomorphic at $z = \infty$. Show that these are the polynomials of degree at most $d$, so $h^0(\mathcal{O}(d)) = d + 1$ for $d
\geq 0$ and $0$ for $d < 0$. Deduce the number of zero modes of the Dirac operator twisted by $\mathcal{O}(M)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$z^{-d}f(z)$ bounded near $\infty$ means $|f(z)| \leq C|z|^d$ for large $|z|$, so $f$ is a polynomial of degree $\leq d$ by the Cauchy estimates for the Taylor coefficients, as in @cor-liouville and @exr-liouville-bounded-growth. There are $d + 1$
coefficients. With $d = M - 1$ (@exm-spd-dolbeault-cp1) there are $M$ zero modes for $M \geq 1$, all of positive chirality,
and by Serre duality $h^1(\mathcal{O}(M - 1)) = h^0(\mathcal{O}(-M - 1))$, which is $|M|$ for $M \leq -1$: the zero modes then
have negative chirality.
:::

The Euler characteristic of a Calabi-Yau threefold is determined by two Hodge numbers. The third exercise computes it for
the quintic in two ways, as in @fig-sd-hodge-diamonds.

::: {#exr-spd-quintic-euler}
#### The Euler characteristic of the quintic

From the Hodge diamond of a Calabi-Yau threefold @greene1997 [Sec. 2.11, p. 32] show $\chi = 2(h^{1, 1} - h^{2, 1})$, and
evaluate it for the quintic ($h^{1, 1} = 1$, $h^{2, 1} = 101$). With Sage, compute $\chi = \int c_3$ from $c(T) = (1 + x)^5/(1 +
5x)$ (the analogue of @aspinwall1996 [eqs. (9)-(12)] for the quintic) and $\int_Xx^3 = 5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Row by row in $\chi = \sum(-1)^{p + q}h^{p, q}$: rows $0$ and $6$ give $h^{0, 0} + h^{3, 3} = 2$, rows $1$ and $5$ vanish,
rows $2$ and $4$ give $2h^{1, 1}$, and row $3$ gives $-(h^{3, 0} + h^{2, 1} + h^{1, 2} + h^{0, 3}) = -(2 + 2h^{2, 1})$, so $\chi =
2h^{1, 1} - 2h^{2, 1}$. For the quintic
$\chi = 2 - 202 = -200$, and $c_3 = -40x^3$ gives $-200$ as well:

{{< sage exr-spd-quintic-euler >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On a Calabi-Yau manifold the holonomy group fixes some spinors, which are then parallel. The proposition counts them, using
the description of holonomy groups in @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.2] and the decomposition of spinors under the holonomy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-calabi-yau-spinors}
#### Parallel spinors on Calabi-Yau manifolds

Let $M$ be a compact simply connected Riemannian spin manifold of real dimension $2m$ with holonomy $SU(m)$ (a Calabi-Yau
manifold, @greene1997 [Sec. 2.11]). The spinor representation of $\mathrm{Spin}(2m)$ restricted to $SU(m)$ contains exactly two
trivial summands, of the same chirality if $m$ is even and of opposite chiralities if $m$ is odd. Hence $M$ has exactly two
linearly independent parallel spinors, these are all its harmonic spinors (@thm-lichnerowicz-vanishing with $R = 0$), and $\dim\ker D^+ - \dim\ker D^- = \pm2$ for $m$ even (the sign fixed by the orientation) and $0$ for $m$ odd @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.2 and Sec. 4.1, eq. (89)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The flat torus has trivial holonomy, so all spinors are parallel. The first example contrasts it with $K3$, whose holonomy
$SU(2)$ fixes only half of them.

::: {#exm-spd-t4-k3}
#### $T^4$ and $K3$

On $T^4$ (holonomy trivial, periodic structure) all four constant spinors are parallel, two of each chirality, and the index
is $0$. On $K3$ (holonomy $SU(2)$, one factor of $\mathrm{Spin}(4) = SU(2) \times SU(2)$) the Weyl spinors of one chirality are
the doublet of the holonomy factor and those of the other are singlets: two parallel spinors, both of the same chirality,
and index $2$, which is $\hat A(K3) = -\tfrac{1}{24}p_1 = -\tfrac18\tau = 2$ with $\tau = -16$ @aspinwall1996 [eq. (20)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In six dimensions $\mathrm{Spin}(6) = SU(4)$ and the holonomy $SU(3) \subset SU(4)$ fixes one vector in $\mathbf{4}$ and one in
$\bar{\mathbf{4}}$. The second example draws the consequence for a Calabi-Yau threefold.

::: {#exm-spd-cy3-spinors}
#### Calabi-Yau threefolds

Under $SU(3) \subset SU(4) = \mathrm{Spin}(6)$, $\mathbf{4} = \mathbf{3} \oplus \mathbf{1}$ and $\bar{\mathbf{4}} =
\bar{\mathbf{3}} \oplus \mathbf{1}$ (@exr-spd-su3-singlets): one parallel spinor of each chirality, complex conjugates of each
other (@prp-weyl-conjugation for $p - q = 6$). The index of the untwisted Dirac operator is $0$, and by
@exr-spd-branch-chirality-count a ten-dimensional Weyl spinor on such a manifold gives one massless four-dimensional spinor of
each chirality, which a Majorana condition identifies: four real supercharges, the minimal supersymmetry of four dimensions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Holonomy groups other than $SU(m)$ also fix spinors. The third example lists the two exceptional cases of Berger's
classification quoted by @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.2].

::: {#exm-spd-g2-spin7}
#### $G_2$ and $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ holonomy

On a seven-manifold with holonomy $G_2 \subset \mathrm{Spin}(7)$ the spinor $\mathbf{8}$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(7)$ decomposes as
$\mathbf{7} \oplus \mathbf{1}$: one parallel spinor, real by @exm-spd-euclidean-table ($r = 7$). On an eight-manifold with
holonomy $\mathrm{Spin}(7) \subset \mathrm{Spin}(8)$ one of the two Weyl spinors decomposes as $\mathbf{7} \oplus \mathbf{1}$:
again one parallel spinor. Eleven-dimensional spinors on a $G_2$ manifold give $32/8 = 4$ real supercharges in four dimensions
(@exm-spd-branch-eleven).
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The $SU(3)$ singlets in the spinors of $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$ can be found from the weights of @fig-sd-weyl-weights. The first
exercise does this with the weights.

::: {#exr-spd-su3-singlets}
#### $SU(3)$ singlets in the spinor of $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$

The roots of $SU(3) \subset U(3) \subset SO(6)$ are $\epsilon_i - \epsilon_j$ in the weight coordinates $(h_1, h_2, h_3)$, and a
weight is $SU(3)$-invariant iff it is orthogonal to all of them, $h_1 = h_2 = h_3$. With Sage, list the Dirac weights and their
chiralities and find the invariant ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ and $(-\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, -\tfrac12)$ have equal entries, and they have opposite
chirality (@fig-sd-weyl-weights): one singlet in each Weyl spinor:

{{< sage exr-spd-su3-singlets >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The value $\hat A(K3) = 2$ can be obtained from the Euler characteristic alone. The second exercise uses the relation between
signature and Euler characteristic quoted by @aspinwall1996 [eq. (20)].

::: {#exr-spd-k3-ahat}
#### $\hat A(K3)$ from $\chi$

For a complex surface with $c_1 = 0$, the signature theorem gives $\tau = \tfrac13\int(c_1^2 - 2c_2) = -\tfrac23\chi$
@aspinwall1996 [eq. (20)], and $p_1 = 3\tau$. Compute $\tau$, $p_1$ and $\hat A = -p_1/24$ for $K3$ ($\chi = 24$) and check
that $\hat A$ equals the number of parallel spinors of @prp-calabi-yau-spinors. What does the formula give for $T^4$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tau = -16$, $p_1 = -48$, $\hat A = 2$, the two parallel spinors of positive chirality. For $T^4$, $\chi = 0$, so $\tau = 0$ and
$\hat A = 0$: two parallel spinors of each chirality cancel in the index.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Supersymmetry in lower dimensions is counted by parallel spinors times the components of the lower-dimensional spinor. The
third exercise counts for the compactifications of this section.

::: {#exr-spd-susy-count}
#### Counting supercharges

A supercharge of $D$ dimensions with $Q$ real components, on a compact space whose Dirac spinor bundle of complex rank $N_K$
has $k$ parallel sections, leaves $Q\,k/N_K$ real supercharges (each parallel spinor keeps a fraction $1/N_K$). Evaluate it for ten dimensions ($Q = 16$) on $T^6$, $K3 \times T^2$ and a Calabi-Yau
threefold, and for eleven dimensions ($Q = 32$) on a $G_2$ manifold.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T^6$: all $8$ internal spinors parallel, $16$ supercharges ($\mathcal{N} = 4$ in four dimensions). $K3 \times T^2$: holonomy
$SU(2)$ fixes half, $8$ supercharges ($\mathcal{N} = 2$). Calabi-Yau threefold: one quarter of the Weyl spinor, $4$
supercharges ($\mathcal{N} = 1$). $G_2$: one of eight, $32/8 = 4$ ($\mathcal{N} = 1$), as in @exm-spd-g2-spin7 and
@aspinwall1996 [Sec. 4.1], where $K3$ preserves half of the supersymmetries of a torus.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Orbifolds

Quotienting a space by a finite group of symmetries projects out the fields that are not invariant. The figure shows the
simplest case, the interval $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$, where the projection keeps a zero mode of one chirality only.

![Modes on the orbifold $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$, $y \sim -y$, on the fundamental domain $[0, \pi]$: even modes $\cos ny$ (solid) and
odd modes $\sin ny$ (dashed). A spinor with $\psi(-y) = \gamma_5\psi(y)$ has even right-handed and odd left-handed components,
so only the right-handed component has a $y$-independent zero mode; odd modes vanish at the fixed points $0$ and $\pi$.
Generated by `figures/sd-orbifold-modes.sage`.](figures/sd-orbifold-modes.svg){#fig-sd-orbifold-modes width=65%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-orbifold-projection}
#### Orbifold projection

Let a finite group $\Gamma$ act on a spin manifold $K$ by isometries $g$ whose action lifts to the spinor bundle, $\psi \mapsto
U_g\,\psi \circ g^{-1}$ with $U_g$ covering the differential of $g$ and $U_gU_h = U_{gh}$ (for orientation-reversing $g$, $U_g$ is
taken in the pin group of @trautman1995 [Sec. 3], and the lifted action commutes with the Dirac operator up to sign). The spinor fields on the
**orbifold** $K/\Gamma$ are the $\Gamma$-invariant spinor fields on $K$, and the Dirac operator of $K/\Gamma$ is the restriction of
that of $K$; its zero modes are the $\Gamma$-invariant zero modes of $K$. Points with non-trivial stabiliser are the fixed
points, where $K/\Gamma$ is locally $\mathbb{R}^n/\Gamma_x$ @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.6], @chatzistavrakidis2010orb [Sec. 2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The circle modulo the reflection $y \mapsto -y$ is an interval with two fixed points. The first example finds its chiral zero
mode.

::: {#exm-spd-s1z2}
#### $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$

For a five-dimensional spinor on $\mathbb{R}^{1, 3} \times S^1$ with $\Gamma^4 = i\gamma_5$ (@exr-spd-five-four), the reflection
$y \mapsto -y$ reverses the orientation of the circle and lifts to the pin transformation $\psi(x, y) \mapsto \gamma_5\psi(x, -y)$:
$\gamma_5$ anticommutes with $\gamma^\mu$ and commutes with $\Gamma^4$, while $\partial_y$ changes sign, so the five-dimensional
Dirac operator changes only by an overall sign and its zero modes are mapped to zero modes. Invariant fields satisfy $\psi(x, -y) = \gamma_5\psi(x, y)$: $\psi_R$ is even, $\psi_L$ odd (@fig-sd-orbifold-modes). The zero modes of the
circle are constant, so only $\psi_R$ survives: one massless chiral fermion; the other lift $U = -\gamma_5$ keeps $\psi_L$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The orbifold $T^4/\mathbb{Z}_2$ is the $K3$ orbifold of @aspinwall1996 [eq. (49)]. The second example counts its invariant
constant spinors and compares with $K3$.

::: {#exm-spd-t4z2}
#### $T^4/\mathbb{Z}_2$

$z \mapsto -z$ on $T^4 = \mathbb{C}^2/\mathbb{Z}^4$ has $16$ fixed points @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.6]. It is the rotation by $\pi$
in two planes, which lifts to $U = \gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3\gamma^4 = \pm\gamma_*$ (a product of the lifts $\gamma^1\gamma^2$ and
$\gamma^3\gamma^4$ of the two rotations, @exm-spd-spin-two), and $U^2 = 1$. The invariant constant spinors are those of one
chirality: two, as on $K3$ (@exm-spd-t4-k3); the orbifold has holonomy $\mathbb{Z}_2 \subset SU(2)$, and blowing up its sixteen
singular points gives a smooth $K3$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Orbifolds by rotations of $\mathbb{C}^3$ in $SU(3)$ preserve one spinor of each chirality, like Calabi-Yau threefolds. The third
example checks this for $\mathbb{Z}_3$, the group used by @chatzistavrakidis2010orb [Sec. 2] to obtain chiral fermions.

::: {#exm-spd-t6z3}
#### $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$

The rotation by angles $2\pi(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, -\tfrac23)$ in three complex planes lies in $SU(3)$ (the angles add to $0$). It
acts on a Dirac weight $(h_1, h_2, h_3)$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(6)$ by $\exp(2\pi i(\tfrac13h_1 + \tfrac13h_2 - \tfrac23h_3))$, which is
$1$ exactly for $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12)$ with equal signs: one invariant spinor of each chirality
(@exr-spd-orbifold-weights). The same $\mathbb{Z}_3$ acting on gauge indices by $\gamma_3 = \operatorname{diag}(1, \omega,
\omega^2)$ projects a gauge theory to chiral bifundamental fermions @chatzistavrakidis2010orb [eqs. (5)-(9)].
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The phases by which a rotation acts on spinors can be listed for any orbifold group. The first exercise does this for several
$\mathbb{Z}_N$ actions on $T^6$.

::: {#exr-spd-orbifold-weights}
#### Invariant spinors of $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_N$

With Sage, for the rotations $2\pi v$ with $v = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, -\tfrac23)$, $(\tfrac14, \tfrac14, -\tfrac12)$, $(\tfrac16,
\tfrac13, -\tfrac12)$ and $(\tfrac13, 0, 0)$, choose the lift $\pm\exp(2\pi iv\cdot h)$ whose $N$th power is $1$, count the
Dirac weights $h$ on which it is $1$, and give their chiralities. Which actions are in $SU(3)$, and what do the counts say?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first three have $\sum v_i = 0$, lie in $SU(3)$ and keep one spinor of each chirality, $h = \pm(\tfrac12, \tfrac12,
\tfrac12)$. The rotation in a single plane is not in $SU(3)$; it needs the lift with the sign $-1$, whose phases $-e^{\pm
i\pi/3}$ are never $1$, so it keeps no spinor:

{{< sage exr-spd-orbifold-weights >}}
:::

The mode expansion on $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ follows from that on the circle by symmetrisation. The second exercise writes it out
and finds the masses.

::: {#exr-spd-s1z2-tower}
#### The tower on $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$

On the circle of radius $R$, expand $\psi_R(x, y) = \sum_n\chi_n(x)\cos(ny/R)$ and $\psi_L(x, y) = \sum_{n \geq 1}\xi_n(x)\sin(
ny/R)$ for the invariant fields of @exm-spd-s1z2. Show that $i\Gamma^4\partial_y$ pairs $\chi_n$ with $\xi_n$ into a Dirac spinor
of mass $n/R$ for $n \geq 1$ and leaves $\chi_0$ massless and right-handed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_y\cos(ny/R) = -\tfrac nR\sin(ny/R)$ and $\partial_y\sin(ny/R) = \tfrac nR\cos(ny/R)$, so the internal operator maps the
$n$th even mode to the $n$th odd mode and back, with factor $\tfrac nR$; together with the chirality-flipping $\Gamma^4 =
i\gamma_5$ this is a mass term coupling $\chi_n$ (right) and $\xi_n$ (left), mass $n/R$ (@exr-spd-branch-mass). The mode $n = 0$
exists only in the even sector, so $\chi_0$ is massless and right-handed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A lift of the orbifold group to spinors must be a homomorphism, and this can fail. The third exercise shows that the rotation
by $\pi$ of the plane does not lift to an action of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ on spinors, while the rotation by $\pi$ in two planes does.

::: {#exr-spd-lift-obstruction}
#### When the group does not lift

Show that the lifts of the rotation by $\pi$ in a plane are $\pm\gamma^1\gamma^2$, which square to $-1$, so $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_2$
(with $z \mapsto -z$) has no $\mathbb{Z}_2$ action on spinors, only a $\mathbb{Z}_4$ one. Show that the rotation by $\pi$ in two
planes lifts to $\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3\gamma^4$, which squares to $+1$, as used in @exm-spd-t4z2.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S(\pi) = \cos\tfrac\pi2 + \sin\tfrac\pi2\gamma^1\gamma^2 = \gamma^1\gamma^2$ (@exm-spd-spin-two) and $(\gamma^1\gamma^2)^2 = -1$:
applying it twice gives $-1$, the lift of the rotation by $2\pi$. For two planes, $(\gamma^1\gamma^2\gamma^3\gamma^4)^2 =
(\gamma^1\gamma^2)^2(\gamma^3\gamma^4)^2 = (-1)(-1) = 1$, since the two factors commute. On $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_2$ fermions must
therefore be combined with an extra phase $i$ (a gauge or fermion-number twist) to define the orbifold.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine group manifolds, coset spaces, Calabi-Yau spaces and orbifolds. They prepare the
twisted Dirac operators of the next part, where gauge fields on these spaces change the zero modes.

The real projective space $\mathbb{R}P^3 = S^3/\mathbb{Z}_2$ is both a group quotient and an orbifold without fixed points. The
first integrative exercise computes its Dirac spectrum from that of $SU(2)$ and compares with @trautman1995 [Prop. 9].

::: {#exr-spd-rp3-spectrum}
#### The spectrum of $\mathbb{R}P^3$

$\mathbb{R}P^3 = SU(2)/\{\pm1\}$, with $-1$ acting by left multiplication. In the left-invariant frame the spinor components
are functions on $SU(2)$, and $-1$ acts on $V_j \otimes V_j^*$ by $(-1)^{2j}$ (times $\pm1$ for the two spin structures). With
Sage, list the eigenvalues and multiplicities of $D$ on $\mathbb{R}P^3$ for the spin structure keeping integer $j$, and compare
with Trautman's spectrum $\{-\tfrac12 \pm (2l + 2)\}$ with multiplicity $2\binom{|\lambda| + 1/2}{|\lambda| - 3/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Integer $j$ gives the eigenvalues $2j + \tfrac32 = \tfrac32, \tfrac72, \dots$ and $-(2j + \tfrac12) = -\tfrac52, -\tfrac92, \dots$
($j \geq 1$), which are $-\tfrac12 + (2l + 2)$ and $-\tfrac12 - (2l + 2)$; the multiplicities agree with Trautman's formula, and
the spectrum is not symmetric. The other spin structure keeps half-integer $j$ and gives the mirror image:

{{< sage exr-spd-rp3-spectrum >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Euler characteristic of a coset $G/H$ with $\operatorname{rank}G = \operatorname{rank}H$ is the ratio of the orders of the
Weyl groups. The second integrative exercise computes it for the three nearly-Kähler cosets of @exm-spd-nearly-kahler.

::: {#exr-spd-nk-euler}
#### Euler characteristics of the nearly-Kähler cosets

With Sage, compute $|W_G|/|W_H|$ for $G_2/SU(3)$, $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ and $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$, and compare with the
Euler characteristics $2, 4, 6$ quoted by @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [Sec. 4]. Why is the Euler characteristic of $S^6 = G_2/SU(3)$
equal to $2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|W_{G_2}| = 12$, $|W_{SU(3)}| = 6$: $2$. $|W_{Sp(4)}| = 8$, $|W_{SU(2) \times U(1)}| = 2$: $4$. $|W_{SU(3)}| = 6$, $|W_{U(1)^2}| =
1$: $6$. These are the values of @chatzistavrakidis2009nk, where half of them counts the generations (@prp-generations-euler).
$G_2/SU(3)$ is the six-sphere, $\chi(S^6) = 1 + 1 = 2$:

{{< sage exr-spd-nk-euler >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Calabi-Yau spaces, orbifolds and tori differ in how many spinors their holonomy preserves. The third integrative exercise
compares the three on the example of $T^4$, $T^4/\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $K3$.

::: {#exr-spd-holonomy-comparison}
#### Holonomy and parallel spinors

For $T^4$, $T^4/\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $K3$, give the holonomy group, the number of parallel spinors of each chirality (for the
orbifold, the invariant constant spinors), and the index $\dim\ker D^+ - \dim\ker D^-$. Which of the three numbers is
topological, and what do the results say about blowing up the orbifold?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T^4$: trivial holonomy, $(2, 2)$ parallel spinors, index $0$. $T^4/\mathbb{Z}_2$: holonomy $\mathbb{Z}_2 \subset SU(2)$, $(2, 0)$
invariant spinors (@exm-spd-t4z2), index $2$ in the orbifold sense. $K3$: holonomy $SU(2)$, $(2, 0)$, index $\hat A = 2$. The
index is topological, and the agreement between the orbifold and $K3$ reflects that resolving the sixteen singularities
produces $K3$ @aspinwall1996 [Sec. 2.6]; the torus has the same topology as neither.
:::

## Twisted Dirac operators and index theorems {#sec-dirac-index}

A gauge field changes the Dirac operator by a potential term and its square by a coupling of the field strength to the
spin, which can cancel the positive curvature term of the Lichnerowicz formula and create zero modes. Their number,
counted with chirality, is the index of the operator, a topological invariant given by the Atiyah-Singer index theorem as
the integral of a characteristic form. This part couples the Dirac operator to gauge fields following @dolan2003 [Sec.
2] and @bilal2008 [Sec. 3.7, 10 and 11], computes the zero modes on the sphere with a monopole by hand, states the index
theorem with the $\hat A$ genus and the Chern character, and evaluates it on spheres, $K3$ and Calabi-Yau threefolds,
where it counts generations. The index is the Fredholm index of @def-fredholm-operator, and its invariance under
deformations is @thm-index-stability; the gauge potentials are those of @def-gauge-potential, anti-Hermitian as in
@sec-conventions-lie.

### Twisted Dirac operators

A spinor that also carries a charge or a gauge index feels the gauge field through its covariant derivative. On the sphere
with a magnetic monopole the spectrum of the resulting operator can be computed exactly; the figure shows it as a function
of the monopole charge.

![The eigenvalues $k(k + |M|)$ of $D_A^2$ on the unit sphere with a monopole of charge $M$ (@thm-monopole-index), for $k =
0, \dots, 4$. The level $k = 0$ consists of the $|M|$ zero modes; at $M = 0$ it is absent and the spectrum is that of the
untwisted sphere, $(j + \tfrac12)^2$ with lowest value $1$. Generated by `figures/sd-monopole-spectrum.sage`.](figures/sd-monopole-spectrum.svg){#fig-sd-monopole-spectrum width=65%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-twisted-dirac-operator}
#### Twisted Dirac operator

Let $E \to M$ be a Hermitian vector bundle with a unitary connection, given locally by an anti-Hermitian matrix-valued
potential $A = A_\mu dx^\mu$ (@def-gauge-potential) with field strength $F = dA + A \wedge A$. The **twisted Dirac
operator** on sections of $S \otimes E$ is
$$
D_A = i\gamma^a\big(\nabla_{e_a} \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes A(e_a)\big) ,
$$ {#eq-spd-twisted-dirac}
with $\nabla$ the spin connection. It is formally self-adjoint, anticommutes with $\gamma_* \otimes 1$ in even dimension, and
satisfies $D_A^2 = \nabla^*\nabla + \tfrac14R - \tfrac12F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b$ (@exm-spd-lichnerowicz-twisted) @dolan2003
[eqs. (2), (5)], @bilal2008 [eq. (11.14)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere a $U(1)$ bundle is a monopole, described by two potentials related by a gauge transformation on the overlap.
The first example writes them down for any charge, generalising the Hopf connection of @def-hopf-connection.

::: {#exm-spd-monopole-potential}
#### The monopole of charge $M$

On the unit sphere let $A = ia$ with $a_N = \tfrac M2(1 - \cos\theta)\,d\varphi$ on the northern patch and $a_S =
-\tfrac M2(1 + \cos\theta)\,d\varphi$ on the southern one; each is regular on its patch, and $a_N - a_S = M\,d\varphi$, the
gauge transformation $e^{iM\varphi}$, single-valued iff $M \in \mathbb{Z}$. The field strength is $F = i\,da = i\tfrac M2
\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, so $F_{12} = \tfrac{iM}{2}$ in the frame of @exm-spd-dirac-sphere, and the Chern number
(@def-chern-number) is $c_1 = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\int da = M$. The Hopf connection of @prp-hopf-chern has $M = -1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On $S^4$ the analogue of the monopole is a homogeneous instanton of $SU(2)$. The second example records it, as given by
@dolan2003 [eqs. (45)-(47)].

::: {#exm-spd-instanton}
#### The instanton on $S^4$

On the unit $S^4 = SO(5)/SO(4)$ with orthonormal coframe $e^1, \dots, e^4$, the $SU(2)$ field strength $F^i = e^i \wedge
e^4 + \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}e^j \wedge e^k$ is self-dual and has the $SO(5)$ symmetry of the sphere; it is the
spin connection of one factor of $\mathrm{Spin}(4) = SU(2) \times SU(2)$ used as a gauge field, and its instanton number is
$1$. For fermions in the spin-$J$ representation the index is $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$, equal to $1$ for $J = \tfrac12$
@dolan2003 [eqs. (45)-(47)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A flat connection has no field strength but can still change the spectrum through its holonomy. The third example identifies
the twisted boundary conditions of the torus as such connections.

::: {#exm-spd-flat-twist}
#### Flat connections

On the circle, the constant potential $A = i\tfrac\alpha R\,dy$ has $F = 0$ and holonomy $e^{-2\pi i\alpha}$; the twisted
Dirac operator on periodic spinors is the Dirac operator with the twisted boundary condition of @def-scherk-schwarz-twist
(@exm-spd-twist-gauge). The term $\tfrac12F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b$ vanishes, so the Lichnerowicz formula is unchanged, but
$\nabla^*\nabla$ now has no zero modes for $\alpha \notin \mathbb{Z}$: flat connections can only remove zero modes, never
create them on a manifold with $R \geq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The two potentials of the monopole must give the same field strength and an integral Chern number. The first exercise checks
both with Sage.

::: {#exr-spd-monopole-flux}
#### The monopole flux

With Sage, compute $da_N$ and $da_S$ for the potentials of @exm-spd-monopole-potential, check that they agree, that $a_N$ is
regular at $\theta = 0$ (its $\varphi$ component vanishes there like $\theta^2$) and $a_S$ at $\theta = \pi$, and compute
$\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_{S^2}da$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both give $\tfrac M2\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$, the components vanish quadratically at the respective poles, and the
flux is $M$:

{{< sage exr-spd-monopole-flux >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spectrum of the twisted operator must not depend on the gauge. The second exercise proves gauge covariance, which also
shows that the two patches of the monopole define one operator.

::: {#exr-spd-gauge-covariance}
#### Gauge covariance

Let $g(x)$ be a unitary matrix-valued function and $A' = gAg^{-1} - dg\,g^{-1}$, $\psi' = g\psi$. Show that $D_{A'}\psi' =
gD_A\psi$, so that $D_{A'} = gD_Ag^{-1}$ has the same spectrum. Apply it to $g = e^{iM\varphi}$ on the overlap of the two
patches of the monopole.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\nabla + A')(g\psi) = (dg)\psi + g\nabla\psi + gA\psi - (dg)\psi = g(\nabla + A)\psi$, and $\gamma^a$ commutes with $g$ (they
act on different indices). For the monopole, $A_N - A_S = i(a_N - a_S) = iM\,d\varphi$, which is $-dg\,g^{-1}$ for $g = e^{-iM\varphi}$; so $A_N$ is the
gauge transform of $A_S$ by $g$, the spinor fields on the two patches are related by $\psi_N = e^{-iM\varphi}\psi_S$ on the overlap,
and the two local operators are conjugate there. The transformation is single-valued exactly when $M$ is an integer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The instanton field strength of @exm-spd-instanton is self-dual, the property that makes it a minimum of the Yang-Mills action.
The third exercise checks self-duality and the index formula on a few representations.

::: {#exr-spd-instanton-check}
#### Self-duality and the instanton index

With Sage, represent the two-forms $F^i = e^i \wedge e^4 + \tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}e^j \wedge e^k$ by antisymmetric $4 \times 4$
matrices in an orthonormal frame, apply the Hodge star ($(\star F)_{ab} = \tfrac12\epsilon_{abcd}F_{cd}$) and check $\star F^i =
F^i$. Then tabulate $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$ for $J = \tfrac12, \dots, 3$ and compare with the zero-mode numbers $\tfrac16(2I +
1)(2I + 2)(2I + 3)$, $I = J - \tfrac12$, of @dolan2003 [eq. (44)].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The three forms are self-dual, and the index and the zero-mode numbers agree for every $J$ ($1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 56$):

{{< sage exr-spd-instanton-check >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

### The index on the sphere

On the sphere with a monopole the zero modes can be found by solving a first-order equation in one variable. The figure shows
the zero modes for $M = 4$: four functions peaked at different latitudes, which form one multiplet of the rotation group.

![The densities $|\psi_k|^2 \propto \sin^{2k}\tfrac\theta2\cos^{2(M - 1 - k)}\tfrac\theta2$ of the $M = 4$ zero modes on the
unit sphere, normalised, for $k = 0, \dots, 3$. They have $U(1)$ charges $m = -\tfrac12 - k$ and span the spin $\tfrac32$
representation of $SU(2)$; the mode $k$ is concentrated at $\theta = 2\arctan\sqrt{k/(M - 1 - k)}$. Generated by
`figures/sd-monopole-zero-modes.sage`.](figures/sd-monopole-zero-modes.svg){#fig-sd-monopole-zero-modes width=65%}

The theorem below is the central computation of this part: it finds all zero modes on the sphere with a monopole and their
chirality, and so evaluates the index directly. The proof is a separation of variables in the coordinates of
@exm-spd-dirac-sphere, and @dolan2003 [eqs. (24)-(32)] obtains the same result from Casimir operators.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-monopole-index}
#### Zero modes and index of the monopole

On the unit sphere with the monopole of charge $M \neq 0$ of @exm-spd-monopole-potential, the twisted Dirac operator has
exactly $|M|$ linearly independent zero modes, all of chirality $\operatorname{sign}(M)$ for $\gamma_* = -\sigma_3$; they form
the irreducible representation of spin $\tfrac{|M| - 1}{2}$ of $SU(2)$. Hence
$$
\operatorname{ind}D_A^+ = \dim\ker D_A^+ - \dim\ker D_A^- = M = c_1 .
$$ {#eq-spd-monopole-index}
The non-zero eigenvalues of $D_A^2$ are $k(k + |M|)$, $k \geq 1$, with multiplicity $2(|M| + 2k)$ @dolan2003 [eqs. (28)-(32)],
@bilal2008 [App. 14].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The zero-mode equation separates in $\theta$ and $\varphi$. The first example solves it for the component that carries the
zero modes when $M > 0$.

::: {#exm-spd-zero-mode-solution}
#### Solving the zero-mode equation

With @eq-spd-dirac-sphere and $\nabla_\varphi \to \nabla_\varphi + ia_N$, the lower component $v = e^{im\varphi}g(\theta)$ of a zero
mode satisfies $g' + \tfrac12\cot\theta\,g + \frac{m + a_\varphi}{\sin\theta}g = 0$, with $a_\varphi = \tfrac M2(1 - \cos\theta)$,
whose solution is $g = \sin^{-m - 1/2}\tfrac\theta2\,\cos^{m + M - 1/2}\tfrac\theta2$. Frame components are antiperiodic, so $m
\in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac12$; regularity at the poles requires $-m - \tfrac12 \geq 0$ and $m + M - \tfrac12 \geq 0$, which allows
$m = -\tfrac12, \dots, -M + \tfrac12$: $M$ solutions for $M > 0$ and none for $M \leq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The zero modes are polynomials in a complex coordinate, as for the Dolbeault operator of @exm-spd-dolbeault-cp1. The second
example rewrites them in the stereographic coordinate.

::: {#exm-spd-zero-modes-polynomial}
#### Zero modes as polynomials

With $m = -\tfrac12 - k$, $k = 0, \dots, M - 1$, the solution is $v_k = e^{-i\varphi/2}\cos^{M - 1}\tfrac\theta2\,\big(\tan
\tfrac\theta2\,e^{-i\varphi}\big)^k = e^{-i\varphi/2}\cos^{M - 1}\tfrac\theta2\,\bar w^k$ with the stereographic coordinate $w =
\tan\tfrac\theta2\,e^{i\varphi}$: a common factor times the polynomials of degree at most $M - 1$ in $\bar w$, the sections of a
line bundle of degree $M - 1$. Their densities are drawn in @fig-sd-monopole-zero-modes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The same counting on the flat plane gives the index only after "marginally normalisable" modes are included. The third
example compares with the computation of @bilal2008 [App. 14], which the sphere makes clean.

::: {#exm-spd-plane-versus-sphere}
#### The plane and the sphere

On $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the field of @bilal2008 [eq. (A.1)], of flux $-2\pi m$, the zero modes of one chirality are $g(\bar z)
(1 + z\bar z)^{-m/2}$ with $g$ holomorphic in $\bar z$; they are square integrable for $\deg g \leq m - 2$ and only marginally
so for $\deg g = m - 1$, and the index $m$ counts both @bilal2008 [eqs. (A.5)-(A.8)]. On the sphere the area element
$\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$ makes all $|M|$ modes genuinely normalisable: compactification removes the subtlety.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Zero modes on the sphere are the lowest Landau level of a charged particle in the monopole field. The fourth example draws the
connection made by @dolan2003 [Sec. 1].

::: {#exm-spd-landau}
#### The lowest Landau level

$D_A^2 = \nabla^*\nabla + \tfrac12 + \tfrac M2\sigma_3$ (@exr-spd-lichnerowicz-check, with $\sigma_3 = -\gamma_*$) is the
Hamiltonian of a non-relativistic spin-$\tfrac12$ particle on the sphere in the monopole field, with a Zeeman term. Its ground
states have energy $0$ and degeneracy $|M|$, the zero modes, and they are Haldane's lowest Landau level on the sphere; the
excited levels $k(k + |M|)$ are the higher Landau levels @dolan2003 [Sec. 1 and eqs. (29)-(31)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The regularity conditions of the first example decide the count. The first exercise checks them numerically for $M = 3$ by
integrating $|v|^2$ near the poles.

::: {#exr-spd-zero-mode-count}
#### Counting regular zero modes

With Sage, for $M = 3$ and the half-integers $m$ from $-\tfrac92$ to $\tfrac72$, form $g_m(\theta)$ of @exm-spd-zero-mode-solution
and decide whether $\int_0^\pi|g_m|^2\sin\theta\,d\theta$ converges and whether $g_m$ is bounded. Do the same for the upper
component, whose solution is $\sin^{m - 1/2}\tfrac\theta2\cos^{-m - M - 1/2}\tfrac\theta2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Exactly three values, $m = -\tfrac12, -\tfrac32, -\tfrac52$, give bounded (indeed smooth) lower components; no value gives an
admissible upper component. The index is $3 - 0 = 3 = M$:

{{< sage exr-spd-zero-mode-count >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The excited levels follow from the Casimir formula of @thm-parthasarathy with the gauge field. The second exercise derives
them as in @dolan2003 [eqs. (27)-(31)].

::: {#exr-spd-monopole-casimirs}
#### The spectrum from Casimirs

On the two components the $U(1)$ charge is $\tfrac{M \pm 1}{2}$, and the Laplacian is $\nabla^*\nabla = j(j + 1) - (\tfrac{M \pm
1}{2})^2$ on $V_j$. Using $D_A^2 = \nabla^*\nabla + \tfrac12 \pm \tfrac M2$, show that both give $E_j = \tfrac14((2j + 1)^2 -
M^2)$, and with $j = \tfrac{|M| - 1}{2} + k$ that $E = k(k + |M|)$. With Sage, list the multiplicities of the first five levels for
$M = 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$j(j + 1) - \tfrac14(M \pm 1)^2 + \tfrac12 \pm \tfrac M2 = j^2 + j + \tfrac14 - \tfrac{M^2}{4} = \tfrac14((2j + 1)^2 - M^2)$.
For $M = 3$ the component of charge $1$ starts at $j = 1$ and that of charge $2$ at $j = 2$, so the level $k = 0$ has
multiplicity $3$ and the level $k \geq 1$ has $2(3 + 2k)$:

{{< sage exr-spd-monopole-casimirs >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sign of the index depends on conventions, while its absolute value does not. The third exercise traces the sign through the
choices made in this chapter and compares with @dolan2003.

::: {#exr-spd-index-sign}
#### The sign of the index

Show that reversing the orientation of the sphere (exchanging $e_1$ and $e_2$) changes $\gamma_*$ to $-\gamma_*$ and the sign of
$c_1$, so @eq-spd-monopole-index is unchanged. @dolan2003 [eq. (32)] writes $\nu = -M$ with $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 =
\sigma_2$ and chirality $\sigma_3$: explain the difference. What happens under $M \mapsto -M$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Exchanging $e_1$ and $e_2$ multiplies $\gamma^1\gamma^2$ by $-1$, hence $\gamma_*$, and reverses the orientation used to integrate
$da$, hence $c_1$: both sides change sign together if one keeps the field fixed, and the formula holds in every orientation.
@dolan2003 counts chirality with $\sigma_3 = -\gamma_*$, which reverses the sign of the index: $\nu = -M$ in his convention is
$+M$ in ours. Under $M \mapsto -M$ the zero modes move to the other component (@exm-spd-zero-mode-solution) and the index
changes sign: the index is odd in the field, as $c_1$ is.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Index theorems

The index on the sphere is the integral of the field strength, a characteristic class of the bundle. In higher dimensions the
curvature of the manifold contributes as well, through the $\hat A$ genus, whose generating function is drawn in the figure.

![The generating function $\frac{x/2}{\sinh(x/2)}$ of the $\hat A$ genus (black) and its Taylor polynomials $1 - \tfrac{x^2}{24}$
(blue) and $1 - \tfrac{x^2}{24} + \tfrac{7x^4}{5760}$ (red). Only even powers occur, so $\hat A$ contributes in dimensions divisible
by four. Generated by `figures/sd-ahat-series.sage`.](figures/sd-ahat-series.svg){#fig-sd-ahat-series width=62%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-a-hat-genus}
#### $\hat A$ genus

For a closed oriented manifold $M$ whose Pontryagin classes are written with formal roots, $\sum_jp_jt^j = \prod_j(1 + x_j^2t)$,
the **$\hat A$ genus** is the characteristic class
$$
\hat A(M) = \prod_j\frac{x_j/2}{\sinh(x_j/2)} = 1 - \frac{p_1}{24} + \frac{7p_1^2 - 4p_2}{5760} - \dots ,
$$ {#eq-spd-ahat}
represented by curvature forms ($\hat A = 1 + \tfrac{1}{(4\pi)^2}\tfrac1{12}\operatorname{tr}R^2 + \dots$); the number $\hat A[M]
= \int_M\hat A(M)$ vanishes unless $\dim M$ is divisible by $4$ @bilal2008 [eqs. (11.15)-(11.16)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Spheres have trivial Pontryagin classes in the degrees that matter. The first example evaluates the genus on them and compares with the absence of zero modes.

::: {#exm-spd-ahat-spheres}
#### Spheres

$S^{4k}$ bounds the ball, so all its Pontryagin numbers vanish and $\hat A[S^{4k}] = 0$; this agrees with the absence of harmonic
spinors on spheres (@thm-lichnerowicz-vanishing), since the index of the untwisted Dirac operator is $\hat A[M]$
(@thm-atiyah-singer). On $S^2$ and $S^6$ the genus vanishes for dimensional reasons.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On a four-manifold the genus is $-p_1/24$, and $p_1$ is three times the signature. The second example evaluates it on $K3$ and on
$CP^2$, where the answer is not an integer.

::: {#exm-spd-ahat-four}
#### $K3$ and $CP^2$

On a four-manifold $\hat A[M] = -\tfrac1{24}\int p_1 = -\tfrac18\tau(M)$ by the signature theorem $\int p_1 = 3\tau$. For $K3$,
$\tau = -16$ @aspinwall1996 [eq. (20)] and $\hat A = 2$, the two parallel spinors of @prp-calabi-yau-spinors. For $CP^2$, $\tau = 1$
and $\hat A = -\tfrac18$, not an integer: the index theorem would be violated, which is another proof that $CP^2$ is not spin
(@exm-spd-cp2-not-spin).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Flat tori have vanishing curvature forms, hence vanishing genus. The third example compares with the zero modes found directly in the part on tori.

::: {#exm-spd-ahat-torus}
#### Tori

On $T^4$ the curvature vanishes, so $\hat A[T^4] = 0$; the periodic structure has two zero modes of each chirality and index $0$
(@exm-spd-torus-six for the analogous count on $T^6$). The genus does not see the spin structure, but the index does not depend on
it either: with the antiperiodic structures there are no zero modes, and the index is $0 - 0 = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The coefficients in @eq-spd-ahat come from multiplying two power series. The first exercise does the multiplication with Sage for two formal roots.

::: {#exr-spd-ahat-expansion}
#### Expanding the genus

With Sage, expand $\frac{x/2}{\sinh(x/2)}$ to order $x^6$, form the product over two roots $x_1, x_2$, and write its parts of degree
$2$ and $4$ in terms of $p_1 = x_1^2 + x_2^2$ and $p_2 = x_1^2x_2^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The series is $1 - \tfrac{x^2}{24} + \tfrac{7x^4}{5760} - \tfrac{31x^6}{967680} + \dots$, and the product gives $-\tfrac{p_1}{24}$ and
$\tfrac{7p_1^2 - 4p_2}{5760}$:

{{< sage exr-spd-ahat-expansion >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The genus is multiplicative, $\hat A(M \times N) = \hat A(M)\hat A(N)$, because the formal roots of a product are the union of
the roots. The second exercise uses this to find manifolds with $\hat A \neq 0$ in dimension eight.

::: {#exr-spd-ahat-products}
#### Products

Show that $\hat A[M \times N] = \hat A[M]\hat A[N]$. Compute $\hat A[K3 \times K3]$ and $\hat A[K3 \times T^4]$, and explain why
$\hat A[S^2 \times \Sigma] = 0$ for every surface $\Sigma$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$TM \oplus TN$ has the roots of both, so the product formula @eq-spd-ahat factorises, and the top-degree part of a product of
forms on $M \times N$ is the product of the top-degree parts. $\hat A[K3 \times K3] = 4$, $\hat A[K3 \times T^4] = 0$. For $S^2
\times \Sigma$ the dimension is $4$ but each factor has dimension $2$, where $\hat A$ has no top-degree part: the product is $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The failure of integrality on $CP^2$ is repaired by the spin-c structure. The third exercise computes the spin-c version of the
genus and recovers @fig-sd-cp2-index.

::: {#exr-spd-spinc-index}
#### The spin-c index of $CP^2$

For a spin-c structure with determinant line $L$, the index is $\int\hat A(M)e^{c_1(L)/2}$. With Sage, take $p_1(CP^2) = 3x^2$,
$c_1(L) = (2Q + 3)x$ and $\int x^2 = 1$, and show that the index is $\tfrac12(Q + 1)(Q + 2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat A = 1 - \tfrac{x^2}{8}$ and $e^{(2Q + 3)x/2}$ has $x^2$ coefficient $\tfrac18(2Q + 3)^2$, so the index is $\tfrac18((2Q +
3)^2 - 1) = \tfrac12(Q + 1)(Q + 2)$, the holomorphic Euler characteristic of @exr-spd-cp2-riemann-roch:

{{< sage exr-spd-spinc-index >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The gauge field enters the index through the Chern character of the bundle. The definition fixes its normalisation in the
conventions of the book, in which the monopole of charge $M$ has first Chern number $M$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-chern-character}
#### Chern character

For a Hermitian vector bundle $E$ with anti-Hermitian curvature $F$, the **Chern character** is the sum of closed forms
$$
\operatorname{ch}(E) = \operatorname{tr}\exp\Big(-\frac{iF}{2\pi}\Big) = \operatorname{rank}E - \frac{i}{2\pi}\operatorname{tr}F
+ \frac12\Big(\frac{-i}{2\pi}\Big)^2\operatorname{tr}(F \wedge F) + \dots ,
$$ {#eq-spd-chern-character}
whose cohomology class does not depend on the connection. For a line bundle with $F = i\,da$, $\operatorname{ch}_1 =
\tfrac{1}{2\pi}da$ and $\int\operatorname{ch}_1 = c_1$ (@def-chern-number); @bilal2008 [eq. (10.53)] writes the same with the
opposite sign convention for the potential.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a line bundle the Chern character is the exponential of the first Chern form. The first example evaluates it for the
monopole.

::: {#exm-spd-ch-monopole}
#### The monopole

For the monopole of charge $M$, $\operatorname{ch} = e^{da/2\pi} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2\pi}da$ on the surface, and $\int_{S^2}
\operatorname{ch}_1 = M$. For the bundle $\mathcal{O}(M)^{\oplus r}$, $\operatorname{ch} = r + \tfrac{r}{2\pi}da$ and the integral is
$rM$: the index of the twisted operator is additive over direct sums.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For an $SU(2)$ bundle the trace of $F$ vanishes and the first non-trivial term is quadratic. The second example evaluates it for
the instanton of @exm-spd-instanton.

::: {#exm-spd-ch-instanton}
#### The instanton

For $SU(2)$, $\operatorname{ch}_1 = 0$ and $\int\operatorname{ch}_2 = -\tfrac{1}{8\pi^2}\int\operatorname{tr}(F \wedge F)$ is the
instanton number $k$ (up to orientation), which is $1$ for the homogeneous instanton in the fundamental representation. In the
spin-$J$ representation the trace is multiplied by the Dynkin index ratio $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$, the number of
@exm-spd-instanton @dolan2003 [eq. (46)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A flat bundle has a Chern character equal to its rank. The third example contrasts this with the non-trivial holonomy of
@exm-spd-flat-twist.

::: {#exm-spd-ch-flat}
#### Flat bundles

If $F = 0$, $\operatorname{ch}(E) = \operatorname{rank}E$, whatever the holonomy: the twisted boundary conditions of the torus do
not change any index. This is consistent with @exr-spd-spectral-flow, where the spectrum changes with the twist but no
eigenvalue crosses zero for a fixed operator: the index $0$ of the circle is preserved along the whole family.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Chern character turns sums and products of bundles into sums and products of forms. The first exercise proves the two rules
for line bundles.

::: {#exr-spd-ch-rules}
#### Sums and products

Show that $\operatorname{ch}(E \oplus E') = \operatorname{ch}E + \operatorname{ch}E'$ and $\operatorname{ch}(E \otimes E') =
\operatorname{ch}E \wedge \operatorname{ch}E'$, using block-diagonal curvature for the sum and $F \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes F'$ for the
product. Deduce $c_1(L \otimes L') = c_1(L) + c_1(L')$ for line bundles.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the sum, $\exp$ of a block-diagonal matrix is block diagonal and the trace adds. For the product, $F \otimes 1$ and $1 \otimes
F'$ commute (they are even forms acting on different factors), so $\exp(-\tfrac{i}{2\pi}(F \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes F')) =
\exp(-\tfrac{i}{2\pi}F) \otimes \exp(-\tfrac{i}{2\pi}F')$, and the trace of a tensor product is the product of traces. For line
bundles the degree-two parts give $c_1(L \otimes L') = c_1(L) + c_1(L')$: the monopole charges add.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

and the resulting index, which is checked against the zero modes in @exr-spd-s2s2-index.

On $S^2 \times S^2$ with charges $M_1$, $M_2$ on the factors, $\operatorname{ch} = e^{M_1\omega_1 + M_2\omega_2}$ with $\int\omega_1
\wedge \omega_2 = 1$ and $\omega_i^2 = 0$. Compute $\int\operatorname{ch}_2$ with Sage and show that it is $M_1M_2$.

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ch}_2 = \tfrac12(M_1\omega_1 + M_2\omega_2)^2 = M_1M_2\,\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2$, integral $M_1M_2$:

{{< sage exr-spd-ch-s2s2 >}}

The quadratic term of the Chern character for $SU(2)$ involves the trace of the square of a generator in each representation.
The third exercise computes the factor $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$ of @exm-spd-ch-instanton from these traces.

::: {#exr-spd-dynkin-ratio}
#### The representation factor

With Sage, compute $\operatorname{tr}(J_3^2)$ in the spin-$J$ representation for $J = \tfrac12, \dots, 3$, divide by its value
$\tfrac12$ in the fundamental, and compare with $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$.

$\operatorname{tr}J_3^2 = \sum_{m = -J}^Jm^2 = \tfrac13J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$; divided by $\tfrac12$ it is $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$:

{{< sage exr-spd-dynkin-ratio >}}

The index theorem states that the analytic index of the twisted Dirac operator, the difference of the numbers of zero modes,
is the integral of the product of the two characteristic forms just defined. We state it in the form used by @bilal2008, with
the sign fixed by the computation on the sphere.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-atiyah-singer}
#### Atiyah-Singer index theorem for Dirac operators

Let $M$ be a closed oriented Riemannian spin manifold of even dimension $2r$ and $E \to M$ a Hermitian bundle with a unitary
connection. The twisted Dirac operator $D_E^+ : \Gamma(S^+ \otimes E) \to \Gamma(S^- \otimes E)$ is Fredholm
(@def-fredholm-operator), its index is invariant under deformations of the metric and the connection (@thm-index-stability),
and
$$
\operatorname{ind}D_E^+ = \dim\ker D_E^+ - \dim\ker D_E^- = \int_M\big[\hat A(M)\operatorname{ch}(E)\big]_{2r} ,
$$ {#eq-spd-atiyah-singer}
with the orientation for which @eq-spd-monopole-index holds. In two dimensions $\operatorname{ind} = \int\operatorname{ch}_1(E) =
c_1(E)$; in four, $\operatorname{ind} = \operatorname{rank}(E)\,\hat A[M] + \int\operatorname{ch}_2(E)$ @bilal2008 [eqs. (3.46)-(3.47),
(11.15), (11.25)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions the theorem reduces to the integral of the field strength. The first example checks it against the explicit
zero modes of the previous section.

::: {#exm-spd-as-sphere}
#### The sphere

On $S^2$, $\hat A = 1$ (no 4-form), so $\operatorname{ind}D_A^+ = \int\operatorname{ch}_1 = M$ for the monopole, as
@thm-monopole-index found by solving the equations. The theorem also gives the answer on every surface: on a surface of genus $g$
with a line bundle of degree $M$ the index is $M$, independently of $g$ and of the metric.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In four dimensions both the manifold and the bundle contribute. The second example evaluates the two contributions on $S^4$ with
the instanton and on $K3$ without gauge field.

::: {#exm-spd-as-four}
#### $S^4$ and $K3$

On $S^4$, $\hat A[S^4] = 0$ and the index is $\int\operatorname{ch}_2$: $\tfrac23J(J + 1)(2J + 1)$ for the instanton in the spin-$J$
representation, matching the zero modes counted by @dolan2003 [eq. (44)] (@exr-spd-instanton-check). On $K3$ with $E$ trivial of rank
one, the index is $\hat A[K3] = 2$, the parallel spinors. With a bundle of rank $r$ and second Chern number $k$ on $K3$, the index
is $2r - k$ up to orientation conventions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem is a statement about a family of operators, and it explains why zero modes can appear and disappear in pairs. The
third example illustrates this with the flat twist of the torus.

::: {#exm-spd-as-stability}
#### Jumping kernels, constant index

On $T^2$ with the flat twist $\alpha$ the kernel has dimension $2$ for $\alpha = 0$ (one zero mode of each chirality) and $0$
otherwise, but the index is $1 - 1 = 0$ and $0 - 0 = 0$: zero modes disappear in pairs of opposite chirality, as the stability of
the index requires (@thm-index-stability). On the sphere with a monopole, by contrast, no deformation can remove the $|M|$ zero
modes, which all have the same chirality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The product of two spheres with monopoles has zero modes that are products of zero modes of the factors. The first exercise counts
them and checks the theorem.

::: {#exr-spd-s2s2-index}
#### $S^2 \times S^2$

On $S^2 \times S^2$ with monopoles $M_1, M_2 > 0$, the Dirac operator squares to $D_1^2 + D_2^2$ (product gamma matrices as in
@eq-spd-product-gammas), so zero modes are products of zero modes of the two factors. Count them and their chirality, compare with
$\int\hat A\operatorname{ch} = M_1M_2$ (@exr-spd-ch-s2s2), and repeat for $M_1 > 0 > M_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\ker D^2 = \ker D_1^2 \otimes \ker D_2^2$ has dimension $M_1M_2$, and the chirality of a product is the product of the
chiralities, $+1 \cdot +1 = +1$: index $M_1M_2$. For $M_1 > 0 > M_2$ the zero modes have chirality $+1 \cdot -1 = -1$, there are
$M_1|M_2|$ of them, and the index is $-M_1|M_2| = M_1M_2$. Since $\hat A(S^2 \times S^2) = 1$ (both factors have $p_1 = 0$), this is
$\int\operatorname{ch}_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The heat-kernel proof of the theorem writes the index as a supertrace that does not depend on time. The second exercise checks this
on $S^2$ with a monopole, using the spectrum of @thm-monopole-index.

::: {#exr-spd-supertrace}
#### The index as a supertrace

Show that $\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma_*e^{-tD_A^2}) = \dim\ker D_A^+ - \dim\ker D_A^-$ for every $t > 0$, because non-zero eigenvalues of
$D_A^2$ have equal multiplicities on the two chiralities (@exr-spd-spectrum-symmetric). With Sage, evaluate the supertrace on $S^2$
with $M = 3$ as a sum over the spectrum for several $t$, assigning half of the multiplicity $2(|M| + 2k)$ to each chirality.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The contributions of each level $k \geq 1$ cancel between the chiralities, and the supertrace equals $3$ for every $t$, while the
ordinary trace grows like $\tfrac{2}{t}$:

{{< sage exr-spd-supertrace >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The index density is a local formula even though the index is global. The third exercise evaluates it in two dimensions as a
function and integrates it, as in @bilal2008 [eq. (3.46)] for $r = 1$.

::: {#exr-spd-index-density}
#### The index density in two dimensions

On a surface, the index density is $\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\tfrac{-i}{1}F_{12}$ times the area form for $F = F_{12}\,e^1 \wedge e^2$
(@eq-spd-chern-character). For the monopole on the unit sphere and for the field of @bilal2008 [eq. (A.1)] on the plane, compute the
density and its integral.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On the sphere $F_{12} = \tfrac{iM}{2}$, the density is $\tfrac{M}{4\pi}$, constant, and the integral over the area $4\pi$ is $M$. On the
plane Bilal's real field $F_{12} = -\tfrac{2m}{(1 + r^2)^2}$ has $\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\int F_{12}\,d^2x = -m$ @bilal2008 [eq. (A.2)], and with
his opposite sign convention for the potential the index is $m$: the density is concentrated near the origin, but its integral is
the same integer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Generations from the index

On a six-dimensional Calabi-Yau space with the gauge field equal to the spin connection, the index of the Dirac operator twisted
by the tangent bundle is half the Euler characteristic. The proposition states the computation, which counts the net number of
chiral multiplets in such backgrounds, and records the same count on the nearly-Kähler cosets of @exm-spd-nearly-kahler.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-generations-euler}
#### Half the Euler number

Let $K$ be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $3$ with $c_1(K) = 0$, and let $T = T^{1, 0}K$ carry the Levi-Civita
(holonomy) connection. Then $\int_K\hat A(K)\operatorname{ch}(T) = \int_K\operatorname{ch}_3(T) = \tfrac12\int_Kc_3 = \tfrac12\chi(K)$,
so the Dirac operator twisted by $T$ has index $\pm\tfrac12\chi(K)$, and its zero modes come in $\tfrac12|\chi(K)|$ net multiplets of one
chirality; with the standard embedding these are the net generations of the heterotic string @braun2009 [Sec. 1]. The same rule, net number of families equal to half the Euler characteristic, holds for the
nearly-Kähler cosets with $\chi = 2, 4, 6$ @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [Sec. 4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The quintic is the simplest Calabi-Yau threefold. The first example evaluates the proposition on it with the Hodge numbers of
@fig-sd-hodge-diamonds.

::: {#exm-spd-generations-quintic}
#### The quintic

$\chi = 2(h^{1, 1} - h^{2, 1}) = -200$ @greene1997 [Sec. 2.11, p. 32], so the index is $\mp100$. In the Dolbeault picture of
@def-dolbeault-dirac the zero modes are $H^{0, q}(T)$, and $T \cong \Lambda^2T^*$ via the holomorphic volume form, so
$H^{0, 1}(T) \cong H^{2, 1}$ and $H^{0, 2}(T) \cong H^{2, 2} \cong H^{1, 1}$: $h^{1, 1} = 1$ zero modes of one chirality and $h^{2, 1} =
101$ of the other, $100$ net. A three-family model needs $|\chi| = 6$, which is why
Calabi-Yau spaces with small Euler characteristic were sought.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The nearly-Kähler cosets give small Euler characteristics. The second example lists the families they produce and compares with the explicit reductions.

::: {#exm-spd-generations-cosets}
#### The six-dimensional cosets

$G_2/SU(3)$, $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ and $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$ have $\chi = 2, 4, 6$ (@exr-spd-nk-euler), hence $1$, $2$ and
$3$ families, the values found by @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [Sec. 4.1-4.3] by an explicit reduction. On $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$ the
three families are the three chiral multiplets associated with its three pairs of roots.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Tori and products with tori have Euler characteristic zero. The third example states the consequence for the index and for the families.

::: {#exm-spd-generations-torus}
#### Tori give no net families

$\chi(T^6) = 0$ and $\chi(K3 \times T^2) = 24 \cdot 0 = 0$, so the twisted index vanishes: these spaces give as many multiplets of one
chirality as of the other, in agreement with the count of @exm-spd-torus-six. A non-zero Euler characteristic is necessary for a net
number of families from this mechanism.
:::

$\sum y_i^3 = e_1^3 - 3e_1e_2 + 3e_3$ by Newton's identity, and $\operatorname{ch}_3 = \tfrac16\sum y_i^3$:

The proposition uses the holonomy connection as the gauge field, and the index is then a property of the manifold alone. The third
exercise checks the formula $\chi = \int c_3$ on $CP^3$, a Kähler manifold that is not Calabi-Yau, and shows where the extra terms
enter.

::: {#exr-spd-cp3-twisted}
#### Beyond $c_1 = 0$

On $CP^3$, $c(T) = (1 + x)^4$, $p_1 = 4x^2$ and $\int x^3 = 1$. With Sage, compute $\chi = \int c_3$, $\int\operatorname{ch}_3(T)$ and
$\int[\hat A\operatorname{ch}(T)]_6$, and compare the last two with $\tfrac12\chi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $T \oplus \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{O}(1)^{\oplus4}$, $\operatorname{ch}(T) = 4e^x - 1$ and $\int\operatorname{ch}_3(T) = \tfrac46 = \tfrac23$;
with $\hat A = 1 - \tfrac{x^2}{6}$ the extra term $-\tfrac{x^2}{6}\operatorname{ch}_1 = -\tfrac{x^2}{6}\cdot4x$ contributes $-\tfrac23$, and
the twisted index is $0$, not $\tfrac12\chi(CP^3) = 2$: the rule of the proposition needs $c_1 = 0$:

{{< sage exr-spd-cp3-twisted >}}
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine twisted operators, the explicit index on the sphere and the general index theorem. They prepare
the last part, where the index decides whether chiral spinors can arise at all.

A constant magnetic field on a torus is the flat-space version of the monopole. The first integrative exercise computes the index and
the zero modes from the theorem and the Lichnerowicz formula.

::: {#exr-spd-torus-flux}
#### Flux on a torus

On $T^2$ of area $A$ with a $U(1)$ field of constant $F_{12} = \tfrac{2\pi iN}{A}$ ($N \in \mathbb{Z}$, the Chern number), show that $D_A^2 = \nabla^*\nabla + \tfrac{2\pi N}{A}\sigma_3$ (with $\gamma^1 = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2 = \sigma_2$), so that for $N > 0$
zero modes can exist only on the lower component; conclude from @thm-atiyah-singer that there are exactly $N$ of them.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R = 0$ and $-\tfrac12F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b = -F_{12}\gamma^1\gamma^2 = -\tfrac{2\pi iN}{A}\cdot i\sigma_3 = \tfrac{2\pi N}{A}\sigma_3$, as in
@exr-spd-lichnerowicz-check. On the upper component $D_A^2 \geq \tfrac{2\pi N}{A} > 0$, so all zero modes lie on the lower component,
of chirality $\gamma_* = -\sigma_3 = +1$. The index is $\int\operatorname{ch}_1 = N$,
so there are exactly $N$ zero modes: the lowest Landau level on the torus, with degeneracy equal to the flux.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spin-c structure of $CP^2$ and the twisted Dirac operator are the same mathematics. The second integrative exercise relates the
two descriptions of the single zero mode of the canonical structure.

::: {#exr-spd-cp2-two-views}
#### Two views of $CP^2$

Explain why the canonical spin-c Dirac operator of $CP^2$ (@exm-spd-dolbeault-cp2), the spin-c index of @exr-spd-spinc-index at $Q = 0$
and the zero-mode count of @dolan2003 [eq. (55)] at $Y = 0$ all give $1$, and identify the zero mode in each description.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the Dolbeault description it is the constant function in $\Omega^{0, 0}$, $h^{0, 0} = 1$. In the index computation $\int\hat
Ae^{3x/2} = \tfrac{9}{8} - \tfrac18 = 1$. In Dolan's description the spinor charge exactly cancels the background charge ($Y = 0$),
so the zero mode is the $SU(3)$ singlet, a constant section: $d(0, 0) = (0 + 2)(0 + 4)/8 = 1$. All three are the same constant
spinor of the canonical structure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The index theorem on $S^4$ and the representation theory of $SO(5)$ count the same zero modes. The third integrative exercise checks
the agreement and the chirality on the instanton.

::: {#exr-spd-s4-instanton-modes}
#### Zero modes of the instanton

Using @exr-spd-instanton-check, show that for $J = \tfrac12$ there is one zero mode, invariant under $SO(5)$, and that its chirality
is the one on which the gauge connection cancels the spin connection. Why are there no zero modes for $J = 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $J = \tfrac12$, $I = 0$ and $d(0, 0) = 1$: a single $SO(5)$-invariant zero mode, the "constant spinor" of @dolan2003 [after eq.
(47)], on the chirality whose $SU(2)$ factor of $\mathrm{Spin}(4)$ is the gauged one, where the gauge connection cancels the spin
connection exactly. For $J = 0$ the operator is the untwisted Dirac operator of $S^4$, which has no zero modes by
@thm-lichnerowicz-vanishing, and the index $\tfrac23\cdot0 = 0$ agrees.
:::
